# Overview



**MLatom** is an open-source Python package for atomistic simulations that unifies machine learning (ML) models with quantum chemical (QC) methods — including DFT, wavefunction-based approaches, and semi-empirical approximations — into a single, coherent workflow. Originally founded by Pavlo O. Dral on 10 September 2013 and currently at version **3.22.0**, MLatom is developed at Xiamen University and commercially supported by [Aitomistic](https://aitomistic.com). It is distributed under a modified MIT license that requests proper citation of the software and its constituent methods in scientific publications.

![MLatom Banner](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9433ac9a-bcc9-4dd4-9128-d834c85603b0)

What makes MLatom distinctive is its ability to serve as a **single entry point** for the full atomistic simulation pipeline: from molecular data management and ML model training, through geometry optimization and molecular dynamics, all the way to spectroscopic predictions and nonadiabatic dynamics on excited-state potential energy surfaces. You interact with it through three complementary usage modes — as a Python library, via declarative input files, or through a command-line interface — each described in detail on the [Usage Modes and Input Files](4-usage-modes-and-input-files) page.

Sources: [MLatom.py](mlatom/MLatom.py#L1-L55), [__init__.py](mlatom/__init__.py#L1-L17), [README.md](README.md#L1-L20)

## What You Can Do with MLatom

MLatom covers a remarkably broad scope of computational chemistry tasks. At the highest level, its capabilities fall into five major pillars:

| Pillar | Key Capabilities | Representative Classes/Functions |
|---|---|---|
| **Machine Learning Models** | Kernel Ridge Regression (KREG), ANI neural networks, PhysNet, MACE, DeePMD, GAP, transfer learning | [`krr`](mlatom/models.py#L17-L82), [`ani`](mlatom/__init__.py#L13), `mace`, `gap_model` |
| **AI-Enhanced QM Methods** | AIQM1, AIQM2, AIQM3, UAIQM, OmniP2x — hybrid ML + semi-empirical/DFT composites | [`aiqm1`](mlatom/aiqm1.py#L18-L60), `aiqm2`, `aiqm3` |
| **Atomistic Simulations** | Geometry optimization, IRC, frequency analysis, molecular dynamics (NVE/NVT), thermochemistry | [`optimize_geometry`](mlatom/simulations.py#L33), [`md`](mlatom/md.py#L27-L60), [`md_parallel`](mlatom/md_parallel.py#L20-L60), [`irc`](mlatom/simulations.py#L33) |
| **Excited-State Dynamics** | Fewest-switches surface hopping (FSSH), LZBL algorithm, nonadiabatic coupling calculations | [`surface_hopping_md`](mlatom/namd.py#L17-L60), [`gap_md`](mlatom/gap_md.py#L35-L50) |
| **Spectroscopy** | IR spectra, Raman spectra, UV/Vis via nuclear ensemble approach (ML-NEA), two-photon absorption | [`spectrum`](mlatom/spectra.py#L17-L45) |

Beyond these pillars, MLatom provides a sophisticated **active learning** framework ([`al`](mlatom/al.py#L15-L80)) that automatically selects which molecular configurations to compute with expensive reference methods, iteratively improving ML model accuracy with minimal quantum chemistry calculations. It also supports **delta-learning** — correcting low-level QM methods with ML — and **composite methods** such as CCSD(T)\*/CBS for high-accuracy single-point energies.

Sources: [__init__.py](mlatom/__init__.py#L1-L17), [namd.py](mlatom/namd.py#L17-L60), [md.py](mlatom/md.py#L17-L60), [spectra.py](mlatom/spectra.py#L17-L45), [al.py](mlatom/al.py#L15-L80)

## High-Level Architecture

MLatom's internal architecture follows a layered design that cleanly separates concerns between data representation, model computation, simulation orchestration, and external program integration. The diagram below illustrates how these layers connect:

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Usage Layer"
        CLI["CLI / Input Files"]
        API["Python API"]
    end

    subgraph "Task Dispatch"
        ARGS["args_class<br/>(Argument Parsing)"]
        TASKS["CLItasks<br/>(Task Router)"]
    end

    subgraph "Core Modules"
        DATA["data<br/>(Molecules, Databases)"]
        MODELS["models + model_cls<br/>(Model Hierarchy)"]
        SIM["simulations<br/>(Opt, Freq, MD, IRC)"]
        SPECTRA["spectra<br/>(IR, UV/Vis)"]
        NAMD["namd<br/>(Surface Hopping)"]
        AL["al<br/>(Active Learning)"]
    end

    subgraph "Model Backends"
        KRR["KRR (SciPy / Julia)"]
        NN["Neural Network Models<br/>(ANI, MACE, PhysNet)"]
        AIQM["AIQM Methods<br/>(AIQM1/2/3, UAIQM)"]
    end

    subgraph "External Interfaces"
        QM["QC Programs<br/>(Gaussian, ORCA, PySCF, xtb)"]
        UML["Universal ML Potentials<br/>(TorchANI, MACE, DeePMD)"]
        SIMTOOLS["Simulation Tools<br/>(ASE, geomeTRIC)"]
    end

    subgraph "Compiled Backends"
        FORT["MLatomF<br/>(Fortran KREG)"]
        JULIA["MLatom.jl<br/>(Julia KRR)"]
    end

    CLI --> ARGS --> TASKS
    API --> TASKS
    TASKS --> DATA
    TASKS --> MODELS
    TASKS --> SIM
    TASKS --> SPECTRA
    TASKS --> NAMD
    TASKS --> AL

    MODELS --> KRR
    MODELS --> NN
    MODELS --> AIQM
    SIM --> QM
    SIM --> SIMTOOLS
    MODELS --> UML
    KRR --> FORT
    KRR --> JULIA
```

The **Usage Layer** provides both a programmatic Python API and a CLI that internally routes through the `args_class` parser and the `CLItasks` dispatcher. The **Core Modules** contain the domain logic: `data` handles molecular representation, `models` and `model_cls` implement the full model hierarchy, `simulations` orchestrates geometry optimization and dynamics, and dedicated modules handle spectroscopy, nonadiabatic dynamics, and active learning. Below that, **Model Backends** implement specific ML algorithms, **External Interfaces** wrap third-party software, and **Compiled Backends** provide high-performance Fortran and Julia implementations for kernel ridge regression.

Sources: [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L1-L45), [args_class.py](mlatom/args_class.py#L1-L50), [__init__.py](mlatom/__init__.py#L1-L17)

## Project Structure at a Glance

The repository is organized around the main `mlatom/` Python package, with compiled backends, external interfaces, and add-on models each living in their own subdirectories:

```
mlatom/                          # Main Python package
├── __init__.py                  # Public API exports & version (3.22.0)
├── MLatom.py                    # Entry point: run() function
├── args_class.py                # CLI argument parsing (AttributeDict)
├── MLtasks.py                   # Task dispatch (CLItasks router)
│
├── data.py                      # atom, molecule, molecular_database, ml_database
├── model_cls.py                 # Base model class hierarchy
├── models.py                    # KRR, ANI, AIQM, method wrappers
├── simulations.py               # Geometry optimization, freq, IRC, thermochemistry
├── md.py / md_parallel.py       # Molecular dynamics (serial & parallel)
├── namd.py                      # Nonadiabatic molecular dynamics (FSSH, LZBL)
├── spectra.py                   # Spectrum generation & analysis
├── al.py / al_utils.py          # Active learning pipeline
├── header.py                    # Reference/citation management
│
├── interfaces/                  # External program wrappers
│   ├── gaussian_interface.py
│   ├── orca_interface.py
│   ├── pyscf_interface.py
│   ├── xtb_interface.py
│   ├── torchani_interface.py
│   ├── mace_interface.py
│   └── ... (20+ interfaces)
│
├── addons/                      # Specialized models
│   ├── aiqm3/                   # AIQM3 method
│   ├── omnip2x/                 # Multi-state potentials
│   └── uaiqm/                   # Universal updatable AI-QM methods
│
├── MLatomF_src/                 # Fortran backend for KREG
│   ├── MLatomF.f90              # Main Fortran program
│   ├── A_KRR.f90                # Kernel Ridge Regression
│   ├── molDescr.f90             # Molecular descriptors
│   └── ...
│
├── julia/                       # Julia backend for KRR
│   ├── KREG.jl / krr.jl
│   └── ...
│
└── fortran/                     # Additional Fortran utilities
```

Sources: [__init__.py](mlatom/__init__.py#L1-L17), [args_class.py](mlatom/args_class.py#L1-L50), [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L1-L45)

## Key Design Principles

Several architectural decisions shape how MLatom works in practice. Understanding these will help you navigate the codebase and use the package effectively.

**Three usage paradigms coexist.** Every capability in MLatom can be accessed through the Python API (for programmatic control and Jupyter workflows), through declarative input files (for reproducible batch jobs), or via the command line (for quick scripting). The `CLItasks` class in [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L17-L45) acts as a router that translates CLI arguments into the same internal function calls used by the Python API, ensuring consistent behavior across all modes.

**A unified model abstraction.** All computational methods — whether they are pure ML models (KRR, ANI), hybrid AI-QM methods (AIQM1/2/3), external QC programs (Gaussian, ORCA), or even composite schemes like CCSD(T)\*/CBS — implement a common `predict()` interface defined in the base [`model`](mlatom/model_cls.py#L21-L65) class. This means you can swap a DFT calculation for a neural network potential without changing your simulation code.

**Multilingual compute backends.** Performance-critical kernel ridge regression is available through three backends: a Fortran implementation ([MLatomF_src/](mlatom/MLatomF_src/)), a Julia implementation ([julia/](mlatom/julia/)), and a pure-Python/SciPy implementation. The system automatically selects the appropriate backend based on configuration, with the Fortran backend serving as the historical default for KREG models.

**Automatic reference tracking.** MLatom's `header` module ([header.py](mlatom/header.py#L1-L200)) automatically detects which methods, models, and external programs you use and prints the corresponding scientific citations. This is driven by a JSON reference database ([ref.json](mlatom/ref.json)) and ensures that all relevant work is properly acknowledged.

> [!TIP]
> The `methods()` factory function (imported from `mlatom.models`) is the simplest way to instantiate any computational method. For example, `ml.methods(method='AIQM1')` or `ml.methods(method='AIQM2', qm_program='xtb')` automatically configures the correct class with sensible defaults, abstracting away the complexity of the model hierarchy.

> [!TIP]
> Active learning ([al.py](mlatom/al.py#L15-L80)) is one of MLatom's most powerful features. It automatically identifies which molecular configurations need expensive reference calculations, iteratively building accurate ML models with minimal computational cost. This is especially valuable when exploring conformational spaces or training reactive potential energy surfaces.

## Quick Installation

MLatom installs as a standard Python package with a single command:

```bash
python3 -m pip install -U mlatom
```

Some features — particularly those involving external quantum chemistry programs (Gaussian, ORCA, MNDO/Sparrow, xtb), neural network potentials (TorchANI, MACE, DeePMD), or the Fortran backend — require additional dependencies. The [Installation and Dependencies](3-installation-and-dependencies) page provides a comprehensive guide to configuring these optional components.

# Quick Start



Get MLatom up and running in minutes. This page walks you through the two primary interaction modes — the **Python API** and the **command-line interface (CLI)** — with concrete, runnable examples for the most common tasks: loading molecular data, predicting properties, training machine learning models, and running simulations.

![MLatom](https://github.com/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/doc/mlatom_logo.png?raw=true)

## The Two Faces of MLatom

MLatom 3.22.0 is a comprehensive package for atomistic simulations powered by machine learning, developed by Pavlo O. Dral and collaborators at Xiamen University. It supports the full lifecycle of computational chemistry workflows — from data management and ML model training to geometry optimization, molecular dynamics, and spectroscopy. Every feature is accessible through two equivalent interfaces, unified by a shared task dispatch architecture.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph User["User Entry Points"]
        PY["Python API<br/>import mlatom"]
        CLI["Command Line<br/>mlatom inputfile.inp"]
    end

    subgraph Core["Core Dispatch Layer"]
        PY --> RUN["mlatom.run(argv)"]
        CLI --> RUN
        RUN --> PARSE["mlatom_args.parse()"]
        PARSE --> TASK["CLItasks(args).run()"]
    end

    subgraph Tasks["Task Modules"]
        TASK --> USE["useMLmodel — Prediction"]
        TASK --> CREATE["createMLmodel — Training"]
        TASK --> EST["estAccMLmodel — Accuracy Estimation"]
        TASK --> OPT["geomopt — Geometry Optimization"]
        TASK --> DYN["MD — Molecular Dynamics"]
        TASK --> FREQ["freq — Frequency Calculation"]
        TASK --> AL["al — Active Learning"]
    end

    subgraph Data["Data Layer"]
        USE --> MDB["molecular_database"]
        CREATE --> MDB
        EST --> MDB
        OPT --> MOL["molecule"]
        DYN --> MOL
    end

    subgraph Models["Model Layer"]
        USE --> MOD["model.predict()"]
        CREATE --> MOD
    end
```

Both entry points converge on the same execution path: the `run()` function in [MLatom.py](mlatom/MLatom.py#L61-L174) parses arguments via the `mlatom_args` class, then delegates to the `CLItasks` dispatcher. This means **anything you can do from the command line, you can also do from Python** — and vice versa.

## Prerequisites and Installation

MLatom is available on PyPI. Install it with a single command:

```bash
pip install mlatom
```

You can verify your installation and check for updates using the built-in version flags:

```bash
mlatom --version          # prints current version, checks PyPi for latest
mlatom --list             # lists all installed mlatom locations on your system
```

These flags are handled directly in the `run()` function before argument parsing begins, as seen in [MLatom.py](mlatom/MLatom.py#L81-L134). For advanced features (specific quantum chemistry program interfaces, GPU acceleration for neural network potentials, etc.), additional dependencies are required — see [Installation and Dependencies](3-installation-and-dependencies) for the complete guide.

## Understanding the Architecture

Before writing code, it helps to understand the three foundational layers that every MLatom workflow touches. Each maps directly to a Python module you'll import:

| Layer | Module | Core Classes | Purpose |
|-------|--------|-------------|---------|
| **Data** | `mlatom.data` | `atom`, `molecule`, `molecular_database`, `ml_database` | Represent and manipulate molecular structures, properties, and datasets |
| **Model** | `mlatom.models` | `ml_model`, `krr`, `kreg`, `methods()` | Create, train, predict with, and save machine learning and quantum chemistry models |
| **Simulation** | `mlatom.simulations` | `optimize_geometry()`, `freq()`, `md()`, `irc()` | Run atomistic simulations using any model as the energy/gradient engine |

The `model` class hierarchy in [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L20-L343) serves as the backbone: `model()` is the root parent, `ml_model(model)` adds training capabilities, and specialized subclasses like `torch_model`, `torchani_model`, and `downloadable_model` provide framework-specific behavior. All of these are re-exported at the top level of the package via [__init__.py](mlatom/__init__.py#L1-L17) so you can access them as `mlatom.molecule`, `mlatom.kreg`, etc.

## Quick Example: Loading and Exploring Molecules

The `molecule` class is your primary data container. It stores atomic species, 3D coordinates, energies, gradients, Hessians, and arbitrary scalar/vector properties. Create one from scratch or load from standard file formats:

```python
import mlatom

# Load from an XYZ file (reads the first molecule)
mol = mlatom.molecule.from_xyz_file('water.xyz')

# Load a full dataset of molecules
molDB = mlatom.molecular_database.from_xyz_file('dataset.xyz')

# Inspect basic properties
print(f'Atoms: {mol.get_number_of_atoms()}')
print(f'Formula: {mol.get_element_symbols()}')
print(f'Coordinates (Å):\n{mol.xyz_coordinates}')

# Access individual atoms
for i, at in enumerate(mol.atoms):
    print(f'  Atom {i}: {at.element_symbol} at {at.xyz_coordinates}')
```

The `molecule` class, defined in [data.py](mlatom/data.py#L356-L1470), supports multiple input formats beyond XYZ — including SMILES strings, NumPy arrays, JSON, and HDF5. You can also construct molecules programmatically from `atom` objects:

```python
at1 = mlatom.atom(element_symbol='O', xyz_coordinates=[0.0, 0.0, 0.1173])
at2 = mlatom.atom(element_symbol='H', xyz_coordinates=[0.0, 0.7572, -0.4692])
at3 = mlatom.atom(element_symbol='H', xyz_coordinates=[0.0, -0.7572, -0.4692])
mol = mlatom.molecule(atoms=[at1, at2, at3])
```

## Quick Example: Predicting Molecular Properties

MLatom provides pre-built and pre-trained methods through the `methods()` factory function. This is the fastest path from structure to property — no training required. The function iterates through a priority list of `known_classes` and returns the first matching model that supports your requested method and has its required program installed.

```python
import mlatom

# Load a molecule
mol = mlatom.molecule.from_xyz_file('ethanol.xyz')

# Create a model — AIQM1 is a pre-trained semiempirical ML method
model = mlatom.methods(method='AIQM1')

# Predict energy and energy gradients
model.predict(molecule=mol, calculate_energy=True, calculate_energy_gradients=True)

# Access results
print(f'Energy: {mol.energy:.6f} Hartree')
print(f'Gradients shape: {mol.energy_gradients.shape}')
```

The `methods()` function in [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L627-L691) supports dozens of methods out of the box — including `AIQM1`, `AIQM2`, `AIQM3`, `ANI-2x`, `GFN2-xTB`, various DFT and ab initio methods through Gaussian, PySCF, ORCA, and more. When you specify a method name without a program, MLatom automatically detects which installed program can handle it.

## Quick Example: Training a Machine Learning Model

For cases where pre-trained methods aren't sufficient, MLatom lets you train your own ML potentials. The most commonly used model type is `kreg` (Kernel Ridge Regression with RE descriptors), which learns molecular energies and gradients from a reference dataset:

```python
import mlatom

# Step 1: Load training data
molDB = mlatom.molecular_database.from_xyz_file('training_data.xyz')
molDB.read_from_y_file('training_energies.txt')            # reference energies
molDB.read_from_xyz_derivative_property_file('training_gradients.xyz')  # reference gradients

# Step 2: Create a KREG model
model = mlatom.kreg(model_file='my_model.json')

# Step 3: Train
model.train(
    molecular_database=molDB,
    property_to_learn='y',                        # energies stored as mol.y
    xyz_derivative_property_to_learn='xyz_derivatives_y'  # gradients
)

# Step 4: Predict on new molecules
test_mol = mlatom.molecule.from_xyz_file('test.xyz')
model.predict(molecule=test_mol, calculate_energy=True, calculate_energy_gradients=True)
print(f'Predicted energy: {test_mol.energy:.6f} Hartree')
```

The `ml_model` base class, defined in [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L343-L816), provides the unified `train()` and `predict()` interface that all trainable models implement. The `kreg` class in [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L343-L595) extends this with kernel-specific hyperparameter optimization, descriptor generation, and support for both the Fortran (MLatomF) and Python backends.

> [!TIP]
> When training KREG models with energy gradients, the `xyz_derivative_property_to_learn` argument must point to the property name where gradients are stored. By convention, the `read_from_xyz_derivative_property_file()` method stores them as `xyz_derivatives_y`. Always ensure this matches what you pass to `train()`.

## Quick Example: Command-Line Interface

For batch processing, scripting, and reproducibility, the CLI mode is often more convenient. You write an input file with keyword-value pairs, then run it with a single command:

```bash
# Predict energies with AIQM1
mlatom useMLmodel XYZfile=molecules.xyz AIQM1 YestFile=energies.txt

# Train a KREG model
mlatom createMLmodel XYZfile=training.xyz Yfile=energies.txt YgradXYZfile=gradients.xyz MLmodelType=KREG MLmodelOut=model.json

# Run geometry optimization
mlatom geomopt XYZfile=initial.xyz AIQM1 optXYZ=optimized.xyz

# Estimate model accuracy with cross-validation
mlatom estAccMLmodel XYZfile=data.xyz Yfile=ref_energies.txt MLmodelIn=model.json CVtest
```

The CLI argument parser in [args_class.py](mlatom/args_class.py#L401-L775) recognizes a comprehensive list of tasks defined in the `_task_list` — currently 25+ tasks spanning ML model creation, PES exploration, dynamics, spectroscopy, and active learning. Key-value pairs can use standard quantum chemistry naming conventions (e.g., `ANI-2x`, `GFN2-xTB`, `CCSD(T)*/CBS`) with automatic alias resolution.

## Quick Example: Geometry Optimization

MLatom wraps geometry optimization into a single high-level function that works with any compatible model. The `optimize_geometry()` function imported from `mlatom.simulations` handles convergence checking, trajectory logging, and result extraction:

```python
import mlatom

# Set up model and initial geometry
model = mlatom.methods(method='AIQM1')
mol = mlatom.molecule.from_xyz_file('ethanol.xyz')

# Run optimization
geomopt = mlatom.optimize_geometry(
    model=model,
    initial_molecule=mol,
    convergence_criterion_for_forces=0.02,  # eV/Å
    maximum_number_of_steps=200
)

# Access results
optimized = geomopt.optimized_molecule
print(f'Optimized energy: {optimized.energy:.6f} Hartree')
optimized.write_file_with_xyz_coordinates('optimized.xyz')
```

Internally, the CLI `geomopt` task in [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L386-L453) follows the same pattern — it loads data, creates a model, calls `simulations.optimize_geometry()`, and writes results. The Python API simply exposes the same pipeline without the argument-parsing layer.

## Quick Example: Molecular Dynamics

Running molecular dynamics follows the same pattern — provide a model and initial conditions, and MLatom handles the integration:

```bash
# CLI: run 1 ps of NVE dynamics at 300 K
mlatom MD XYZfile=init.xyz AIQM1 initTemp=300 dt=0.1 trun=1000 \
    trajXYZout=traj.xyz trajEpot=energy.dat
```

The MD parameters are pre-configured in the `mlatom_args` class with sensible defaults — `dt=0.1 fs`, `trun=1000 fs`, `ensemble='nve'`, and various output file paths for trajectories, energies, and temperatures, as seen in [args_class.py](mlatom/args_class.py#L595-L632).

## Summary: Which Mode to Use

| Scenario | Recommended Mode | Why |
|----------|-----------------|-----|
| Interactive exploration, Jupyter notebooks | Python API | Immediate feedback, easy plotting, step-by-step debugging |
| Reproducible batch jobs, HPC clusters | CLI with input files | Self-documenting, easy to version-control, no Python overhead |
| Custom ML pipelines, integration with other tools | Python API | Full programmatic control over data flow |
| Quick property calculations on a few molecules | Either — CLI is faster for single commands | |
| Training and hyperparameter optimization | Python API for flexibility, CLI for standard workflows | Python allows custom validation loops |

# Installation and Dependencies



This page provides a complete guide to installing MLatom and understanding its dependency structure. MLatom is a versatile atomistic simulation package that supports multiple execution modes — as a Python library, through input files, or via the command line. Its modular architecture means most features work immediately after a simple pip install, while advanced capabilities (external quantum chemistry programs, GPU-accelerated ML models, Fortran/Julia backends) require additional setup.

![MLatom-banner](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9433ac9a-bcc9-4dd4-9128-d834c85603b0)

The current version is **3.22.0**, distributed under a modified MIT license [Sources: [__init__.py](mlatom/__init__.py#L17-L17)].

## Dependency Architecture Overview

MLatom's dependencies are organized in a layered architecture. The core package has minimal requirements, while each optional capability pulls in additional libraries or external programs only when needed. Understanding this structure helps you install exactly what you need — nothing more, nothing less.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Core Layer (pip install mlatom)"
        A[mlatom Python package]
        A --> B[numpy]
        A --> C[scipy]
    end

    subgraph "ML Models Layer"
        A --> D[PyTorch<br/>TorchANI, MACE,<br/>AIMNet2, GICnet]
        A --> E[TensorFlow<br/>PhysNet, DeePMD-kit]
        A --> F[Julia + PyJulia<br/>KRR (mlatom.jl)]
        A --> G[e3nn + torch-ema<br/>MACE-specific]
    end

    subgraph "External QM Programs"
        A --> H[PySCF]
        A --> I[xtb]
        A --> J[MNDO / Sparrow]
        A --> K[Gaussian / ORCA / Turbomole]
        A --> L[DFTB+]
        A --> M[D4 dispersion]
        A --> N[COLUMBUS]
    end

    subgraph "Simulation & Optimization"
        A --> O[ASE]
        A --> P[geomeTRIC]
        A --> Q[PySCF freq]
        A --> R[pysisyphus]
    end

    subgraph "Spectroscopy"
        A --> S[RDKit<br/>MLTPA]
    end

    subgraph "Fortran Backend"
        A --> T[Intel/gfortran<br/>MKL / OpenBLAS]
    end

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#6db56d,color:#fff
    style C fill:#6db56d,color:#fff
```

## Quick Installation

The simplest way to install MLatom is via pip, which installs the core Python package along with its essential dependencies [Sources: [README.md](README.md#L33-L34)]:

```bash
python3 -m pip install -U mlatom
```

After installation, verify it works by importing the package:

```python
import mlatom as ml
print(ml.__version__)  # Should print 3.22.0
```

The core package imports reveal the foundational modules available immediately after installation: `MLatom`, `args_class`, `MLtasks`, `header`, `data`, `models`, `plot`, `simulations`, `stats`, `xyz`, `namd`, `constants`, `spectra`, `model_cls` [Sources: [__init__.py](mlatom/__init__.py#L4-L4)].

> [!TIP]
> If you plan to use ML models that involve training (KREG, ANI) or matrix operations (KRR with scipy solver), ensure `numpy` and `scipy` are installed — these are typically pulled in automatically as pip dependencies but may need manual installation in minimal environments.

## Core Dependencies

The following table lists the packages required for MLatom's core functionality. These are either installed automatically with pip or are part of the Python standard library.

| Dependency | Purpose | Used By |
|---|---|---|
| **numpy** | Array operations, linear algebra | Nearly every module — kernel matrices in KRR [Sources: [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L17-L17)], molecular coordinate handling, statistics |
| **scipy** | Sparse/dense linear solvers (Cholesky, LU decomposition) | KRR training with `ml_program='scipy'` [Sources: [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L207-L218)] |
| **json** (stdlib) | Reference metadata, model serialization | Header printing [Sources: [header.py](mlatom/header.py#L5-L5)], model dump/load |
| **os / sys / subprocess** (stdlib) | File I/O, environment variables, process spawning | External program interfaces, MLatomF bridge |

The `krr` class with the `scipy` solver uses `scipy.linalg.cho_factor` and `cho_solve` as its primary matrix decomposition strategy, falling back to LU decomposition when the kernel matrix is not positive definite [Sources: [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L207-L214)].

## Machine Learning Model Dependencies

MLatom integrates with a rich ecosystem of ML potential frameworks. These dependencies are only required when you use the corresponding model types.

### PyTorch-Based Models

PyTorch is the most widely required optional dependency, powering several universal ML potential interfaces:

| Model / Interface | Additional Requirements | Import Location |
|---|---|---|
| **TorchANI** (ANI-1x, ANI-1ccx, ANI-2x, MS-ANI) | `torchani` | [Sources: [torchani_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/torchani_interface.py#L1-L50)] |
| **MACE** | `mace`, `e3nn`, `torch_geometric`, `torch_ema` | [Sources: [mace_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/mace_interface.py#L1-L50)] |
| **AIMNet2** | `torchani` (shared infrastructure) | [Sources: [aimnet2_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/aimnet2_interface.py#L1-L50)] |
| **KRR (scipy, gradient kernel)** | `torch` (for autograd in kernel derivatives) | [Sources: [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L318-L319)] |
| **GICnet** | `torch` | [Sources: [GICnet.py](mlatom/GICnet.py)] |
| **MDtrajNet** | `torch` | [Sources: [__init__.py](mlatom/__init__.py#L12-L12)] |

The model class hierarchy includes dedicated base classes for PyTorch integration: `torch_model` extends `model` with thread configuration, and `torchani_model` further extends `torch_model` with multiprocessing setup for TorchANI [Sources: [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L139-L154)].

Installation command for the full PyTorch ML stack:

```bash
pip install torch torchani mace-torch e3nn torch_geometric torch-ema
```

### TensorFlow-Based Models

| Model / Interface | Additional Requirements | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **PhysNet** | `tensorflow`, PhysNet source code | Expects `$PhysNet` environment variable pointing to installation directory [Sources: [physnet_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/physnet_interface.py#L17-L31)] |
| **DeePMD-kit** | `tensorflow`, DeePMD-kit | Expects `$DeePMDkit` environment variable [Sources: [dpmd_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/dpmd_interface.py#L18-L22)] |

Both PhysNet and DeePMD-kit use TensorFlow v1 compatibility mode. The `tensorflow_model` base class inherits from `model` and handles thread configuration for TF [Sources: [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L157-L157)].

### sGDML Interface

The symmetric Gradient Domain Machine Learning (sGDML) package provides its own GDML models. MLatom's interface converts molecular databases to sGDML data format and wraps the GDML train/predict pipelines [Sources: [sgdml_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/sgdml_interface.py#L1-L60)].

```bash
pip install sgdml
```

### GAP/SOAP Interface

The Gaussian Approximation Potential (GAP) with SOAP descriptors requires external executables rather than Python packages. You must set two environment variables [Sources: [gap_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/gap_interface.py#L18-L26)]:

```bash
export gap_fit=/path/to/gap_fit_executable
export quip=/path/to/quip_executable
```

### Julia Backend for KRR

MLatom can delegate KRR computations to a Julia implementation (`mlatom.jl`), which requires both Julia and the `PyJulia` Python bridge. The Julia KRR module supports Gaussian, periodic Gaussian, decaying periodic Gaussian, and Matern kernels [Sources: [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L128-L171)].

```bash
# Install Julia (e.g., via juliaup or system package manager)
pip install julia
python -c "import julia; julia.install()"
```

> [!TIP]
> When choosing between KRR solvers: `scipy` is the most portable (pure Python), `mlatom.jl` may offer performance benefits for large datasets, and `MLatomF` (Fortran) provides the highest performance but requires Fortran compilation. The solver is selected via the `ml_program` parameter.

## External Quantum Chemistry Program Interfaces

MLatom can use external QM programs as reference methods, baseline calculators (for AIQM methods), or standalone energy/gradient engines. Each interface requires the corresponding program to be installed and accessible via an environment variable or PATH.

### Program Installation Summary

| Program | Environment Variable | Interface | Supported Methods |
|---|---|---|---|
| **PySCF** | (Python import) | [Sources: [pyscf_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/pyscf_interface.py#L1-L50)] | HF, MP2, DFT, CCSD, TD-DFT, CISD, FCI, DM21 |
| **xtb** | (PATH) | [Sources: [xtb_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/xtb_interface.py#L1-L50)] | GFN2-xTB, GFN2-xTB* |
| **MNDO** | `mndobin` | [Sources: [mndo_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/mndo_interface.py#L1-L50)] | ODM2, ODM2*, ODM3, OM1-3, PM3, AM1, MNDO/d, SCC-DFTB |
| **Sparrow** | `sparrowbin` | (via MNDO interface) | ODM2, ODM2* |
| **Gaussian** | `GAUSS_EXEDIR` | [Sources: [gaussian_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/gaussian_interface.py)] | DFT, ab initio, TD-DFT |
| **ORCA** | (PATH) | [Sources: [orca_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/orca_interface.py)] | CCSD(T)*, DFT |
| **Turbomole** | (PATH) | [Sources: [turbomole_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/turbomole_interface.py)] | DFT, MP2 |
| **DFTB+** | (PATH) | [Sources: [dftbplus_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/dftbplus_interface.py)] | DFTB, TD-DFTB |
| **COLUMBUS** | `COLUMBUS` | [Sources: [columbus_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/columbus_interface.py#L1-L50)] | CASSCF, MRCI |
| **D4 dispersion** | (via d4 Python package) | [Sources: [dftd4_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/dftd4_interface.py)] | DFT-D4 |

Example environment setup for commonly used programs:

```bash
# xtb (usually installed via conda)
conda install -c conda-forge xtb

# PySCF
pip install pyscf

# MNDO/Sparrow (external binaries)
export mndobin=/path/to/mndo/bin
export sparrowbin=/path/to/sparrow/bin

# D4 dispersion correction
pip install d4
```

The `method_model` base class provides a unified pattern for external program interfaces: it implements `is_method_supported()`, `is_program_found()`, and `get_bin_env_var()` class methods that child interfaces override to declare their capabilities [Sources: [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L175-L206)].

## Simulation and Optimization Dependencies

### Geometry Optimization Engines

MLatom supports multiple optimization backends. The `header.py` module demonstrates an automatic fallback mechanism: it first attempts to import `geometric`, then falls back to `scipy` for optimization, and checks for `ase` as an additional option [Sources: [header.py](mlatom/header.py#L147-L158)].

| Engine | Package | Install Command |
|---|---|---|
| **geomeTRIC** | `geometric` | `pip install geometric` |
| **ASE** | `ase` | `pip install ase` |
| **PySCF** | `pyscf` | `pip install pyscf` (for PySCF-based optimization) |
| **Gaussian** | (external) | Must be installed separately |

The geomeTRIC interface wraps MLatom models into a `geometric.engine.Engine` subclass (`MLatomEngine`), converting between MLatom's internal molecule representation and geomeTRIC's coordinate system (Bohr ↔ Ångström) [Sources: [geometric_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/geometric_interface.py#L1-L50)].

The ASE interface provides an `MLatomCalculator` (extending ASE's `Calculator` base class) that allows any MLatom model to be used within ASE's workflow, including geometry optimization, frequency calculations, and thermochemistry [Sources: [ase_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/ase_interface.py#L1-L50)].

### Molecular Dynamics

The built-in MD engine (`mlatom/md.py`) requires only `numpy` and the internal `thermostat` module, supporting NVE and NVT ensembles with Andersen, Nosé-Hoover, and Langevin thermostats [Sources: [md.py](mlatom/md.py#L1-L60)].

For parallel molecular dynamics batch execution, no additional dependencies are needed beyond the core package [Sources: [__init__.py](mlatom/__init__.py#L9-L9)].

## Spectroscopy and Analysis Dependencies

| Feature | Dependency | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| IR/Raman spectra | `scipy` (interpolation), optional QM program | Linear/cubic interpolation via `scipy.interpolate.interp1d` [Sources: [spectra.py](mlatom/spectra.py#L38-L42)] |
| UV-Vis / ML-NEA | `numpy` | Nuclear ensemble approach with Wigner sampling |
| MLTPA (two-photon absorption) | `RDKit` | Referenced in header printing [Sources: [header.py](mlatom/header.py#L116-L117)] |
| Hyperparameter optimization | `hyperopt` | Tree-Structured Parzen Estimator algorithm [Sources: [header.py](mlatom/header.py#L119-L120)] |

## Add-on Models

MLatom includes an add-on system (`mlatom/addons/`) for premium models that require separate licensing or download. Currently, three add-on packages are structured in the repository [Sources: [addons/__init__.py](mlatom/addons/__init__.py)]:

| Add-on | Models | Status | Requirement |
|---|---|---|---|
| **AIQM3** | AIQM3, AIQM3@DFT | Requires Aitomistic subscription | Raises `ValueError` directing users to [mlatom.com/aitomic](http://mlatom.com/aitomic) [Sources: [aiqm3.py](mlatom/addons/aiqm3/aiqm3.py#L26-L35)] |
| **UAIQM** | Universal updatable AI-enhanced QM methods | Requires Aitomistic subscription | Multiple method variants (ODM2*, GFN2-xTB*, DFT, CC baselines) [Sources: [uaiqm.py](mlatom/addons/uaiqm/uaiqm.py#L36-L44)] |
| **OmniP2x** | Multi-state potentials (vecMSANI) | Requires Aitomistic subscription | Excited-state dynamics [Sources: [addons/__init__.py](mlatom/addons/__init__.py)] |

The `downloadable_model` class in `model_cls.py` provides infrastructure for downloading model files from remote URLs, handling zip extraction and path flattening — used by universal models like ANI-1x, ANI-1ccx, MACE-OFF, and AIMNet2 [Sources: [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L208-L313)].

## Fortran Backend (MLatomF)

MLatom includes a Fortran backend called **MLatomF** located in `mlatom/MLatomF_src/`. This is a standalone Fortran executable that handles kernel ridge regression (KREG), descriptor generation (Coulomb Matrix, RE, ID), and model training with hyperparameter optimization [Sources: [MLatomF_src/Makefile](mlatom/MLatomF_src/Makefile#L1-L61)].

### Compilation Requirements

The MLatomF Makefile includes multiple compiler configuration files:

| Makefile | Compiler | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `Makefile.intel` | Intel Fortran (ifort) + MKL | Default; highest performance with Intel MKL for BLAS/LAPACK |
| `Makefile.gnu` | GNU Fortran (gfortran) + OpenBLAS | Open-source alternative |
| `Makefile.cygwin` | Intel Fortran (Cygwin) | Windows via Cygwin |

The build produces two artifacts: the `MLatomF` executable and `cs.so` (a shared library for ML-NEA cross-section calculations via C++) [Sources: [MLatomF_src/Makefile](mlatom/MLatomF_src/Makefile#L37-L40)].

### Compilation Steps

```bash
cd mlatom/MLatomF_src/

# Edit Makefile to select your compiler:
# Change "include Makefile.intel" to "include Makefile.gnu" if using gfortran
vim Makefile

# Compile
make clean
make
```

The Python interface to MLatomF (`mlatom/interface_MLatomF.py`) invokes the compiled binary via `subprocess.Popen`, passing command-line arguments and parsing stdout for timing and result information [Sources: [interface_MLatomF.py](mlatom/interface_MLatomF.py#L1-L50)].

### Fortran KREG Module (Optional)

A separate Fortran KREG module exists in `mlatom/fortran/` with its own compilation script. The compile script in `compile.py` shows it uses `f2py` (from NumPy) to build a Python-callable shared object from `KREG.f90`, linking against Intel MKL and OpenMP for parallel execution [Sources: [compile.py](mlatom/fortran/compile.py#L1-L10)].

## Verifying Your Installation

After installing MLatom and your desired dependencies, run this verification script to check what's available:

```python
import mlatom as ml

# Check core version
print(f"MLatom version: {ml.__version__}")

# Check optional dependencies
checks = {
    'numpy': lambda: __import__('numpy'),
    'scipy': lambda: __import__('scipy'),
    'torch': lambda: __import__('torch'),
    'ase': lambda: __import__('ase'),
    'geometric': lambda: __import__('geometric'),
    'pyscf': lambda: __import__('pyscf'),
}

for name, check in checks.items():
    try:
        check()
        print(f"  ✓ {name} available")
    except ImportError:
        print(f"  ✗ {name} not installed")

# Check environment variables for external programs
import os
env_checks = ['mndobin', 'sparrowbin', 'GAUSS_EXEDIR', 'COLUMBUS',
              'DeePMDkit', 'PhysNet', 'gap_fit', 'quip']
for var in env_checks:
    path = os.environ.get(var, None)
    if path:
        print(f"  ✓ ${var} = {path}")
    else:
        print(f"  ✗ ${var} not set")
```

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

| Problem | Likely Cause | Solution |
|---|---|---|
| `ImportError: cannot import name 'torch'` | PyTorch not installed | `pip install torch` |
| `please set $mndobin` | MNDO not configured | `export mndobin=/path/to/mndo/bin` |
| MLatomF binary not found | Fortran backend not compiled | `cd mlatom/MLatomF_src && make` |
| `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'julia'` | PyJulia not installed | `pip install julia && python -c "import julia; julia.install()"` |
| CUDA out of memory | Model too large for GPU | Set `device='cpu'` in model constructor |
| `cho_factor` LinAlgError | Non-positive-definite kernel matrix | MLatom falls back to LU automatically [Sources: [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L213-L216)] |

# Usage Modes and Input Files



MLatom 3.22.0 offers two primary usage modes — a **command-line interface (CLI)** driven by keyword-based input files, and a **Python API** for programmatic integration. Both modes ultimately funnel through the same internal pipeline: argument parsing → task dispatch → execution. Understanding how these modes work and how input files are structured is the essential first step before exploring any specific ML workflow.

## High-Level Architecture

Every MLatom invocation follows a single, predictable path regardless of the usage mode you choose. Arguments are parsed into a structured dictionary, a task is identified, and the corresponding function in the task engine is invoked.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["User Input"] --> B{"Which mode?"}
    B -->|CLI| C["mlatom input_file.inp"]
    B -->|Python API| D["mlatom.run(argv=[...])"]
    
    C --> E["mlatom_args.parse()"]
    D --> E
    
    E --> F["parse_input_file() / parse_input_content()"]
    F --> G["ArgsBase._checkArgs()"]
    G --> H["Task identified"]
    
    H --> I{"MLatomF task?"}
    I -->|Yes| J["run_with_mlatomF()"]
    I -->|No| K["CLItasks.run() → globals()[task](args)"]
    
    J --> L["Fortran Backend Execution"]
    K --> M["Python Task Functions"]
    
    L --> N["Results"]
    M --> N
```

This diagram illustrates the core insight: **both usage modes converge on the same `mlatom_args` parser and `CLItasks` dispatcher**. The CLI mode is simply a thin wrapper that reads an input file and passes the extracted tokens to the same machinery the Python API uses directly.
Sources: [MLatom.py](mlatom/MLatom.py#L61-L174), [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L14-L29)

## The Command-Line Interface (CLI)

The CLI is the most common way to use MLatom. You invoke it by passing a single input file name as an argument. If the file exists, MLatom reads it; if you pass inline keyword-value pairs instead, those are parsed directly.

### Basic Invocation

```bash
# Using an input file (most common)
mlatom my_calculation.inp

# Using inline arguments (less common, but supported)
mlatom useMLmodel XYZfile=molecules.xyz AIQM1

# Check version or list installations
mlatom -v
mlatom -l
```

When a single argument is provided and it corresponds to an existing file, MLatom automatically reads it as an input file and echoes its contents to the console for reproducibility [MLatom.py](mlatom/MLatom.py#L145-L152). If the argument is not a file, it is treated as a space-separated list of keyword-value pairs.

### The Input File Format

MLatom input files use a flat, **keyword=value** syntax — one keyword per logical unit, separated by whitespace or newlines. Comments begin with `#` and are stripped out during parsing. This deliberately simple format means there are no section headers, no nested blocks, and no indentation rules to remember.

Here is a representative input file that trains a KREG model and estimates its accuracy:

```text
# my_calculation.inp - Train and test a ML model

# Task: estimate accuracy (trains + predicts on test set)
estAccMLmodel

# Input data
XYZfile=training_data.xyz
Yfile=reference_energies.dat

# Model type
MLmodelType=KREG
MLmodelOut=my_model.unf

# Sampling settings
Ntrain=800
Nvalidate=100
Ntest=100

# Kernel and descriptor
kernel=Gaussian
molDescriptor=RE
```

### Keyword-Value Syntax Rules

The argument extractor in `ArgsBase._args_extractor()` processes the raw text with a few important rules [args_class.py](mlatom/args_class.py#L202-L233):

| Rule | Behavior | Example |
|------|----------|---------|
| **Whitespace separation** | Keywords are separated by spaces, tabs, or newlines | `XYZfile=data.xyz Ntrain=100` works |
| **Equals sign for values** | `key=value` assigns a value; `key` alone sets it to `True` | `createMLmodel` → `True`; `Ntrain=500` → `500` |
| **Comments** | Everything after `#` on a line is ignored until the next newline | `Ntrain=100 # use 100 structures` |
| **Bracket matching** | Parentheses `()`, brackets `[]`, braces `{}`, and quotes are balanced before splitting | `hyperopt.sigma=(1,10)` is kept intact |
| **Dot notation** | Periods create nested dictionaries | `ase.fmax=0.02` becomes `{'ase': {'fmax': '0.02'}}` |

The `parse_input_content` method further distinguishes between flag-only keywords and keyword-value pairs. If a string contains no `=` sign, it is treated as a boolean flag set to `True` [args_class.py](mlatom/args_class.py#L240-L267).

> [!TIP]
> **Inline multi-line data**: If a keyword value contains newline characters (e.g., inline XYZ geometries), MLatom automatically writes the data to a temporary file using an MD5-based hash for the filename and replaces the value with the file path. This is handled transparently in `_multi_lines_to_file()` [args_class.py](mlatom/args_class.py#L679-L689).

## Supported Tasks

The task system is the backbone of MLatom's CLI. When `mlatom_args._checkArgs()` runs, it scans the parsed arguments against a master task list to determine which workflow to execute [args_class.py](mlatom/args_class.py#L706-L748).

### Complete Task Reference

The `_task_list` in `mlatom_args` defines every available task [args_class.py](mlatom/args_class.py#L410-L437):

| Category | Task Keyword | Description |
|----------|-------------|-------------|
| **ML Tasks** | `useMLmodel` | Predict properties with an existing model or method |
| | `createMLmodel` | Train a new ML model from data |
| | `estAccMLmodel` | Train and evaluate model accuracy on test set |
| | `selfCorrect` | Multi-layer self-correction (delta learning) |
| | `learningCurve` | Generate learning curves with varying training sizes |
| **Data Tasks** | `XYZ2X` | Convert XYZ geometries to descriptor vectors |
| | `XYZ2SMI` | Convert XYZ to SMILES notation |
| | `SMI2XYZ` | Convert SMILES to 3D XYZ geometries |
| | `analyze` | Analyze prediction statistics |
| | `sample` | Sample molecular data into train/validate/test subsets |
| | `slice` / `sampleFromSlices` / `mergeSlices` | Advanced data slicing operations |
| **Potential Energy Surface** | `geomopt` | Geometry optimization |
| | `ts` | Transition state search |
| | `freq` | Frequency and thermochemistry calculation |
| | `irc` | Intrinsic reaction coordinate analysis |
| | `ir` / `raman` | Vibrational spectra calculation |
| **Dynamics** | `MD` | Molecular dynamics simulation |
| | `MD2vibr` | Convert MD trajectories to vibrational spectra |
| | `crossSection` | UV-Vis cross-section via ML-NEA |
| | `MLQD` | Machine learning quantum dynamics |
| | `MLTPA` | ML-based triplet pair annihilation |
| **Active Learning** | `al` | Active learning pipeline |

### Task Resolution Logic

When multiple tasks are specified in a single input file, MLatom applies precedence rules [args_class.py](mlatom/args_class.py#L706-L728):

1. If only **one** task is detected, it is used directly.
2. If `selfCorrect` is among multiple tasks, `selfCorrect` takes priority.
3. The combination `geomopt` + `freq` is resolved to the composite task `optfreq`.
4. The combination `ts` + `freq` is resolved to `tsfreq`.
5. If `useMLmodel` appears alongside other tasks, it is silently omitted.
6. Otherwise, the **first** task in the list wins, and a warning is printed.

If no explicit task is specified but a `method` (like `AIQM1`) is present, MLatom automatically infers `useMLmodel` as the task. If neither a task nor a method is provided, the help documentation is displayed and execution stops [args_class.py](mlatom/args_class.py#L743-L748).

## Key Input Parameters

Beyond the task keyword, input files specify data sources, model configuration, and task-specific settings. The `mlatom_args.__init__()` method registers hundreds of default parameters, all accessible as keyword=value pairs [args_class.py](mlatom/args_class.py#L491-L650).

### Data Input/Output Parameters

These parameters control where MLatom reads data from and writes results to:

| Parameter | Purpose | Default |
|-----------|---------|---------|
| `XYZfile` | Input molecular geometries (XYZ format) | `''` (empty) |
| `jsonfile` | Input molecular database (JSON format) | `''` (empty) |
| `Yfile` | Reference scalar properties (e.g., energies) | `''` (empty) |
| `YgradXYZfile` | Reference gradient properties | `''` (empty) |
| `YestFile` | Output file for predicted scalar values | `''` (empty) |
| `YgradXYZestFile` | Output file for predicted gradients | `''` (empty) |
| `HessianEstFile` | Output file for predicted Hessians | `''` (empty) |
| `MLmodelIn` | Input (pre-trained) ML model file | `''` (empty) |
| `MLmodelOut` | Output (newly trained) ML model file | `''` (empty) |

When both `XYZfile` and `jsonfile` are provided, the JSON file takes precedence with a warning message [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L672-L696).

### Model Configuration Parameters

| Parameter | Purpose | Default |
|-----------|---------|---------|
| `MLmodelType` | Type of ML model (e.g., `KREG`, `ANI`, `sGDML`) | `''` (auto: `MLatomF`) |
| `MLprog` | ML program backend | `''` (auto-determined from model type) |
| `method` | Computational method (e.g., `AIQM1`, `ANI-2x`) | `''` (none) |
| `kernel` | Kernel function type for KRR/KREG | `'Gaussian'` |
| `molDescriptor` | Molecular descriptor type | `'RE'` |
| `nthreads` | Number of CPU threads | `None` (system default) |

### Sampling Parameters

| Parameter | Purpose | Default |
|-----------|---------|---------|
| `Nuse` | Total number of data points to use | `None` |
| `Ntrain` | Number of training points | `None` |
| `Nvalidate` | Number of validation points | `None` |
| `Ntest` | Number of test points | `None` |
| `Sampling` | Sampling strategy (`'random'`, `'structure-based'`, etc.) | `'random'` |
| `iTrainIn` / `iTrainOut` | Custom train subset index file in/out | `''` |

## Method Keyword Aliases

MLatom supports a rich set of computational methods and provides convenient aliases so you can use the notation most familiar to you. These aliases are registered via `set_keyword_alias()` in the `mlatom_args` constructor [args_class.py](mlatom/args_class.py#L457-L485):

| Preferred Alias | Internal Key | Example Input |
|----------------|-------------|---------------|
| `AIQM1@DFT*` | `AIQM1DFTstar` | `AIQM1@DFT* XYZfile=mol.xyz` |
| `AIQM2@DFT` | `AIQM2DFT` | `AIQM2@DFT XYZfile=mol.xyz` |
| `AIQM3@DFT` | `AIQM3DFT` | `AIQM3@DFT XYZfile=mol.xyz` |
| `ANI-1ccx` | `ani1ccx` | `ANI-1ccx XYZfile=mol.xyz` |
| `ANI-2x` | `ani2x` | `ANI-2x XYZfile=mol.xyz` |
| `GFN2-xTB` | `gfn2xtb` | `GFN2-xTB XYZfile=mol.xyz` |
| `CCSD(T)*/CBS` | `CCSDTstarCBS` | `CCSD(T)*/CBS XYZfile=mol.xyz` |
| `AIMNet2@B973c` | `aimnet2atb973c` | `AIMNet2@B973c XYZfile=mol.xyz` |
| `omni-p1` | `omnip1` | `omni-p1 XYZfile=mol.xyz` |

The `methods()` function in `models.py` resolves these keywords into the appropriate model class instances [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L627-L693).

## The Python API Mode

For integration into larger workflows, Jupyter notebooks, or custom scripts, MLatom exposes a full Python API. The public interface is re-exported from `__init__.py` [mlatom/__init__.py](mlatom/__init__.py#L1-L17):

### Programmatic Invocation

You can replicate any CLI invocation in Python using `mlatom.run()`:

```python
import mlatom

# Equivalent to: mlatom input_file.inp
mlatom.run(['input_file.inp'])

# Or pass arguments directly (no file needed)
mlatom.run(['useMLmodel', 'XYZfile=molecules.xyz', 'AIQM1'])
```

The `run()` function handles module loading, version checks, argument parsing, task dispatch, and timing — exactly mirroring the CLI path [MLatom.py](mlatom/MLatom.py#L61-L174).

### Direct Python Usage (Advanced)

For finer control, you can import individual components and build your pipeline:

```python
import mlatom

# Load molecules
mol_db = mlatom.molecular_database.from_xyz_file('molecules.xyz')

# Create and use a method
model = mlatom.methods(method='AIQM1')
model.predict(molecular_database=mol_db,
              calculate_energy=True,
              calculate_energy_gradients=True)

# Access results
for mol in mol_db:
    print(f'Energy: {mol.energy:.6f} Hartree')
```

Key imports available from the top-level `mlatom` namespace include: `atom`, `molecule`, `molecular_database`, `kreg`, `ani`, `methods`, `aiqm1`, `aiqm2`, `aiqm3`, `optimize_geometry`, `freq`, `md`, `irc`, `al`, and more [mlatom/__init__.py](mlatom/__init__.py#L2-L14).

## Fortran Backend (MLatomF) Dispatch

Certain tasks are automatically routed to the Fortran backend `MLatomF` for performance. The `CLItasks` class maintains a whitelist of tasks eligible for Fortran execution [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L15-L22):

| MLatomF-eligible Tasks | Conditions |
|----------------------|------------|
| `useMLmodel`, `createMLmodel`, `estAccMLmodel`, `XYZ2X`, `sample` | No custom `method`, no `hyperparameter_optimization`, no `uaiqm`, and `MLprog=mlatomf` |

If any of those conditions are violated (e.g., you specify `AIQM1` as the method, or request hyperparameter optimization), execution falls back to the Python implementation via `globals()[self.args.task](self.args)` [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L25-L29).

## Putting It All Together: Example Input Files

### Predicting energies with AIQM1

```text
# inp - Calculate energies with the AIQM1 method
useMLmodel
XYZfile=molecules.xyz
AIQM1
```

### Training a KREG model

```text
# train.inp - Train a kernel ridge regression model
createMLmodel
XYZfile=training_data.xyz
Yfile=energies.dat
YgradXYZfile=gradients.dat
MLmodelType=KREG
MLmodelOut=my_model.unf
kernel=Gaussian
molDescriptor=RE
Ntrain=800
Nvalidate=100
```

### Geometry optimization with a trained model

```text
# opt.inp - Optimize geometry with a pre-trained model
geomopt
XYZfile=initial_geometry.xyz
MLmodelIn=my_model.unf
optXYZ=optimized.xyz
ase.fmax=0.0005
ase.steps=500
```

### Estimating model accuracy with cross-validation

```text
# cv.inp - Evaluate model with k-fold cross-validation
estAccMLmodel
XYZfile=data.xyz
Yfile=energies.dat
YgradXYZfile=gradients.dat
MLmodelType=KREG
kernel=Gaussian
molDescriptor=RE
NcvTestFolds=5
hyperopt.max_evals=20
hyperopt.algorithm=tpe
```

> [!TIP]
> **Hyperparameter search syntax**: Hyperparameter optimization uses the dot-notation prefix `hyperopt.`. Ranges are specified with parentheses using a comma-separated format, e.g., `hyperopt.sigma=(1,10)`. The optimization algorithm and loss function are configured separately via `hyperopt.algorithm=tpe` and `hyperopt.losstype=geomean` [args_class.py](mlatom/args_class.py#L540-L547).

## Quick Reference: Common Input Patterns

| Goal | Key Parameters |
|------|---------------|
| **Use a pre-trained model** | `useMLmodel` + `XYZfile` + `MLmodelIn` |
| **Use a built-in method** | `useMLmodel` + `XYZfile` + `method` (e.g., `AIQM1`) |
| **Train a new model** | `createMLmodel` + `XYZfile` + `Yfile` + `MLmodelType` + `MLmodelOut` |
| **Estimate accuracy** | `estAccMLmodel` + `XYZfile` + `Yfile` + `Ntest` |
| **Geometry optimization** | `geomopt` + `XYZfile` + `MLmodelIn` (or `method`) |
| **Run dynamics** | `MD` + `XYZfile` (or `initXYZ`) + `method` + `dt` + `trun` |

---

With these fundamentals in place, you are ready to explore MLatom's deeper systems. The natural next step is understanding the [Architecture Overview](5-architecture-overview) to see how the parsed arguments flow through the model and data layers. From there, depending on your workflow, you may want to jump to [Model Class Hierarchy](9-model-class-hierarchy) for how models are constructed, or [Molecule and Atom Classes](6-molecule-and-atom-classes) for how molecular data is represented internally.

# Architecture Overview



MLatom 3.22.0 is a comprehensive Python package for atomistic simulations powered by machine learning. It unifies molecular data management, a polyglot model system spanning kernel methods and neural network potentials, quantum chemistry program interfaces, and simulation engines (geometry optimization, molecular dynamics, spectroscopy, and nonadiabatic dynamics) under a single coherent framework. This page maps the architectural decisions that make this integration possible, providing the conceptual map you need before diving into any individual subsystem.

## High-Level System Architecture

The entire MLatom runtime can be understood as a pipeline with five functional layers, each with well-defined boundaries and data contracts. Execution enters through a CLI entry point, flows through argument parsing and task dispatch, then branches into one of several domain-specific engines depending on the requested operation.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Entry["Entry Layer"]
        CLI["mlatom command / Python API"]
        RUN["MLatom.run()"]
    end

    subgraph Dispatch["Dispatch Layer"]
        ARGS["mlatom_args<br/>args_class.py"]
        TASKS["CLItasks<br/>MLtasks.py"]
    end

    subgraph Core["Core Layers"]
        direction LR
        subgraph Data["Data Layer"]
            ATOM["atom"]
            MOL["molecule"]
            MOLDB["molecular_database"]
            MLDB["ml_database"]
            TRAJ["molecular_trajectory"]
        end
        subgraph ModelSystem["Model System"]
            MODEL["model"]
            MLMODEL["ml_model"]
            METHOD["method_model"]
            TREENODE["model_tree_node"]
            KRR["krr / kreg"]
            METHODS["methods() factory"]
        end
    end

    subgraph Engines["Simulation Engines"]
        GEOPT["optimize_geometry"]
        FREQ["freq / thermochemistry"]
        MD["md / nve"]
        NAMD["surface_hopping_md"]
        SPEC["spectra / uvvis / ir"]
        AL["active learning"]
    end

    subgraph External["External Layer"]
        direction LR
        QC["QC Programs<br/>Gaussian, ORCA, PySCF…"]
        MLP["ML Potentials<br/>ANI, MACE, DPMD…"]
        ASE["ASE / Geometric"]
        FORTRAN["MLatomF<br/>Fortran + OpenMP"]
    end

    CLI --> RUN --> ARGS --> TASKS
    TASKS --> Data & TASKS --> ModelSystem
    ModelSystem --> Engines
    Engines --> External
    Data --> Engines
```

The dispatch layer receives raw CLI input, normalizes it through the `mlatom_args` parser, and routes execution to the appropriate task function. All tasks consume data objects from the data layer and invoke models from the model system. Simulation engines orchestrate iterative model calls (e.g., geometry optimization loops, MD propagation) and can delegate to external programs through the interface layer.

Sources: [MLatom.py](mlatom/MLatom.py#L61-L175), [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L14-L31), [args_class.py](mlatom/args_class.py#L401-L408)

## Project Structure Map

The source tree is organized into clearly separated concerns. The top-level `mlatom/` package contains the core Python modules, while `MLatomF_src/` houses the legacy Fortran backend that still handles high-performance kernel ridge regression.

```
mlatom/
├── MLatom.py                 # CLI entry point & runtime bootstrap
├── __init__.py               # Package version (3.22.0) & public API
├── args_class.py             # Argument parsing infrastructure
├── MLtasks.py                # Task registry & dispatch functions
│
├── data.py                   # atom, molecule, molecular_database, trajectories
├── model_cls.py              # Abstract model hierarchy & hyperparameter system
├── models.py                 # krr, kreg, methods() factory, model I/O
│
├── simulations.py            # Geometry optimization, frequency, DMC
├── md.py                     # Molecular dynamics (NVE, thermostats)
├── namd.py                   # Nonadiabatic / surface-hopping dynamics
├── spectra.py                # IR, Raman, UV-Vis, spectrum comparison
├── al.py                     # Active learning pipeline
│
├── interfaces/               # 25+ external program adapters
│   ├── gaussian_interface.py
│   ├── orca_interface.py
│   ├── pyscf_interface.py
│   ├── torchani_interface.py
│   ├── mace_interface.py
│   ├── dpmd_interface.py
│   ├── ase_interface.py
│   └── ...                   # xtb, xtb_interface, columbus, dftbplus, etc.
│
├── addons/                   # Extended models (separate distribution)
│   ├── aiqm3/                # AIQM3 neural network potential
│   ├── uaiqm/                # Universal AIQM variants
│   └── omnip2x/              # Multi-state OmniP2x potentials
│
├── MLatomF_src/              # Fortran backend (MLatomF)
│   ├── MLatomF.f90           # Main Fortran program
│   ├── MLmodel.f90           # ML model management
│   ├── A_KRR.f90             # Kernel ridge regression (OpenMP)
│   ├── dataset.f90           # Dataset handling
│   └── ...
│
└── interface_MLatomF.py      # Python ↔ Fortran bridge
```

Sources: [__init__.py](mlatom/__init__.py#L16-L17), [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L14-L43)

## Entry Point and Dispatch

Execution begins in `MLatom.run()`, which performs a careful dynamic import of the `mlatom` package to guarantee the correct instance is loaded regardless of the invocation context. It then initializes three key objects: `header` (citation output), `CLItasks` (the task router), and `mlatom_args` (the argument parser). The flow proceeds as: parse CLI arguments → print header → execute `CLItasks(args).run()` → report wall-clock time.

The `CLItasks` class maintains a mapping between task keywords (e.g., `'geomopt'`, `'MD'`, `'createMLmodel'`) and their corresponding handler functions defined in the same module. Each handler follows a consistent pattern: load data, load or create a model, perform the computation, and save results. The `run_with_mlatomF()` function provides a fallback path that delegates certain tasks entirely to the Fortran backend for legacy compatibility.

Sources: [MLatom.py](mlatom/MLatom.py#L61-L174), [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L14-L31), [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L43-L86), [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L31-L42)

## Argument Parsing Infrastructure

The argument system is built on a two-tier class hierarchy in `args_class.py`. The base class `ArgsBase` provides a case-insensitive, attribute-style dictionary (`AttributeDict`) with support for nested key-value extraction from input files. It handles type coercion (strings to integers, floats, booleans, lists), multi-level dictionary construction from dotted keys, keyword aliases, and input file parsing that tolerates both `key = value` and `key value` syntaxes.

The concrete `mlatom_args` subclass specializes this for MLatom's domain, adding post-processing steps such as multi-line argument expansion (`_multi_lines_to_file`), hyperparameter optimization detection (`_check_hyperopt`), and argument validation (`_checkArgs`). It also exposes a `task` property that identifies which simulation task was requested, and a `copy()` method that allows task handlers to fork argument sets with selective key filtering.

Sources: [args_class.py](mlatom/args_class.py#L53-L153), [args_class.py](mlatom/args_class.py#L401-L770)

## Data Layer

The data layer in `data.py` is the foundational substrate for every computation in MLatom. It defines two parallel hierarchies: a simple ML-oriented path and a chemistry-oriented path, connected by the model system.

| Class | Purpose | Key Properties |
|-------|---------|---------------|
| `entry` | Generic (x, y) data point | `x`, `y` |
| `ml_database` | Collection of entries | `entries`, `x`, `y`, `size` |
| `atom` | Single atom with identity and coordinates | `nuclear_charge`, `element_symbol`, `xyz_coordinates`, `nuclear_mass` |
| `molecule` | Full molecular system with dynamic properties | `atoms`, `xyz_coordinates`, `energy`, `energy_gradients`, `charges`, `velocities` |
| `molecular_database` | Ordered collection of molecules | `molecules`, plus iteration, indexing, slicing |
| `molecular_trajectory` | Time-series from dynamics/optimization | HDF5-backed storage, step access, checkpointing |

The `molecule` class is notably rich — it uses Python's dynamic attribute system to attach arbitrary scalar, vectorial, and tensor properties (energies, gradients, Hessians, dipole moments, nonadiabatic couplings). It supports periodic boundary conditions (`pbc`, `cell` properties), SMILES parsing, geometric operations (rotate, translate, align, proliferate), and physical property calculations (kinetic energy, angular momentum, moment of inertia). The `molecular_trajectory` class wraps HDF5-based I/O for efficient storage of large trajectory datasets, and the `h5dataloader` provides batched access for training workflows.

Sources: [data.py](mlatom/data.py#L23-L164), [data.py](mlatom/data.py#L191-L315), [data.py](mlatom/data.py#L356-L409), [data.py](mlatom/data.py#L2738-L2741)

## Model Class Hierarchy

The model system is the architectural heart of MLatom, designed to present a uniform `predict()` interface across an enormously diverse set of computational methods — from semiempirical quantum chemistry to deep neural network potentials to composite delta-learning schemes.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class model {
        +predict(molecular_database, molecule)
        +dump(filename, format)
        +parse_args(args)
        +set_num_threads(nthreads)
    }
    class ml_model {
        +train(molecular_database)
        +predict(molecular_database)
        +optimize_hyperparameters()
        +cross_validation()
        +holdout_validation()
        +calculate_validation_loss()
        +reset()
    }
    class torch_model {
        +set_num_threads(nthreads)
        +config_multiprocessing()
    }
    class torchani_model
    class tensorflow_model
    class method_model {
        +is_method_supported(method)$
        +is_program_found()$
        +get_bin_env_var()$
        +supported_methods : list
    }
    class downloadable_model {
        +download(links, target)
        +check_model_path()
        +model_dir : str
    }
    class MKL_model
    class OMP_model
    class model_tree_node {
        +name : str
        +operator : str
        +children : list
        +model : model
        +weight : float
    }

    model <|-- ml_model
    model <|-- torch_model
    model <|-- tensorflow_model
    model <|-- method_model
    model <|-- downloadable_model
    model <|-- MKL_model
    model <|-- OMP_model
    model <|-- model_tree_node
    torch_model <|-- torchani_model
```

The root `model` class establishes the universal contract: every model must implement `predict()` and can optionally override `dump()`, `parse_args()`, and `set_num_threads()`. The `ml_model` subclass extends this with training capabilities (`train()`, `reset()`) and a comprehensive hyperparameter optimization framework that supports grid search, cross-validation, and holdout validation. The `method_model` class adds program-discovery logic — it can check whether a required external binary is available via environment variables and whether a given method string is in its `supported_methods` list. The `model_tree_node` class enables the construction of composite model expressions (e.g., delta-learning corrections like `AIQM1 + Δ-ML`) by combining child models with arithmetic operators.

Sources: [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L20-L137), [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L343-L420), [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L175-L207), [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L208-L313), [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L960-L994)

## Model Factory and Registry

The `models.py` module provides the central `methods()` factory function and a `known_classes` registry that together implement an auto-discovery pattern for computational methods. When `methods(method='AIQM1')` is called without specifying a program, the factory iterates through `known_classes` in priority order and returns the first class that both (a) has its required program installed and (b) supports the requested method string. This design allows users to write program-agnostic code while still supporting explicit program specification when needed.

The `known_classes` list is ordered by priority: `aiqm1 → aiqm2 → aiqm3 → dens → ani_methods → aimnet2_methods → mace_methods → ccsdtstarcbs → gaussian_methods → pyscf_methods → orca_methods → turbomole_methods → mndo_methods → sparrow_methods → xtb_methods → dftbplus_methods → columbus_methods → dftd3_methods → dftd4_methods → uaiqm → omnip2x → omnip1`. The module also provides `load()` / `load_json()` / `load_pickle()` functions for deserializing saved model objects, capable of reconstructing the full class hierarchy including nested `model_tree_node` structures.

Sources: [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L18-L20), [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L624-L627), [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L627-L693), [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L700-L766)

## Interface Layer

The `interfaces/` directory contains 25+ adapter modules, each wrapping an external computational program behind MLatom's `method_model` interface. These adapters follow a consistent structural pattern: they define a class (or classes) inheriting from `method_model`, specify `supported_methods`, implement program-discovery logic via `get_bin_env_var()`, and provide the `predict()` method that handles file I/O, subprocess invocation, and result parsing.

| Category | Interfaces | External Dependency |
|----------|-----------|-------------------|
| **Ab initio / DFT** | `gaussian_interface`, `orca_interface`, `pyscf_interface`, `turbomole_interface`, `columbus_interface` | Gaussian, ORCA, PySCF, Turbomole, Columbus |
| **Semiempirical** | `mndo_interface`, `sparrow_interface`, `xtb_interface`, `dftbplus_interface` | MNDO, Sparrow, xtb, DFTB+ |
| **ML Potentials** | `torchani_interface`, `mace_interface`, `dpmd_interface`, `physnet_interface`, `sgdml_interface`, `gap_interface`, `aimnet2_interface` | TorchANI, MACE, DPMD, PhysNet, sGDML, GAP, AIMNet2 |
| **Dispersion** | `dftd3_interface`, `dftd4_interface` | DFT-D3, DFT-D4 |
| **Simulation Tools** | `ase_interface`, `geometric_interface`, `pysisyphus_interface` | ASE, Geometric, PySisyphus |

The `ase_interface` deserves special mention as a cross-cutting integration layer — it converts MLatom's `molecule` objects to/from ASE's `Atoms` objects, enabling access to ASE's extensive ecosystem of optimizers, dynamics engines, and calculators. This is the bridge that allows MLatom's simulation engines to delegate to ASE when needed.

Sources: [interfaces/](mlatom/interfaces/), [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L175-L207), [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L624-L625)

## Simulation Engines

MLatom provides a suite of simulation engines, each implemented as a self-contained class that accepts a model and data objects, then drives an iterative computation loop.

**Geometry Optimization** (`simulations.py` → `optimize_geometry`): Supports multiple backends — internal ASE-based optimization, Gaussian's built-in optimizer, and the external Geometric program. It handles both minima and transition state searches, accepts constraints, and can dump trajectory data at configurable intervals. The class delegates model evaluation to the supplied model's `predict()` method at each optimization step.

**Frequency Analysis** (`simulations.py` → `freq`): Calculates harmonic vibrational frequencies via numerical differentiation of energy gradients (or analytical Hessians from external programs). It also provides IR and Raman intensity calculations through dipole and polarizability derivative evaluation. The `thermochemistry` class extends this with partition-function-based thermochemical analysis.

**Molecular Dynamics** (`md.py` → `md`): Implements velocity Verlet integration with support for NVE, NVT (Andersen, Nosé-Hoover, Langevin thermostats), and periodic boundary conditions. The `propagate()` method drives the main integration loop with configurable time steps, maximum propagation times, and trajectory dumping. Momentum elimination and angular momentum management are built in.

**Nonadiabatic Dynamics** (`namd.py` → `surface_hopping_md`): A full fewest-switches surface hopping (FSSH) implementation with Landau-Zener-based hopping (`LZBL` algorithm), multiple integrators for the electronic wavefunction (Butcher 5th order, Adams-Moulton 5th order, RK4), decoherence corrections (simple decay model), and frustrated hop handling. It supports multi-state potentials and outputs population analysis over trajectories.

Sources: [simulations.py](mlatom/simulations.py#L92-L405), [simulations.py](mlatom/simulations.py#L440-L613), [md.py](mlatom/md.py#L17-L264), [namd.py](mlatom/namd.py#L21-L178)

## Spectroscopy Module

The `spectra.py` module provides a complete spectroscopy toolkit built on top of the simulation results. The base `spectrum` class handles raw spectral data (x/y pairs), interpolation, normalization, and convolution with various broadening functions (Gaussian, Lorentzian). Specialized subclasses implement domain-specific logic:

- **`uvvis`**: UV-Vis spectra via single-point convolution (SPC) and nuclear ensemble approach (NEA)
- **`ir`**: IR spectra from vibrational frequencies and intensities
- **`raman`**: Raman spectra from vibrational frequencies and Raman activities
- **`spectrum_comparison`**: 15+ spectral similarity metrics including Pearson/Spearman correlation, Tanimoto coefficient, KL/Jeffery/JS divergence, Earth mover's distance, cosine similarity, and spectral information divergence

Sources: [spectra.py](mlatom/spectra.py#L17-L220), [spectra.py](mlatom/spectra.py#L539-L624), [spectra.py](mlatom/spectra.py#L626-L997)

## Fortran Backend (MLatomF)

The `MLatomF_src/` directory contains the original Fortran implementation of MLatom, which remains actively used for high-performance kernel ridge regression calculations. The main program (`MLatomF.f90`) handles tasks like descriptor generation (`getX`), model creation, accuracy estimation, and data sampling. It communicates with the Python layer through the `interface_MLatomF.py` bridge module, which manages subprocess execution, input file generation, and output parsing.

Key Fortran modules include `A_KRR.f90` (OpenMP-parallel kernel ridge regression), `A_KRR_kernel.f90` (kernel function implementations), `MLmodel.f90` (model lifecycle management), `dataset.f90` (data I/O), and `molDescr.f90` (molecular descriptors). The Python `kreg` model class can delegate training and prediction to MLatomF when specified via `ml_program='KREG_API'`, leveraging Fortran's superior performance for the matrix algebra-intensive KRR computations.

Sources: [MLatomF.f90](mlatom/MLatomF_src/MLatomF.f90#L69-L80), [interface_MLatomF.py](mlatom/interface_MLatomF.py#L13-L16), [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L343-L364)

## Add-ons System

The `addons/` directory hosts extended models that are distributed separately from the core package. These include `aiqm3` (the AIQM3 neural network potential), `uaiqm` (universal AIQM variants), and `omnip2x` (multi-state potentials for excited-state simulations). Each add-on is structured as a self-contained Python package with its own `__init__.py`, allowing independent versioning and optional installation. The core `models.py` references these add-ons in `known_classes`, and the `methods()` factory will use them if they are installed.

Sources: [addons/](mlatom/addons/), [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L624-L625)

## Cross-Cutting Concerns

Several architectural patterns recur across the entire codebase and are worth understanding before working with any specific subsystem.

**Dynamic property attachment**: Both the `molecule` and `model` classes use Python's `__setattr__` / `__getattr__` to allow arbitrary named properties. In `molecule`, this means calling `mol.some_property = value` creates a new property accessible as `mol.some_property`. This pattern avoids the need for extensive schema definitions but requires awareness that property names are not statically checked.

**Parallel execution**: The `run_in_parallel()` function in `simulations.py` provides a generic multiprocessing wrapper that distributes model predictions across CPU cores. Thread-level parallelism is managed through the `set_num_threads()` interface on model classes, with framework-specific implementations for PyTorch (`torch_model`), TensorFlow (`tensorflow_model`), OpenMP (`OMP_model`), and MKL (`MKL_model`).

**Serialization**: All core objects support JSON serialization via `dump()` methods. The `model_tree_node` class serializes its full tree structure recursively, enabling complex composite models (like delta-learning corrections) to be saved and restored. The `molecular_trajectory` class uses HDF5 for efficient binary serialization of large trajectory datasets.

Sources: [simulations.py](mlatom/simulations.py#L25-L92), [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L139-L171), [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L109-L116)

---

- To understand the data structures that flow through every computation, proceed to [Molecule and Atom Classes](6-molecule-and-atom-classes) and [Molecular Database Management](7-molecular-database-management)
- To learn how models are constructed, trained, and composed, read [Model Class Hierarchy](9-model-class-hierarchy) and [AIQM Methods and Delta Learning](11-aiqm-methods-and-delta-learning)
