| `ani_methods` | [torchani_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/torchani_interface.py#L1637-L1896) | `torchani_model` | ANI-1x, ANI-1ccx, ANI-2x, ANI-1x-D4, ANI-2x-D4 |

> [!TIP]
> The distinction between `ani` (trainable) and `ani_methods` (pre-trained) is intentional. `ani` supports `train()`, `save()`, and `load()` for building new ANI models from scratch, while `ani_methods` wraps pre-trained checkpoints for immediate prediction with named methods like `'ANI-2x'`. Both share the `torchani_model` mixin but serve fundamentally different workflows.

## The Model Tree: Composite and Delta-Learning Models

The `model_tree_node` class at [line 960](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/model_cls.py#L960-L1139) extends `model` to enable **composite model construction**—the mechanism behind delta learning, ensemble averaging, and weighted combinations of models. Each node in the tree has a `name`, optional `parent` and `children` references, an `operator` (one of `'sum'`, `'weighted_sum'`, `'average'`, or `'predict'`), and an optional `model` reference to a concrete model instance.

When `predict()` is called on a tree node at [line 994](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/model_cls.py#L994-L1083), the node recursively invokes prediction on all children, then applies its operator to combine their results. A leaf node (with `operator='predict'` and no children) simply delegates to its wrapped `model`. An internal node with `operator='sum'` adds the energy/gradient contributions of all children—this is the pattern used for delta-learning (e.g., AIQM1 = baseline semiempirical + Δ-ML correction). The `weighted_sum` operator applies per-child weights, while `average` divides the sum by the number of children.

The tree also handles **multi-state prediction** (`nstates > 1`), creating `properties_tree_node` objects on each molecule's `electronic_states` to track per-state property values. Thread configuration propagates recursively from parent to children through `set_num_threads()` at [line 985](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/model_cls.py#L985-L992).

Serialization of model trees is handled by the recursive `dump()` at [line 1120](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/model_cls.py#L1120-L1137), which produces nested JSON. The complementary `load_dict()` function in [models.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/models.py#L721-L764) reconstructs the full tree from such JSON by recursively deserializing children and the wrapped model.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Delta Learning: AIQM1 Structure"
        root["model_tree_node<br/>operator='sum'"]
        baseline["model_tree_node<br/>operator='predict'<br/>model = mndo_methods(method='OM2')"]
        delta["model_tree_node<br/>operator='predict'<br/>model = ani_nns_in_aiqm1"]
        root --> baseline
        root --> delta
    end
    
    subgraph "Weighted Ensemble"
        ens["model_tree_node<br/>operator='weighted_sum'"]
        m1["model_tree_node<br/>weight=0.7<br/>model = ani(method='ANI-2x')"]
        m2["model_tree_node<br/>weight=0.3<br/>model = kreg(model_file='...')"]
        ens --> m1
        ens --> m2
    end
```

## The `methods()` Factory and Model Resolution

The `methods()` function at [line 627](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/models.py#L627-L691) is the primary entry point for creating model instances by method name. It operates in two modes:

1. **Program-specified**: If `program` is provided (e.g., `program='gaussian'`), it looks up `gaussian_methods` in the module's global namespace and instantiates it with the requested `method`.
2. **Auto-discovery**: If only `method` is provided, it iterates over the `known_classes` list at [line 625](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/models.py#L625-L626), calling `is_program_found()` (to skip unavailable programs) and then `is_method_supported()` (to match the method name). The first class that claims the method wins, and the ordering of `known_classes` determines priority.

This factory pattern means that adding a new method model to MLatom requires only: (a) defining a class that extends `method_model`, (b) setting `supported_methods` as a class attribute, (c) implementing `predict()`, and (d) adding the class to `known_classes` in `models.py`.

## Summary: Architectural Principles

The model hierarchy follows three key design principles that developers extending MLatom should understand:

**Polymorphic uniformity**. Every model—whether a neural network, a Gaussian wrapper, or a composite delta-learning tree—satisfies the same `predict()` signature. This allows simulation workflows to accept any model without type checking.

**Composable mixins**. Backend-specific behavior (threading, downloading, method lookup) is factored into orthogonal mixin classes rather than embedded in monolithic base classes. A model like `kreg` combines four parents (`krr`, `OMP_model`, `MKL_model`) to inherit training logic and two independent threading strategies.

**Separation of trainability from predictability**. The split between `ml_model` (trainable) and `method_model` (pre-trained/wrapper) reflects a fundamental distinction: trainable models own their parameters and lifecycle, while method models are stateless delegates to external programs. The `model_tree_node` bridges both worlds by wrapping any model type in a composable graph.


# Kernel Ridge Regression Models



Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR) is a foundational machine learning method in MLatom for constructing molecular machine learning potentials and property predictors. MLatom provides two tightly integrated classes—`krr` for general-purpose kernel regression and `kreg` for molecular potentials built on the RE (Reverse Equilibrium) descriptor—each with multiple computational backends ranging from pure Python to high-performance Fortran compiled via NumPy bindings. This page documents their architecture, supported kernels, gradient learning, and backend strategies.

## Class Hierarchy and Architectural Overview

The KRR subsystem is built on two classes defined in [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L18-L555) that share a clear division of labor. The base class `krr` provides a generic kernel ridge regression implementation, while the specialized subclass `kreg` extends it with molecular-specific functionality: the RE descriptor, OMP (OpenMP) threading support, and MKL (Intel Math Kernel Library) acceleration through the `OMP_model` and `MKL_model` mixin classes from [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L163-L169).

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class model {
        +predict()
        +set_num_threads()
        +dump()
    }
    class ml_model {
        +train()
        +predict()
        +optimize_hyperparameters()
        +cross_validation()
        +holdout_validation()
    }
    class OMP_model {
        +set_num_threads()
    }
    class MKL_model {
        +set_num_threads()
    }
    class krr {
        +kernel_function: str
        +ml_program: str
        +hyperparameters: hyperparameters
        +train()
        +predict()
        +gaussian_kernel_function()
        +RE_descriptor_tensor()
    }
    class kreg {
        +equilibrium_molecule
        +ml_program: str = 'KREG_API'
        +hyperparameters: sigma, lambda
        +get_descriptor()
        +get_equilibrium_distances()
        +train()
        +predict()
    }
    class KREG_API {
        +sigma, lambdav, lambdagradxyz
        +kreg_api: KREG Fortran module
        +train()
        +predict()
        +save_model()
        +load_model()
    }
    class KRR_julia {
        +model: Julia krr object
        +train()
        +predict()
        +save_model()
        +load_model()
    }

    model <|-- ml_model
    model <|-- OMP_model
    model <|-- MKL_model
    ml_model <|-- krr
    krr <|-- kreg
    OMP_model <|-- kreg
    MKL_model <|-- kreg
    kreg ..> KREG_API : delegates to
    krr ..> KRR_julia : delegates to
```

The `kreg` class inherits from both `krr` (for regression logic) and `OMP_model`/`MKL_model` (for thread control), giving it access to the Fortran backend's parallel capabilities. When the `ml_program` parameter is set to `'KREG_API'`, the class delegates computation to the `KREG_API` wrapper in [kreg_api.py](mlatom/kreg_api.py#L11-L178), which interfaces with the compiled Fortran module in [KREG.f90](mlatom/fortran/KREG.f90#L1-L665).

## Supported Kernel Functions and Hyperparameters

The `krr` class supports four kernel functions, each with its own set of hyperparameters registered at initialization time in [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L50-L73):

| Kernel Function | Hyperparameters | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `Gaussian` | `sigma`, `lambda` | Standard radial basis function; `sigma` controls the kernel width (bandwidth) |
| `periodic_Gaussian` | `sigma`, `lambda`, `period` | Gaussian kernel with periodicity for angular/cyclic coordinates |
| `decaying_periodic_Gaussian` | `sigma`, `lambda`, `period`, `sigmap` | Periodic Gaussian with an additional decay envelope controlled by `sigmap` |
| `Matern` | `sigma`, `lambda`, `nn` | Matern family kernel; `nn` is the smoothness order (default 2) |

All hyperparameters are encapsulated as `hyperparameter` objects from [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L856-L905), carrying optimization metadata such as `minval`, `maxval`, and `optimization_space` (log or linear). The regularization parameter `lambda` (spelled `lambdav` in Fortran contexts) is always present with a default value of 2⁻³⁵ and a log-scale optimization range from 2⁻³⁵ to 1.0, as defined in [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L51-L58).

> [!TIP]
> The `kreg` subclass declares its own class-level `hyperparameters` at [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L354-L363) containing only `lambda` and `sigma`. This class-level definition serves as the default set, but instance-level `__init__` merges any user-provided hyperparameters via `self.hyperparameters.update(hyperparameters)`, so additional keys like `lambdaGradXYZ` can be injected at construction time.

## Backend Strategies: scipy, mlatom.jl, KREG_API, and MLatomF

MLatom routes KRR computation to one of four backends, selected via the `ml_program` constructor parameter. Each backend has distinct capabilities and trade-offs:

| Backend | `ml_program` value | Kernel functions | Gradient learning | Hessian | Threading | Implementation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SciPy | `'scipy'` | Gaussian (analytic derivatives via PyTorch) | ✓ (joint value+gradient) | ✗ | Single-threaded | Pure Python + SciPy/PyTorch |
| Julia | `'mlatom.jl'` | Gaussian, periodic_Gaussian, decaying_periodic_Gaussian, Matern | ✗ (values only) | ✗ | Julia threads | Julia via PyJulia |
| KREG API | `'KREG_API'` | Gaussian (RE descriptor) | ✓ (joint value+gradient) | ✓ | OpenMP | Fortran f2py + MKL/LAPACK |
| MLatomF | `'MLatomF'` | Gaussian (RE descriptor) | ✓ | ✓ | Varies | Standalone Fortran process |

### SciPy Backend

When `ml_program='scipy'`, the `krr.train()` method constructs the kernel matrix entirely in Python, starting at [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L157-L221). It subtracts the prior from training labels, builds the kernel matrix by evaluating the kernel function pairwise across all training geometries, adds the regularization term λ·I to the diagonal, then solves the linear system **Kα = y** using either Cholesky or LU decomposition from `scipy.linalg`. The default strategy tries Cholesky first and falls back to LU if the matrix is not positive definite—a pattern mirrored in the Fortran backend's `solveSysLinEqs` at [mathUtils.f90](mlatom/fortran/mathUtils.f90#L8-L33).

For gradient learning under the scipy backend, the kernel matrix is extended to include both energy and force blocks. The matrix dimension becomes `N_train + 3 × N_atoms × N_train`, with cross-terms encoding the kernel derivatives with respect to nuclear coordinates. These analytic derivatives are computed using PyTorch's autograd in the `gaussian_kernel_function` method at [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L286-L319), which leverages automatic differentiation through the RE descriptor computation in `RE_descriptor_tensor` at [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L321-L333).

### KREG_API Backend (Fortran via f2py)

The `KREG_API` class in [kreg_api.py](mlatom/kreg_api.py#L11-L178) wraps a compiled Fortran module that provides the highest performance for molecular potential construction. It selects the correct NumPy-version-specific binary at import time—either `fortran.np1.KREG` or `fortran.np2.KREG` based on the major NumPy version—in [kreg_api.py](mlatom/kreg_api.py#L6-L9).

The Fortran kernel in [KREG.f90](mlatom/fortran/KREG.f90#L1-L665) implements the full KREG workflow: RE descriptor computation, kernel matrix assembly with analytic value and gradient covariances, regression coefficient calculation, and prediction of energies, gradients (forces), and Hessians. Key functions include:

- **`kernel()`** at [KREG.f90](mlatom/fortran/KREG.f90#L87-L95): The Gaussian kernel `exp(-d²/(2σ²))` computed over RE descriptor space
- **`calc_RE_descriptors()`** at [KREG.f90](mlatom/fortran/KREG.f90#L257-L271): Batch computation of RE descriptors `R_eq/R_ij` for all training geometries
- **`calc_kernel_matrix()`** at [KREG.f90](mlatom/fortran/KREG.f90#L293-L346): Full kernel matrix assembly including value-value, value-gradient, and gradient-gradient covariances, with OpenMP parallelization (`!$OMP PARALLEL DO`)
- **`calcAlpha()`** at [KREG.f90](mlatom/fortran/KREG.f90#L598-L627): Solves the regularized linear system using LAPACK's Cholesky (`dpotrf`/`dpotrs`) with Bunch-Kaufman fallback (`dsytrf`/`dsytrs`) via [mathUtils.f90](mlatom/fortran/mathUtils.f90#L24-L31)
- **`predict()`** at [KREG.f90](mlatom/fortran/KREG.f90#L534-L596): Predicts energies, forces, and Hessians for new geometries with OpenMP parallelization over prediction points

> [!TIP]
> The Fortran backend uses separate regularization parameters for values (`lambdav`) and gradients (`lambdagradxyz`), applied independently to the diagonal blocks of the augmented kernel matrix in `calcAlpha()` at [KREG.f90](mlatom/fortran/KREG.f90#L617-L622). The `kreg` class maps its `lambda` hyperparameter to `lambdav` by default, but supports an optional `lambdaGradXYZ` key in the hyperparameters dict at [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L508-L509).

### Julia Backend

The Julia backend is accessible through two code paths. For the general `krr` class, the `KRR_julia` wrapper in [krr_julia.py](mlatom/krr_julia.py#L8-L97) loads the Julia implementation from [julia/krr.jl](mlatom/julia/krr.jl) and supports all four kernel functions (Gaussian, periodic Gaussian, decaying periodic Gaussian, Matern). For the molecular `kreg` class, the `KREG_julia` wrapper in [julia/kreg_julia.py](mlatom/julia/kreg_julia.py#L13-L234) loads the mirror implementation in [julia/KREG.jl](mlatom/julia/KREG.jl#L1-L247), which implements the identical RE descriptor and gradient kernel functions as the Fortran version. Both wrappers use `PyJulia` (`julia.Main`) for cross-language invocation.

## RE Descriptor: The Molecular Representation

The **RE descriptor** (Reverse Equilibrium descriptor) is the core molecular representation used by the `kreg` class. For a molecule with N atoms, it produces a vector of dimension N(N−1)/2, where each element is the ratio of an equilibrium interatomic distance to the current interatomic distance:

**RE_ij = R_eq_ij / R_ij**

This descriptor provides translational and rotational invariance by construction, and its derivatives with respect to nuclear coordinates are analytically computable—essential for force learning. The descriptor is computed in the Fortran backend by the `RE_descriptor` subroutine at [KREG.f90](mlatom/fortran/KREG.f90#L241-L255), using a precomputed atom-pair index array `ac2dArray` that maps atom indices to descriptor vector indices.

The equilibrium geometry can be provided explicitly via the `equilibrium_molecule` constructor argument, or automatically selected as the geometry with the lowest energy (or lowest `y` value) from the training database, as implemented in `get_equilibrium_molecule()` at [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L447-L457).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Training
        A[Training Database] --> B[Select Equilibrium Geometry]
        B --> C[Compute R_eq distances]
        A --> D[Compute R_ij for each geometry]
        C --> E[RE descriptor = R_eq / R_ij]
        D --> E
        E --> F[Build Kernel Matrix K]
        F --> G[Solve K + λI α = y]
        G --> H[Store α, X, R_eq, σ, λ]
    end
    subgraph Prediction
        I[New Geometry] --> J[Compute R_ij]
        J --> K[RE descriptor = R_eq / R_ij]
        K --> L[Compute k* = K X predict]
        L --> M[y* = k* · α + prior]
    end
    H --> R_eq
    R_eq --> K
    H --> α
    α --> M
```

## Training Workflow

The training workflow diverges depending on the selected backend. The `krr.train()` method at [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L76-L223) handles the `scipy` and `mlatom.jl` paths, while `kreg.train()` at [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L459-L521) adds the `KREG_API` and `MLatomF` paths. The common steps are:

1. **Data extraction**: Load xyz coordinates, descriptors, and target properties from the molecular database
2. **Prior subtraction**: Subtract the prior value (default 0.0, or `'mean'` for the training set mean) from reference values at [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L107-L125)
3. **Kernel matrix construction**: Compute the kernel matrix, optionally augmented with gradient blocks
4. **Linear system solution**: Solve (K + λI)α = y for regression coefficients
5. **Model persistence**: Save the model to an `.npz` file (scipy/Julia) or `.unf` file (MLatomF)

For the KREG_API backend, step 3 is delegated entirely to the Fortran `train` subroutine at [KREG.f90](mlatom/fortran/KREG.f90#L495-L532), which internally handles descriptor computation, kernel matrix assembly, and coefficient calculation. The Julia backend follows a similar delegation pattern through `KRR_julia.train()` at [krr_julia.py](mlatom/krr_julia.py#L13-L46).

## Prediction and Gradient Computation

Prediction follows the standard KRR formula: **y\*(x) = Σᵢ αᵢ K(x, xᵢ) + prior**. For models trained with gradients, the prediction formula extends to include gradient-weighted kernel terms, enabling analytic force prediction without numerical differentiation.

The `kreg.predict()` method at [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L523-L552) dispatches to the appropriate backend. The Fortran backend's `predict` subroutine at [KREG.f90](mlatom/fortran/KREG.f90#L534-L596) can simultaneously compute energies, forces, and full Hessians in a single call, with OpenMP parallelization over prediction points. The scipy backend iterates over molecules in Python at [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L258-L281), computing kernel vectors and their derivatives via PyTorch autograd.

## Prior Function

The prior acts as a baseline value subtracted during training and added back during prediction. Supported prior types are defined in [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L107-L125):

| Prior value | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `None` / `0` | Zero prior (raw regression) |
| `'mean'` | Mean of training target values |
| Float/Int | User-specified constant |
| NumPy array | 1-D array of per-property priors |

Both the Python (`krr`) and Fortran (`KREG_API`) backends implement prior handling during training at [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L107-L125) and [kreg_api.py](mlatom/kreg_api.py#L55-L62) respectively.

## Model Serialization

All Python-accessible backends use NumPy's `.npz` format for model persistence. The `KREG_API.save_model()` at [kreg_api.py](mlatom/kreg_api.py#L134-L150) stores sigma, Natoms, Xsize, RE descriptors, equilibrium distances, and regression coefficients. The `KRR_julia.save_model()` at [krr_julia.py](mlatom/krr_julia.py#L53-L66) additionally stores kernel type metadata and kernel-specific parameters. The MLatomF backend uses a proprietary `.unf` (unformatted Fortran) binary format via the `MLatomF` standalone executable interface.

## Navigating Further

- For the broader model class hierarchy that `krr` and `kreg` participate in, see [Model Class Hierarchy](9-model-class-hierarchy)
- To understand how hyperparameters like `sigma` and `lambda` are optimized, see [Hyperparameter Optimization](12-hyperparameter-optimization)
- For molecular databases that feed into KRR training, see [Molecular Database Management](7-molecular-database-management)
- For the Fortran backend internals beyond KRR, see [Fortran Backend MLatomF](28-fortran-backend-mlatomf)

# AIQM Methods and Delta Learning



This page documents MLatom's family of **Artificial Intelligence-Quantum Mechanical (AIQM)** methods and the underlying **delta learning** architecture that powers them. AIQM methods are composite computational approaches that combine low-cost quantum mechanics (QM) baselines with neural network corrections, achieving near-CCSD(T) accuracy at semiempirical cost. The implementation centers on a **model tree composition framework** expressed through the `model_tree_node` class, which orchestrates how baseline methods, ML corrections, and dispersion terms are combined.

## The Delta Learning Paradigm

Delta learning is a strategy in which a machine learning model is trained to predict the *difference* between a high-level reference method and a lower-level baseline method, rather than learning absolute properties directly. In MLatom's AIQM family, this manifests as a composite computational pipeline: a semiempirical or density functional baseline provides the bulk of the energy, while an ensemble of neural networks corrects the systematic errors of that baseline. The final prediction is the algebraic sum of all components, including an optional dispersion correction and an atomic energy shift.

The critical architectural insight is that **the user never interacts with the tree structure directly**. Each AIQM class (`aiqm1`, `aiqm2`) assembles its own model tree internally during initialization, and the `predict()` call simply traverses that tree. The `model_tree_node` class in [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L960-L1140) provides the recursive traversal logic, supporting operators such as `'sum'`, `'average'`, `'weighted_sum'`, and `'predict'` (leaf node invocation). Correspondingly, the `properties_tree_node` class in [data.py](mlatom/data.py#L1471-L1524) mirrors this tree structure on the molecular data side, accumulating energy, gradient, and hessian contributions from each child before reducing them with the appropriate operator.

Sources: [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L960-L1140), [data.py](mlatom/data.py#L1471-L1524)

## Model Composition Architecture

The following diagram illustrates how the model tree is structured for both AIQM methods, showing the relationship between the computational components and the operators that combine their outputs:

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "AIQM1 Model Tree"
        AIQM1_ROOT["aiqm1 (operator: sum)"]
        AIQM1_ROOT --> ANI_NNS["ani_nns (operator: average)"]
        AIQM1_ROOT --> SHIFT["atomic_energy_shift (operator: predict)"]
        AIQM1_ROOT --> ODM2STAR["odm2star (operator: predict)"]
        AIQM1_ROOT --> D4["d4_wb97x (operator: predict)"]
        ANI_NNS --> NN0["nn0 (predict)"]
        ANI_NNS --> NN1["nn1 (predict)"]
        ANI_NNS --> NDot["nn7 (predict)"]
        NDot -.->|"×8 models"| NN1
    end

    subgraph "AIQM2 Model Tree"
        AIQM2_ROOT["aiqm2 (operator: sum)"]
        AIQM2_ROOT --> NN_AVG["aiqm2_nn (operator: average)"]
        AIQM2_ROOT --> GFN2["gfn2xtbstar (operator: predict)"]
        AIQM2_ROOT --> D4B["d4wb97x (operator: predict)"]
        NN_AVG --> NN2_0["nn_0 (predict)"]
        NN_AVG --> NN2_1["nn_1 (predict)"]
        NN2_1 -.->|"×8 models"| NN2_0
    end
```

Both AIQM1 and AIQM2 share the same high-level pattern: an ensemble of neural networks provides the delta correction (averaged to reduce variance), a semiempirical baseline supplies the reference energy, and a D4 dispersion term adds long-range correction. The differences lie in the baseline method and the neural network architecture used.

Sources: [aiqm1.py](mlatom/aiqm1.py#L60-L75), [aiqm2.py](mlatom/aiqm2.py#L94-L99)

## AIQM1: ODM2*-Based Delta Learning

The `aiqm1` class in [aiqm1.py](mlatom/aiqm1.py#L15-L152) implements the original AIQM1 method as described in the [AIQM1 paper](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-27340-2). It inherits from both `torchani_model` and `method_model`, combining PyTorch-based neural network inference with the generic method dispatch machinery.

### Model Assembly

During initialization, `load_model()` constructs a four-component (or three-component, depending on variant) model tree [aiqm1.py](mlatom/aiqm1.py#L60-L75):

1. **Neural Network Ensemble** — Eight `ani_nns_in_aiqm1` instances are created (indices 0–7), each wrapped in a `model_tree_node` with `operator='predict'`. These are collected under a parent node with `operator='average'`, producing an ensemble-averaged ML correction.
2. **Atomic Energy Shift** — A constant per-element correction applied via the `atomic_energy_shift` class [aiqm1.py](mlatom/aiqm1.py#L153-L188). Different shift values are stored for the CC and DFT training targets.
3. **ODM2* Baseline** — The semiempirical ODM2* method, invoked through the generic `methods()` factory with `program` set to MNDO or Sparrow [aiqm1.py](mlatom/aiqm1.py#L70).
4. **D4 Dispersion** — The DFT-D4 dispersion correction with ωB97X functional, added for AIQM1 and AIQM1@DFT variants but **omitted** for AIQM1@DFT* (the asterisk convention indicates the dispersion term is absent) [aiqm1.py](mlatom/aiqm1.py#L72-L74).

The `@DFT` and `@DFT*` suffixed variants differ in which neural network weights and atomic energy shifts are loaded, corresponding to whether the NN was trained against DFT or CCSD(T) reference data. The `@DFT*` variant further excludes the D4 dispersion term.

### Neural Network Architecture

The `ani_nns_in_aiqm1` class [aiqm1.py](mlatom/aiqm1.py#L190-L335) defines a TorchANI-compatible architecture with element-specific networks for H, C, N, and O. The AEV (Atomic Environment Vector) computation uses the standard TorchANI `AEVComputer` with radial cutoff Rcr = 5.2 Å and angular cutoff Rca = 4.0 Å [aiqm1.py](mlatom/aiqm1.py#L205-L218). Each element has a dedicated feedforward network with GELU activations and element-specific hidden layer widths (H: 160→128→96, C: 144→112→96, N/O: 128→112→96) [aiqm1.py](mlatom/aiqm1.py#L250-L295).

### Supported Methods and Atomic Energies

AIQM1 supports three method variants, each with distinct per-element atomic energy references [aiqm1.py](mlatom/aiqm1.py#L43-L46):

| Method | Training Target | D4 Dispersion | Elements |
|--------|----------------|---------------|----------|
| `AIQM1` | CCSD(T)/CBS | ✓ | H, C, N, O |
| `AIQM1@DFT` | DFT (ωB97X/6-31G*) | ✓ | H, C, N, O |
| `AIQM1@DFT*` | DFT (ωB97X/6-31G*) | ✗ | H, C, N, O |

### Prediction Flow

When `predict()` is called, AIQM1 delegates to the model tree's recursive prediction engine. For single-atom molecules, a special-case path directly returns the stored atomic energy (with an ODM2*-based correction for non-standard charge/multiplicity states) [aiqm1.py](mlatom/aiqm1.py#L104-L115). For multi-atom molecules, the full model tree evaluates all components. After prediction, the standard deviation across the 8 NN ensemble members is computed and stored on the molecule object for uncertainty quantification [aiqm1.py](mlatom/aiqm1.py#L127-L140).

Sources: [aiqm1.py](mlatom/aiqm1.py#L15-L152), [aiqm1.py](mlatom/aiqm1.py#L153-L188), [aiqm1.py](mlatom/aiqm1.py#L190-L335)

## AIQM2: GFN2-xTB*-Based Delta Learning

The `aiqm2` class in [aiqm2.py](mlatom/aiqm2.py#L5-L199) represents the second generation of AIQM methods. It inherits from `method_model` and `downloadable_model`, reflecting its design as a self-contained, downloadable model package.

### Model Assembly

AIQM2's model tree has a simpler three-component structure assembled in the `load()` method [aiqm2.py](mlatom/aiqm2.py#L140-L195):

1. **GFN2-xTB* Baseline** — A semiempirical tight-binding method serving as the baseline, wrapped in a `model_tree_node` with `operator='predict'` [aiqm2.py](mlatom/aiqm2.py#L78-L84).
2. **Neural Network Ensemble** — Eight TorchANI model instances loaded from checkpoint files (`cv0.pt` through `cv7.pt`), wrapped in an `ani_wrapper` that silently removes unsupported prediction kwargs (dipole derivatives, polarizability derivatives), and combined under an `operator='average'` node [aiqm2.py](mlatom/aiqm2.py#L163-L189).
3. **D4 Dispersion** — Same DFT-D4/wB97X dispersion correction as in AIQM1 [aiqm2.py](mlatom/aiqm2.py#L86-L92).

The key architectural difference from AIQM1 is that AIQM2 does **not** include an explicit atomic energy shift component — the NN correction is trained to absorb whatever shifts are necessary. Additionally, AIQM2 provides a reloadable architecture: the `reload_baseline()`, `reload_dispersion()`, and `reload()` methods allow re-initializing individual tree components, which is useful when changing the working directory or reconfiguring external program paths [aiqm2.py](mlatom/aiqm2.py#L78-L99).

### Model Download and Storage

AIQM2 leverages the `downloadable_model` mixin [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L208-L313) for automatic model download from Zenodo and a mirror URL. The `check_model_path()` method first verifies whether model files already exist locally; if not, `download()` fetches and extracts the zip archive [aiqm2.py](mlatom/aiqm2.py#L155-L156). Two model variants exist — CC-trained and DFT-trained — each with its own download URL and model directory [aiqm2.py](mlatom/aiqm2.py#L142-L153).

### Supported Methods

| Method | Training Target | D4 Dispersion | Elements |
|--------|----------------|---------------|----------|
| `AIQM2` | CCSD(T) | ✓ | H, C, N, O |
| `AIQM2@DFT` | DFT | ✓ | H, C, N, O |
| `AIQM2@DFT*` | DFT | ✗ | H, C, N, O |

Sources: [aiqm2.py](mlatom/aiqm2.py#L5-L199), [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L208-L313)

## Model Tree Node: The Composition Engine

The `model_tree_node` class [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L960-L1140) is the structural backbone of all AIQM methods. It implements a tree data structure where each node either wraps a concrete model (leaf) or aggregates child results (branch). The `predict()` method [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L994-L1083) implements recursive depth-first evaluation:

**Leaf nodes** (`self.children is None and self.operator == 'predict'`) invoke the wrapped model's `predict()` directly, then transfer computed properties (energy, energy_gradients, hessian) from the molecule to a `properties_tree_node` attached to the molecule's attribute dictionary.

**Branch nodes** recursively call `predict()` on all children, then apply the specified operator to aggregate results. The `properties_tree_node` class [data.py](mlatom/data.py#L1471-L1524) provides three aggregation methods — `sum()` [L1484-L1492], `average()` [L1506-L1514], and `weighted_sum()` [L1494-L1504] — plus `standard_deviation()` [L1516-L1524] for uncertainty quantification across ensemble members.

> [!TIP]
> The model tree is evaluated **bottom-up**: leaf models compute first, then results bubble up through branch operators. The final molecular properties (energy, gradients, hessian) are only written back to the molecule object at the **root node** level via `update_molecular_properties()`, which means intermediate components store their results in `properties_tree_node` objects attached to the molecule's `__dict__` as named attributes (e.g., `mol.aiqm1_nn`, `mol.odm2star`). This design enables post-hoc analysis of individual component contributions.

### Supported Operators

| Operator | Behavior | Use in AIQM |
|----------|----------|-------------|
| `'predict'` | Leaf node: delegates to the wrapped model's `predict()` | Every leaf component |
| `'sum'` | Sums child property values element-wise | Top-level root node of AIQM1/AIQM2 |
| `'average'` | Computes mean across child property values | NN ensemble aggregation |
| `'weighted_sum'` | Weighted sum using per-child `weight` attribute | Not used in current AIQM methods |

### Multi-State Support

The model tree natively supports excited-state and multi-state calculations via the `nstates` and `current_state` kwargs. When `nstates > 1`, the prediction loop iterates over `molecule.electronic_states`, creating and evaluating a full `properties_tree_node` tree for each electronic state [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L1016-L1034). The `update_molecular_properties()` method then writes the current state's properties back to the parent molecule.

Sources: [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L960-L1140), [data.py](mlatom/data.py#L1471-L1524)

## Uncertainty Quantification via Ensemble Standard Deviation

Both AIQM1 and AIQM2 use an ensemble of 8 neural networks trained on different data splits (cross-validation). After prediction, the standard deviation across these 8 predictions is computed and stored as an uncertainty estimate. In AIQM1, this is done by calling `standard_deviation()` on the NN ensemble's `properties_tree_node` [aiqm1.py](mlatom/aiqm1.py#L136-L140]. In AIQM2, the same operation is performed on the NN component [aiqm2.py](mlatom/aiqm2.py#L138). The resulting `energy_standard_deviation` is accessible on the molecule object (e.g., `mol.aiqm1_nn.energy_standard_deviation` or `mol.aiqm2_model_nn.energy_standard_deviation`).

Sources: [aiqm1.py](mlatom/aiqm1.py#L136-L140), [aiqm2.py](mlatom/aiqm2.py#L138), [data.py](mlatom/data.py#L1516-L1524)

## Method Dispatch Through the Factory Function

The `methods()` factory function in [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L627-L691) is the unified entry point for creating any model instance, including AIQM methods. When `method='AIQM1'` is requested without a `program` argument, the factory iterates through `known_classes` [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L625-L625) — an ordered list where `aiqm1` and `aiqm2` appear first. Each class's `is_method_supported()` classmethod is checked against the requested method string, and the first match is instantiated. This priority ordering ensures that AIQM classes take precedence over more generic interfaces when method names overlap.

Sources: [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L624-L691)

## AIQM3 and UAIQM: Add-On Methods

AIQM3 ([addons/aiqm3/aiqm3.py](mlatom/addons/aiqm3/aiqm3.py#L5-L48)) and UAIQM ([addons/uaiqm/uaiqm.py](mlatom/addons/uaiqm/uaiqm.py#L16-L72)) are implemented as add-on stubs. When instantiated, they detect whether the requested method is in their `supported_methods` list and, if so, raise a `ValueError` directing the user to the Aitomic commercial platform at `MLatom.com/aitomic`. This indicates that AIQM3 and UAIQM are **proprietary extensions** with the same delta-learning architecture but not available in the open-source distribution.

UAIQM declares a notably broader set of supported methods spanning different baselines (`gfn2xtbstar`, `odm2star`, `wb97x631gp`, `wb97xdef2tzvpp`) and training targets (`dft`, `cc`) [addons/uaiqm/uaiqm.py](addons/uaiqm/uaiqm.py#L41-L41], suggesting a parameterized delta-learning framework where users can compose custom AIQM variants by selecting baseline and training data independently.

Sources: [addons/aiqm3/aiqm3.py](mlatom/addons/aiqm3/aiqm3.py#L5-L48), [addons/uaiqm/uaiqm.py](mlatom/addons/uaiqm/uaiqm.py#L16-L72)

## Comparison of AIQM Implementations

| Feature | AIQM1 | AIQM2 | AIQM3 / UAIQM |
|---------|-------|-------|---------------|
| **File** | [aiqm1.py](mlatom/aiqm1.py) | [aiqm2.py](mlatom/aiqm2.py) | [addons/](mlatom/addons/) (stub) |
| **Baseline** | ODM2* (MNDO/Sparrow) | GFN2-xTB* | Multiple options |
| **NN Framework** | TorchANI (custom AEV) | TorchANI (wrapper) | Proprietary |
| **NN Architecture** | Element-specific GELU FFN | TorchANI checkpoint | Proprietary |
| **Ensemble Size** | 8 | 8 | — |
| **Atomic Energy Shift** | Yes | No | — |
| **D4 Dispersion** | Yes (except `@DFT*`) | Yes (except `@DFT*`) | — |
| **Auto-Download** | Yes (via `downloadable_model`) | Yes (via `downloadable_model`) | No (proprietary) |
| **Reloadable Components** | No (full reload) | Yes (per-component) | — |
| **Element Coverage** | H, C, N, O | H, C, N, O | Expanded |
| **License** | Open source | Open source | Commercial (Aitomic) |

## Usage Patterns

Both AIQM1 and AIQM2 follow the same calling convention through MLatom's unified interface. The examples below demonstrate the standard workflow:

```python
import mlatom as ml

# --- AIQM1 example ---
mol = ml.data.molecule()
mol.read_from_xyz_file(filename='ethanol.xyz')
aiqm1 = ml.methods(method='AIQM1', qm_program='MNDO')
aiqm1.predict(molecule=mol, calculate_energy=True, calculate_energy_gradients=True)
energy = mol.energy
gradient = mol.energy_gradients
uncertainty = mol.aiqm1_nn.energy_standard_deviation

# --- AIQM2 example ---
mol2 = ml.data.molecule()
mol2.read_from_xyz_file(filename='ethanol.xyz')
aiqm2 = ml.methods(method='AIQM2')
aiqm2.predict(molecule=mol2, calculate_energy=True, calculate_energy_gradients=True, calculate_hessian=True)
energy2 = mol2.energy
gradient2 = mol2.get_energy_gradients()
hessian2 = mol2.hessian
uncertainty2 = mol2.aiqm2_model_nn.energy_standard_deviation
```

> [!TIP]
> Both AIQM1 and AIQM2 are restricted to molecules containing **only H, C, N, O** atoms. Attempting to predict on molecules with other elements will raise a `ValueError` [aiqm1.py](mlatom/aiqm1.py#L92-L96), [aiqm2.py](mlatom/aiqm2.py#L127-L130). For broader element coverage, consider the UAIQM add-on or universal ML potentials described in [Universal ML Potential Interfaces](15-universal-ml-potential-interfaces).

Sources: [aiqm1.py](mlatom/aiqm1.py#L17-L39), [aiqm2.py](mlatom/aiqm2.py#L7-L29)
