# Hyperparameter Optimization



Effective machine learning models depend critically on well-chosen hyperparameters. MLatom provides a unified, extensible hyperparameter optimization framework embedded directly within the `ml_model` superclass, enabling any trainable ML model to search its parameter space without external tooling. This system integrates seamlessly with the model's training and prediction lifecycle, supports multiple optimization algorithms and validation strategies, and exposes a clean declarative API for defining searchable parameter spaces.

## Architectural Overview

The hyperparameter optimization subsystem is built around four core components: the **`hyperparameter`** data class, the **`hyperparameters`** collection container, the **`optimize_hyperparameters()`** orchestration method on `ml_model`, and the **`calculate_validation_loss()`** evaluation engine. These four elements form a closed loop: hyperparameters define the search space, the optimizer proposes candidates, the validation loss evaluator scores them, and the loop iterates until convergence or exhaustion.

```mermaid
graph TD
    A["ml_model.optimize_hyperparameters()"] --> B{Algorithm Router}
    B -->|"grid / brute"| C["optimize_grid()"]
    B -->|"TPE"| D["hyperopt.tpe.suggest"]
    B -->|"scipy methods"| E["scipy.optimize.minimize"]
    
    C --> F["calculate_validation_loss()"]
    D --> F
    E --> F
    
    F --> G{Validation Strategy}
    G -->|Holdout| H["holdout_validation()"]
    G -->|Cross-validation| I["cross_validation()"]
    
    H --> J["model.train() → model.predict()"]
    I --> J
    
    J --> K["geomRMSE loss aggregation"]
    K --> F
    
    subgraph "Hyperparameter Definitions"
        L["hyperparameter"] --> M["hyperparameters (UserDict)"]
    end
    
    M --> A
    M -.->|"value updates"| F
    
    style A fill:#2d6a4f,color:#fff
    style F fill:#d4a373,color:#fff
    style L fill:#457b9d,color:#fff
    style M fill:#457b9d,color:#fff
```

Sources: [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L609-L728), [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L856-L955)

## The `hyperparameter` and `hyperparameters` Data Model

The `hyperparameter` class encapsulates a single tunable parameter with all metadata needed for search space definition. Each instance carries its current value, bounds (`minval`/`maxval`), a search space type (`optimization_space`), and a dtype enforcement mechanism. The `hyperparameters` container extends `collections.UserDict` to provide dict-like access while automatically wrapping bare values as `hyperparameter` instances.

The `optimization_space` field is particularly important: it controls how grid points are distributed and how the TPE sampler constructs its probability model. The value `'linear'` produces evenly spaced samples between bounds, while `'log'` produces logarithmically spaced samples — essential for parameters like regularization strength that span many orders of magnitude. The `dtype` field enforces type coercion on every value assignment, preventing silent type corruption during optimization iterations. When a `hyperparameter` is updated via `__setattr__`, the incoming value is cast through the dtype if it doesn't already match [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L875-L880).

The `hyperparameters` class provides transparent attribute access: reading `model.hyperparameters.sigma` returns the raw `.value` of the underlying `hyperparameter` object, while assigning `model.hyperparameters.sigma = 2.0` updates the `.value` in-place or creates a new wrapped instance [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L922-L941). The `.copy(keys=...)` method enables selective deep-copying of a subset of hyperparameters, which is used by `kreg.__init__` to create per-instance hyperparameter collections from the class-level defaults [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L380).

| Attribute | Type | Purpose |
|-----------|------|---------|
| `value` | `Any` | Current parameter value (dtype-enforced) |
| `optimization_space` | `str` | `'linear'` or `'log'` — controls search space geometry |
| `minval` / `maxval` | `Any` | Search boundaries for bounded optimization |
| `step` | `Any` | Step size for discrete search (reserved) |
| `choices` | `Iterable[Any]` | Discrete value set for categorical search |
| `dtype` | `Callable` | Type caster; auto-derived from initial value if `None` |
| `name` | `str` | Human-readable identifier for debugging output |

Sources: [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L856-L905), [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L907-L955)

## Model-Specific Hyperparameter Definitions

Each ML model class declares its own tunable hyperparameters with physically meaningful defaults and bounds. The **KRR** model (`krr`) maintains a registry of kernel-specific candidates and activates the relevant subset based on the `kernel_function` argument [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L50-L73). The **KREG** model (`kreg`) defines its hyperparameters as a class-level attribute, enabling shared defaults across all instances while supporting per-instance override via constructor arguments [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L354-L381).

The KREG class provides the most concrete example. It declares `lambda` (regularization) and `sigma` (kernel width) with logarithmic search spaces spanning [2⁻³⁵, 1.0] and [2⁻⁵, 2⁹] respectively. These bounds reflect the physical scale of molecular potential energy surfaces: regularization must be capable of approaching machine epsilon for well-conditioned problems, while the kernel width must accommodate both tightly bound and loosely scattered configurations. During `__init__`, the class-level `hyperparameters` is copied and then merged with any user-provided overrides, ensuring that instance mutations never contaminate the class default [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L380-L381).

The KRR model is more nuanced. It defines a dictionary of all possible hyperparameters — `sigma`, `lambda`, `sigmap`, `period`, and `nn` — and selects the active set based on kernel function type. Gaussian kernels activate `sigma`; periodic Gaussian kernels additionally activate `period`; decaying periodic Gaussian kernels add `sigmap`; Matern kernels use `nn` instead of `sigma` [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L50-L73).

| Model | Hyperparameter | Default | Search Space | Physical Role |
|-------|---------------|---------|--------------|---------------|
| `krr` (Gaussian) | `sigma` | 1.0 | log [2⁻⁵, 2⁹] | Gaussian kernel width |
| `krr` (any) | `lambda` | 2⁻³⁵ | log [2⁻³⁵, 1.0] | L2 regularization strength |
| `krr` (periodic) | `period` | 1.0 | log [2⁻⁵, 2⁹] | Periodic kernel period |
| `krr` (decaying periodic) | `sigmap` | 100.0 | log [2⁻⁵, 2⁹] | Periodic kernel width |
| `krr` (Matern) | `nn` | 2 | linear [1, 50] | Matern smoothness order |
| `kreg` | `sigma` | 1.0 | log [2⁻⁵, 2⁹] | Kernel width (RE descriptor) |
| `kreg` | `lambda` | 2⁻³⁵ | log [2⁻³⁵, 1.0] | Regularization (values + gradients) |

Sources: [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L50-L73), [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L354-L383)

## Optimization Algorithms

The `optimize_hyperparameters()` method routes to one of three algorithm families based on the `optimization_algorithm` argument. All three share a common interface: they accept an initial parameter vector, invoke `calculate_validation_loss()` as the objective function, and write the optimal parameter values back into `self.hyperparameters`.

### Grid Search

Grid search is implemented via the standalone `optimize_grid()` function, which uses a recursive coordinate descent over the parameter grid. For each parameter dimension, it fixes all other dimensions at their first values, sweeps the remaining parameter, and recurses inward until the final dimension is exhausted [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L819-L854). Grid resolution defaults to 9 points per dimension but is configurable via `optimization_algorithm_kwargs['grid_size']`. The grid spacing respects each hyperparameter's `optimization_space`: linear spaces use `np.linspace`, while log spaces use `np.logspace` with natural logarithm base [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L680-L686). Grid search does not respect `maximum_evaluations` — it exhaustively evaluates all grid points, making it suitable only for low-dimensional spaces or coarse preliminary sweeps.

### Bayesian Optimization (TPE)

The Tree-structured Parzen Estimator is available through the `hyperopt` library. When `optimization_algorithm='tpe'`, the system maps each hyperparameter's search space to a `hyperopt.hp` distribution: `'linear'` maps to `hp.uniform`, and `'log'` maps to `hp.loguniform` with bounds transformed through `np.log` [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L690-L722). The `hyperopt.fmin()` call uses `hyperopt.tpe.suggest` as the acquisition function and respects `maximum_evaluations` as the budget. This makes TPE the recommended algorithm for moderate-dimensional spaces (2–10 parameters) where the validation loss evaluation is expensive — such as training kernel ridge regression models on molecular databases with gradient learning.

### scipy.optimize Gradient-Based Methods

For problems where the loss landscape is relatively smooth, the framework delegates to `scipy.optimize.minimize` with any of 14 scipy methods: Nelder-Mead, BFGS, L-BFGS-B, Powell, CG, Newton-CG, TNC, COBYLA, SLSQP, trust-constr, dogleg, trust-krylov, and trust-exact [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L662-L671). Bounds are extracted from `minval`/`maxval` on each hyperparameter and passed directly to scipy. The `maximum_evaluations` parameter maps to scipy's `maxiter`. These methods are most effective when combined with log-space parameterization (since the loss surface is often smoother in log-space for kernel parameters) and when the number of hyperparameters is small enough for gradient estimation to be tractable.

| Algorithm | Family | Budget Control | Gradient Required | Best For |
|-----------|--------|---------------|-------------------|----------|
| `grid` / `brute` | Exhaustive | `grid_size` per dim | No | Coarse 1–3D sweeps |
| `tpe` | Bayesian | `maximum_evaluations` | No | Expensive 2–10D targets |
| `Nelder-Mead` | Derivative-free | `maximum_evaluations` | No | Noisy, non-smooth losses |
| `L-BFGS-B` | Quasi-Newton | `maximum_evaluations` | Approx. | Smooth bounded problems |
| `Powell` | Direction set | `maximum_evaluations` | No | Moderate dimensions |

Sources: [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L658-L727)

## Validation Loss Computation

The `calculate_validation_loss()` method is the objective function that all optimizers evaluate. Its default loss metric is a **geometric mean RMSE** (referred to internally as `geomRMSE`), which balances scalar properties (e.g., energies) and vectorial properties (e.g., gradients) on equal footing [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L577-L585). When both energy and gradient errors are available, the combined loss is `sqrt(RMSE_energy × RMSE_gradients)`; when only one is available, it reduces to the individual RMSE. This formulation ensures that neither error component dominates the optimization signal, which is critical for models trained on both energies and forces.

The method supports two validation strategies selected by the caller's arguments:

- **Holdout validation**: accepts separate `subtraining_*` and `validation_*` databases, trains on the subtraining set, predicts on the validation set, and computes the loss. This is routed through `holdout_validation()` [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L729-L740).
- **Cross-validation**: accepts `cv_splits_molecular_databases` (a list of pre-split folds), iterates over leave-one-out splits, trains on each subtraining combination, predicts on the held-out fold, and aggregates results. This is routed through `cross_validation()` [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L742-L770).

Critically, `calculate_validation_loss()` calls `self.reset()` after computing the error [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L590), which cleans up the trained model artifact. This prevents stale model files from interfering with subsequent optimization iterations — each evaluation starts from a clean slate. The entire `optimize_hyperparameters()` method further wraps its work in a `tempfile.TemporaryDirectory` context, redirecting model file writes to a temporary location so the original model file is never corrupted during search [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L658-L661).

For advanced use cases, a custom `validation_loss_function` callable can be provided along with `validation_loss_function_kwargs`, bypassing the default geomRMSE entirely [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L587-L588).

> [!TIP]
> When optimizing hyperparameters for models that learn both energies and gradients, the default geometric-mean RMSE ensures balanced treatment. If you need to weight energies more heavily (e.g., for thermochemistry), provide a custom `validation_loss_function` that applies your preferred weighting scheme.

Sources: [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L450-L607), [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L577-L585)

## CLI Integration and TPE Argument Parsing

The framework integrates with MLatom's input file system through `parse_hyperparameter_optimization()`, which translates TPE distribution specifications from the command line into `hyperparameter` objects. When the optimization algorithm is `'tpe'`, the parser expects hyperparameter specifications in hyperopt's DSL format — e.g., `loguniform(-35, 0)` or `uniform(0, 10)` — and extracts the space type and bounds from the string [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L432-L448). For log-space parameters, the raw bounds (which hyperopt expects in log₂ space) are transformed via `2**lb` and `2**hb` to produce absolute values for `minval` and `maxval` [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L443-L445).

The `mlatom_args._check_hyperopt()` method (in `args_class.py`) handles pre-validation of hyperopt-specific syntax before it reaches the model parser [args_class.py](mlatom/args_class.py#L691-L705). This two-stage parsing ensures that malformed hyperopt specifications are caught early with meaningful error messages.

## End-to-End Optimization Workflow

The complete optimization lifecycle proceeds as follows. The user defines hyperparameters on the model, provides training data and validation strategy, selects an algorithm, and invokes `optimize_hyperparameters()`. Internally, the system: (1) redirects model file I/O to a temporary directory, (2) iterates parameter proposals through the chosen algorithm, (3) for each proposal, sets hyperparameter values, trains the model on the subtraining set, predicts on the validation set, and computes the loss, (4) feeds the loss back to the optimizer, and (5) upon convergence, restores the original model file path, trains one final time with the optimal parameters, and stores the validation loss in `self.validation_loss` [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L726-L727).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Define model with hyperparameters"] --> B["Provide data + validation splits"]
    B --> C["Select optimization algorithm"]
    C --> D["Call model.optimize_hyperparameters()"]
    
    D --> E["Redirect model_file to tmpdir"]
    E --> F["Read initial parameter values"]
    F --> G["Propose candidate parameters"]
    G --> H["Set model.hyperparameters values"]
    H --> I["model.train() on subtraining set"]
    I --> J["model.predict() on validation set"]
    J --> K["Compute geomRMSE loss"]
    K --> L{"Converged or exhausted?"}
    
    L -- "No" --> G
    L -- "Yes" --> M["Restore original model_file"]
    M --> N["Final train + predict with optimal params"]
    N --> O["Store model.validation_loss"]
    
    style A fill:#457b9d,color:#fff
    style D fill:#2d6a4f,color:#fff
    style O fill:#e76f51,color:#fff
```

Sources: [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L609-L728), [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L658-L661)

## Practical Considerations

**Temporary directory isolation** is a critical safety mechanism. During optimization, the model's `model_file` attribute is redirected to `tmpdirname/saved_name` inside a `with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()` block [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L658-L661). This ensures that intermediate model files — which may be large kernel matrices or regression coefficient arrays — are automatically cleaned up when the search completes, regardless of success or failure. The original `model_file` is restored before the method returns [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L724).

**Model reset between iterations** is enforced by `self.reset()` at the end of each `calculate_validation_loss()` call [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L590). For KREG models using the KREG_API backend, this calls `clean_up()` which re-invokes `__init__()` to deallocate all Fortran arrays [kreg_api.py](mlatom/kreg_api.py#L174-L175). Without this reset, stale kernel matrices and alpha coefficients from previous iterations would corrupt subsequent training runs.

**Debug output** can be activated by passing `debug=True` to either `calculate_validation_loss()` or `optimize_hyperparameters()`. When enabled, each evaluation prints the current hyperparameter values and the computed validation loss [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L599-L602).

> [!TIP]
> For production hyperparameter optimization runs, start with a coarse grid search (grid_size=5) to identify the approximate region of the minimum, then refine with TPE (maximum_evaluations=100–500) for precise convergence. This two-stage approach dramatically reduces total evaluation count compared to pure TPE with a wide initial search space.

Sources: [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L658-L661), [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L590), [kreg_api.py](mlatom/kreg_api.py#L174-L175)

## Navigation

This page covered the hyperparameter optimization framework at its architectural core. To understand how these optimized hyperparameters flow into model training, see [Kernel Ridge Regression Models](10-kernel-ridge-regression-models). For strategies on preparing the cross-validation splits consumed by this system, consult [Data Sampling and Cross-Validation Strategies](25-data-sampling-and-cross-validation-strategies). To learn how optimized models are re-used through serialization, proceed to [Transfer Learning and Model Fine-Tuning](13-transfer-learning-and-model-fine-tuning).

# Transfer Learning and Model Fine-Tuning



This page documents how MLatom enables **transfer learning** — reusing knowledge from pretrained models to accelerate training on new chemical domains — and **model fine-tuning** — selectively adjusting portions of an existing model to adapt it to target tasks. These capabilities are critical for molecular machine learning, where generating high-level reference data (e.g., CCSD(T)) is expensive and data-efficient learning strategies directly impact research throughput.

## Architectural Overview

MLatom implements transfer learning through two complementary mechanisms: **neural network fine-tuning** (applicable to TorchANI, PhysNet, and MACE models) and **delta learning via model composition** (the `model_tree_node` system). The former operates at the parameter level within a single model architecture, while the latter composes multiple models arithmetically at prediction time. Both approaches are grounded in MLatom's unified model class hierarchy, where `ml_model` defines the `train()`/`predict()`/`load()`/`save()` contract and each interface specializes these methods.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    direction TB
    class model {
        +predict()
        +set_num_threads()
    }
    class ml_model {
        +train()
        +predict()
        +load()
        +save()
        +reset()
    }
    class torch_model {
        +set_num_threads()
        +config_multiprocessing()
    }
    class tensorflow_model {
        +set_num_threads()
    }
    class ani {
        +train(reset_parameters, reset_network, reset_optimizer, reset_energy_shifter, check_point, use_last_model)
        +load(model_file, reset_parameters, method)
        +fix_layers(layers_to_fix)
        +NN_initialize()
        +load_ani_model(method)
        +NN_setup()
        +optimizer_setup()
    }
    class msani {
        +train(reset_parameters, reset_network, reset_optimizer, reset_energy_shifter)
        +load(model_file, reset_parameters, method)
        +fix_layers(layers_to_fix)
    }
    class physnet {
        +train(check_point, use_last_model)
        +load(model_file)
        +save(model_file)
        +reset()
    }
    class mace {
        +train(hyperparameters)
        +load(model_file)
        +save(model_file)
    }
    class model_tree_node {
        +predict()
        +operator: str
        +parent: model_tree_node
        +children: list
    }
    class downloadable_model {
        +download(download_links, target)
        +check_model_path(model_dir, model_files)
    }

    model <|-- ml_model
    model <|-- model_tree_node
    model <|-- downloadable_model
    ml_model <|-- torch_model
    ml_model <|-- tensorflow_model
    torch_model <|-- ani
    torch_model <|-- msani
    tensorflow_model <|-- physnet
    ml_model <|-- mace

    ani ..> model_tree_node : composable via
    physnet ..> model_tree_node : composable via
    mace ..> model_tree_node : composable via
```

## Pretrained Model Loading

The entry point for any transfer learning workflow is loading a pretrained model. MLatom provides two distinct loading paths: loading a saved custom model from disk, and loading a published universal ML potential (e.g., ANI-1x, ANI-1ccx, ANI-2x). The `downloadable_model` mixin class further automates the acquisition of pretrained model files by checking standard filesystem locations (`$MODELSPATH`, `[mlatom_dir]/mlatom_models/`, `~/.mlatom/models/`) and downloading from remote URLs when necessary [Sources: [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L208-L340)].

For **TorchANI models**, the `ani.load()` method accepts a `.pt` model file and deserializes the complete model state — AEV computer parameters, network architecture dictionaries, energy shifter, and neural network weights. Crucially, it accepts a `reset_parameters` flag that, when `True`, triggers `NN_initialize()` to re-randomize all network weights via Kaiming normal initialization while preserving the architecture. This enables the "load architecture, train from scratch" pattern. Alternatively, `load_ani_model(method)` loads a named pretrained model (ANI-1x, ANI-1ccx, ANI-2x) directly from TorchANI's built-in model zoo, setting up `species_order`, `aev_computer`, `networkdict`, and `energy_shifter` automatically [Sources: [torchani_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/torchani_interface.py#L204-L312)].

For **MACE models**, the loading path is simpler — `mace.load()` uses `torch.load()` to deserialize the model state dict and maps it to the configured device. MACE's `train()` method always constructs a fresh model from the training data's `z_table` and hyperparameters, meaning fine-tuning with MACE requires re-initialization from data statistics rather than warm-starting from weights [Sources: [mace_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/mace_interface.py#L245-L248)].

For **PhysNet models**, `physnet.load()` restores from a directory containing TensorFlow checkpoint files (`best_model.ckpt`) alongside metadata (`best_loss.npz`, `NAS.npz`). If `self.model` already exists when `train()` is called, PhysNet **reuses the existing model** rather than constructing a new one, enabling natural fine-tuning from a loaded checkpoint [Sources: [physnet_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/physnet_interface.py#L170-L202)].

| Model Interface | Load Format | Reset Weights on Load | Reuses Model in `train()` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ani` / `msani` | `.pt` (TorchANI dict) | Via `reset_parameters=True` | Yes, with optional resets |
| `mace` | `.pt` (PyTorch state) | No built-in flag | No — always rebuilds |
| `physnet` | Directory (TF checkpoint) | No built-in flag | Yes — if `self.model` exists |

## Neural Network Fine-Tuning Strategies

### Selective Layer Freezing

The most granular fine-tuning mechanism in MLatom is **per-element layer freezing**, implemented exclusively in the TorchANI `ani` and `msani` classes via the `fix_layers()` method. This method accepts a specification of which linear layers should be made non-trainable (`requires_grad=False`) for each elemental sub-network, enabling strategies such as freezing lower-level feature extractors while keeping higher-level output layers adaptive [Sources: [torchani_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/torchani_interface.py#L704-L770)].

The method operates on TorchANI's named parameter structure (`{species}.{layer_index}.{weight_or_bias}`) and interprets layer indices relative to the `Linear` layers within each elemental sub-network. When a single list is provided, it is broadcast across all species. When a list of lists is provided, each sub-list targets a specific element in `species_order`.

> [!TIP]
> Layer freezing is invoked **during** `train()` when the `hyperparameters` dict contains a `'fixed_layers'` key. The check occurs after confirming `self.model` exists but before training begins, making it a natural hook for transfer learning workflows. The AEV computation layers (index 0 in the outer `Sequential`) are unaffected since they operate on indices within each elemental sub-network.

### Training Control Flags

The `ani.train()` and `msani.train()` methods expose a comprehensive set of flags that control what gets reset — and what gets preserved — when fine-tuning begins on a loaded model:

| Flag | Effect | Use Case |
|---|---|---|
| `reset_parameters` | Re-initializes all network weights via `NN_initialize()` (Kaiming normal) | Architecture transfer without weight reuse |
| `reset_network` | Reconstructs the neural network entirely via `NN_setup()` | Architecture change during fine-tuning |
| `reset_optimizer` | Re-creates the optimizer via `optimizer_setup()` | New learning rate schedule on existing weights |
| `reset_optim_state` | Clears optimizer momentum/adaptive state | Prevents stale gradient statistics |
| `reset_energy_shifter` | Replaces or clears the atomic self-energy shifter | New chemical domain with different atomization energies |
| `check_point` | Path to a checkpoint file; loads both model weights and optimizer state | Resume interrupted training |
| `use_last_model` | If `False`, restores best validation model at end; if `True`, keeps last epoch | Controlling final model selection |

These flags compose independently. For example, a standard fine-tuning workflow would load a pretrained model (preserving all weights) and call `train()` with `reset_optimizer=True` (fresh Adam/SGD state) and `reset_energy_shifter=True` (recalibrate for new domain), while leaving `reset_parameters=False` and `reset_network=False` [Sources: [torchani_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/torchani_interface.py#L313-L430)].

The energy shifter deserves special attention: it stores per-element self-energies that serve as a baseline correction. When transferring between chemical domains (e.g., from organic molecules to organometallics), `reset_energy_shifter=True` causes MLatom to recompute or clear these values. If a list is provided, a new `EnergyShifter` is constructed from those values; if a `torchani.utils.EnergyShifter` instance is provided, it replaces the existing one directly [Sources: [torchani_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/torchani_interface.py#L367-L373)].

### PhysNet Fine-Tuning via Model Persistence

PhysNet follows a simpler but effective fine-tuning path. Since `train()` checks `if not self.model` before constructing a new `NeuralNetwork`, any previously loaded model is reused with its learned weights intact. The `check_point` parameter enables resuming training from a saved checkpoint, restoring both model weights and optimizer state. The `use_last_model` flag controls whether the final model in memory is the best-validation model or the model from the final epoch [Sources: [physnet_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/physnet_interface.py#L221-L300)].

PhysNet also performs neural architecture search (NAS) statistics normalization (`Eshift`, `Escale`) from the training data on every `train()` call, which implicitly adapts the output scaling to the new domain even when weights are preserved [Sources: [physnet_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/physnet_interface.py#L252-L253)].

## Delta Learning via Model Composition

Beyond parameter-level fine-tuning, MLatom provides a **delta learning** framework through the `model_tree_node` class. This enables building models of the form `E_target = E_base + ΔE`, where `E_base` is a pretrained lower-level method and `ΔE` is a learned correction. This is the architectural foundation of AIQM methods and similar composite approaches documented in [AIQM Methods and Delta Learning](11-aiqm-methods-and-delta-learning) [Sources: [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L960-L1040)].

The `model_tree_node` class implements a tree structure where each node holds either a child `model` or a set of child nodes. Each node carries an `operator` string (e.g., `'+'`, `'-'`) that determines how predictions from its children are combined. During prediction, the tree is traversed recursively: leaf nodes invoke their model's `predict()`, and parent nodes combine child results using the specified operator.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "Delta Learning Model Tree"
        root["model_tree_node\noperator='+'\nname='AIQM'"]
        base["model_tree_node\nmodel=ani_method('ANI-2x')\nname='base'"]
        delta["model_tree_node\nmodel=krr()\nname='delta'"]
        root --> base
        root --> delta
    end

    subgraph "Prediction Flow"
        P1[Input molecule] --> P2[base.predict → E_base]
        P1 --> P3[delta.predict → ΔE]
        P2 --> P4["E_target = E_base + ΔE"]
        P3 --> P4
    end

    root -.-> P1
```

The prediction pipeline stores intermediate results on the molecule object itself using the node's `name` attribute, enabling parent nodes to access child results without explicit return value threading. For multi-state calculations, the tree traversal extends across electronic states [Sources: [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L994-L1090)].

This design means delta models can mix model types freely — a neural network base (ANI, MACE, PhysNet) can be corrected by a kernel ridge regression delta, or vice versa. The only requirement is that all models in the tree produce compatible output properties.

## Practical Workflow: Fine-Tuning a Pretrained ANI Model

The following flowchart illustrates a complete fine-tuning workflow, from loading a pretrained universal potential through selective training to deployment:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Load pretrained ANI model\nani.load_ani_model('ANI-2x')"] --> B{"Select strategy"}
    B -->|Full fine-tuning| C["Train on target data\nreset_optimizer=True\nreset_energy_shifter=True"]
    B -->|Frozen lower layers| D["Fix layers\nani.fix_layers([[0, 2]])\nthen train()"]
    B -->|Architecture only| E["Reset weights\ntrain(reset_parameters=True)"]
    B -->|Delta learning| F["Build model_tree_node\nbase=ANI-2x, delta=KRR"]
    C --> G["Validate & select model"]
    D --> G
    E --> G
    F --> G
    G --> H["Save or deploy\nmodel.save(model_file)"]
```

## Model Persistence and Checkpointing

All trainable models in MLatom support `save()` and `load()` for serialization. TorchANI models save as `.pt` files containing the complete state (AEV computer, network dict, energy shifter, optimizer state). PhysNet saves as directories containing TensorFlow checkpoints and metadata. MACE saves as `.pt` files via `torch.save()`.

The `ani` and `msani` classes additionally support `save_every_epoch` and `save_epoch_interval` parameters during training, enabling the creation of epoch-level checkpoints. Combined with `check_point` loading, this provides full training resumption capability — essential for long-running fine-tuning jobs on GPU clusters [Sources: [torchani_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/torchani_interface.py#L313-L336)].

## Integration with Hyperparameter Optimization

When fine-tuning, the interplay between transfer learning controls and hyperparameter optimization becomes important. The `ml_model` base class provides `optimize_hyperparameters()` and `calculate_validation_loss()` methods that search over `hyperparameters` objects. During optimization, each evaluation invokes a full `train()` → `predict()` → `loss()` cycle. Fine-tuning flags (`reset_optimizer`, `reset_energy_shifter`) are orthogonal to this process — they control *initialization behavior*, while hyperparameter optimization controls *search behavior*. Practitioners should typically fine-tune with `reset_optimizer=True` during hyperparameter search to ensure each evaluation starts from a consistent optimizer state [Sources: [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L609-L728)].

## Summary: Transfer Learning Capability Matrix

| Capability | `ani` / `msani` | `physnet` | `mace` | `kreg` / `krr` |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Load pretrained model | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Fine-tune from weights | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ |
| Per-element layer freezing | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ | N/A |
| Reset weights, keep architecture | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ | N/A |
| Reset optimizer state only | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ | N/A |
| Reset energy shifter | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ | N/A |
| Checkpoint resume | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ | N/A |
| Delta learning composition | ✓ (via tree) | ✓ (via tree) | ✓ (via tree) | ✓ (via tree) |
| Universal model zoo loading | ✓ (ANI-1x/1ccx/2x) | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ |

For deeper exploration of how these mechanisms connect to specific methods, see [Model Class Hierarchy](9-model-class-hierarchy) for the inheritance structure, [AIQM Methods and Delta Learning](11-aiqm-methods-and-delta-learning) for production delta-learning workflows, and [Hyperparameter Optimization](12-hyperparameter-optimization) for search strategies during fine-tuning.

# Quantum Chemistry Program Interfaces



MLatom provides a unified abstraction layer over a diverse ecosystem of quantum chemistry programs, enabling any supported external method to be invoked through a single consistent API. Whether you need a ground-state DFT single point, excited-state gradients for nonadiabatic dynamics, or spin-orbit coupling vectors, the interface architecture routes your request to the correct program, translates molecular data into its input format, executes the calculation, and parses results back into MLatom's standard molecule objects. This page dissects the architectural patterns, dispatch mechanism, property coverage, and practical usage of every interfaced quantum chemistry program.

## Architectural Overview

All quantum chemistry program interfaces inherit from a common base class hierarchy rooted in the `model` class at [model_cls.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/model_cls.py#L20-L137). The critical intermediate class is `method_model`, which extends `model` with introspection capabilities specific to external chemistry programs: method validation, binary discovery via environment variables, and structured error reporting.

Sources: [model_cls.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/model_cls.py#L175-L206)

The dispatch mechanism lives in the `models.methods()` factory function, which resolves a method name (with an optional program hint) to the correct interface class. When called without `program`, it iterates through `known_classes` in priority order—the first class whose `is_program_found()` returns `True` and whose `is_method_supported()` matches the requested method wins. This priority ordering is defined at [models.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/models.py#L624-L625) and determines default behavior when multiple programs support the same method name.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    direction TB
    
    class model {
        +nthreads: int
        +set_num_threads(nthreads)
        +predict(molecular_database, molecule, ...)
        +dump(filename, format)
    }
    
    class OMP_model {
        +set_num_threads(nthreads)
    }
    
    class MKL_model {
        +set_num_threads(nthreads)
    }
    
    class method_model {
        +bin_env_name: str
        +supported_methods: list
        +is_method_supported(method)$ bool
        +is_program_found()$ bool
        +get_bin_env_var()$ str
        +raise_unsupported_method_error(method)$
    }
    
    class gaussian_methods {
        +method: str
        +chkfilename: str
        +predict(..., nstates, gaussian_keywords)
    }
    
    class orca_methods {
        +bin_env_name: "orcabin"
        +solvent, solvation_model
        +predict(..., active_space, casscf_kwargs)
    }
    
    class pyscf_methods {
        +supported_methods: list
        +predict_for_molecule(...)
        +predict_for_molecule_DM21(...)
        +check_convergence(...)
    }
    
    class columbus_methods {
        +bin_env_name: "COLUMBUS"
        +level_of_theory: str
        +predict(..., nsinglets, ntriplets, calculate_nacv, calculate_soc)
    }
    
    class turbomole_methods {
        +predict(method='ADC(2)', ...)
        +set_num_threads(nthreads)
    }
    
    class mndo_methods {
        +bin_env_name: "mndobin"
        +supported_methods: list
        +predict(..., read_density_matrix)
    }
    
    class dftbplus_methods {
        +generate_dftbplus_input(...)
        +parse_output(...)
    }
    
    class xtb_methods {
        +supported_methods: list
        +predict(..., calculate_dipole_derivatives)
        +error_handle(stds)
    }
    
    model <|-- OMP_model
    model <|-- MKL_model
    model <|-- method_model
    OMP_model <|-- orca_methods
    OMP_model <|-- dftbplus_methods
    OMP_model <|-- xtb_methods
    OMP_model <|-- dftd4_methods
    method_model <|-- gaussian_methods
    method_model <|-- orca_methods
    method_model <|-- columbus_methods
    method_model <|-- turbomole_methods
    method_model <|-- mndo_methods
    method_model <|-- dftbplus_methods
    method_model <|-- xtb_methods
    method_model <|-- dftd3_methods
    method_model <|-- dftd4_methods
```

The inheritance pattern reveals two distinct design strategies. **External-process interfaces** (Gaussian, ORCA, COLUMBUS, Turbomole, MNDO, xTB, DFTB+) inherit from `method_model` and communicate with the quantum chemistry program through file I/O and subprocess execution. **Library interfaces** (PySCF) operate entirely in-process, importing the target program as a Python package and calling its API directly—this is reflected by the `OMP_pyscf` subclass that handles OpenMP thread configuration through PySCF's own runtime settings.

Sources: [pyscf_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/pyscf_interface.py#L23-L52), [model_cls.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/model_cls.py#L169-L174)

## The Method Dispatch Mechanism

The `models.methods()` function is the single entry point for creating any quantum chemistry model instance. Its resolution logic operates in two phases, controlled by whether the `program` argument is provided.

When `program` is specified, the function constructs a class name string (`f'{program.casefold()}_methods'`) and looks it up in the module globals. If found, it instantiates the class with the provided method and keyword arguments. When `program` is omitted, the function iterates through `known_classes` (a priority-ordered list) and for each class: skips it if it lacks `is_method_supported`; skips it if `is_program_found()` returns `False` (meaning the environment variable for its binary is not set); and returns the first class where `is_method_supported(method)` matches. If no class matches, it raises a descriptive `ValueError` listing three possible causes: method name misspelling, program not installed, or need for explicit `program` specification.

Sources: [models.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/models.py#L627-L691)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["models.methods(method, program, **kwargs)"] --> B{program specified?}
    B -- Yes --> C["Resolve '{program}_methods' class from globals"]
    C --> D["Instantiate with method + kwargs"]
    B -- No --> E["Iterate known_classes in priority order"]
    E --> F{class has is_method_supported?}
    F -- No --> E
    F -- Yes --> G{is_program_found? == False}
    G -- Yes --> E
    G -- No/None --> H{is_method_supported?}
    H -- No --> E
    H -- Yes --> I["Instantiate class(method=method, **kwargs)"]
    D --> J["Return model instance"]
    I --> J
    E -- exhausted --> K["Raise ValueError"]
```

The `method_model` base class provides three class methods that power this dispatch. `is_method_supported()` checks the class's `supported_methods` list using case-insensitive comparison. `is_program_found()` checks whether the class's `bin_env_name` exists as an environment variable. `get_bin_env_var()` returns the environment variable's value or `None`. For in-process interfaces like PySCF that don't rely on external binaries, `is_program_found()` may return `None` (meaning "not applicable"), which the dispatch loop treats as a pass-through rather than a rejection.

Sources: [model_cls.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/model_cls.py#L176-L203)

> [!TIP]
> The `known_classes` list order in [models.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/models.py#L624-L625) acts as a **precedence chain**. When multiple installed programs support the same method name (e.g., both MNDO and Sparrow support `PM6`), whichever appears first in the list wins. If you need to override the default, always pass `program=` explicitly.

## Program Interface Catalog

The following table provides a consolidated reference of every quantum chemistry program interface, its discovery mechanism, supported methods, and property calculation capabilities. Interfaces marked with "In-process" execute as Python library calls rather than subprocess launches.

Sources: [models.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/models.py#L636-L660), [gaussian_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/gaussian_interface.py#L19-L47), [orca_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/orca_interface.py#L23-L67), [pyscf_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/pyscf_interface.py#L31-L92), [columbus_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/columbus_interface.py#L13-L42), [turbomole_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/turbomole_interface.py#L20-L52), [mndo_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/mndo_interface.py#L37-L78), [dftbplus_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/dftbplus_interface.py#L33-L60), [xtb_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/xtb_interface.py#L19-L76), [dftd3_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/dftd3_interface.py#L20-L48), [dftd4_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/dftd4_interface.py#L18-L44)

| Interface | Class | Discovery | Execution | Method Examples | Key Capabilities |
|-----------|-------|-----------|-----------|-----------------|------------------|
| **Gaussian** | `gaussian_methods` | `GAUSS_EXEDIR` env var | Subprocess | `B3LYP/6-31G*`, TD-DFT, ab initio | Multi-state TD-DFT, Hessian, dipole derivatives, external potential mode |
| **ORCA** | `orca_methods` | `orcabin` env var | Subprocess | `TD-wb97x/def2-SVP`, `qd-nevpt2`, `CCSD(T)*/CBS` | TD-DFT/TDA, QD-NEVPT2, CASSCF, solvation (SMD/CPCM), per-state gradients |
| **PySCF** | `pyscf_methods` | Python import (In-process) | In-process | `HF`, `MP2`, `CCSD`, `CCSD(T)`, `FCI`, `CISD`, `DM21*` | Full wavefunction methods, convergence check, DM21 functionals |
| **COLUMBUS** | `columbus_methods` | `COLUMBUS` env var | Subprocess (`runc`) | `CASSCF`, `MRCI` | NACV, SOC, singlet/triplet multi-state, MO coefficient export |
| **Turbomole** | `turbomole_methods` | `TURBODIR` env var | Subprocess (`dscf`+`ricc2`) | `ADC(2)`, CASSCF | Multi-state gradients via module pipeline |
| **MNDO** | `mndo_methods` | `mndobin` env var | Subprocess | `ODM2*`, `OM2`, `OM3`, `PM3`, `MNDO/d`, `SCC-DFTB` | Semiempirical OMx/NDDO, density matrix reading |
| **DFTB+** | `dftbplus_methods` | `dftbplusbin` env var | Subprocess | `DFTB` | Slater-Koster file management, SCF tolerance control |
| **xTB** | `xtb_methods` | `xtbbin` env var | Subprocess | `GFN2-xTB`, `GFN2-xTB*` | Solvation, dipole/polarizability derivatives, structured error handling |
| **DFT-D3** | `dftd3_methods` | `dftd3bin` env var | Subprocess | `d3zero`, `d3bj`, `d3bjm`, `d3zerom`, `d3op` | Dispersion corrections, numerical Hessian |
| **DFT-D4** | `dftd4_methods` | `dftd4bin` env var | Subprocess | `D4` | Dispersion corrections with OMP threading |

## Property Calculation Capabilities

Each interface implements a `predict()` method that accepts a standard set of flags controlling which quantum chemical properties are computed. While the base `model.predict()` signature defines `calculate_energy`, `calculate_energy_gradients`, and `calculate_hessian`, individual interfaces extend this with program-specific properties such as nonadiabatic coupling vectors, spin-orbit coupling, and dipole derivatives. The following matrix summarizes which properties each interface can compute based on its `predict()` method signature.

Sources: [gaussian_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/gaussian_interface.py#L72-L79), [orca_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/orca_interface.py#L89-L98), [pyscf_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/pyscf_interface.py#L91-L92), [columbus_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/columbus_interface.py#L44-L56), [turbomole_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/turbomole_interface.py#L43-L52), [mndo_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/mndo_interface.py#L68-L78), [xtb_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/xtb_interface.py#L105-L106), [dftbplus_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/dftbplus_interface.py#L286-L293)

| Property | Gaussian | ORCA | PySCF | COLUMBUS | Turbomole | MNDO | DFTB+ | xTB | DFT-D3/4 |
|----------|----------|------|-------|----------|-----------|------|-------|-----|----------|
| Energy | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Energy Gradients | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Hessian | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅¹ |
| Multi-State Energies | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | — | — | — |
| Multi-State Gradients | — | ✅² | — | ✅ | ✅ | — | — | — | — |
| Dipole Derivatives | ✅ | — | ✅ | — | — | ✅ | — | ✅ | — |
| NACV | — | — | — | ✅ | — | ✅ | — | — | — |
| SOC | — | — | — | ✅ | — | — | — | — | — |
| Polarizability Derivatives | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | ✅ | — |
| Density Matrix | — | — | — | — | — | ✅ | — | — | — |
| Solvation | — | ✅ | — | — | — | — | — | ✅ | — |
