## Interface Lifecycle: From Invocation to Result

All subprocess-based interfaces follow the same operational lifecycle, implemented within each class's `predict()` method. Understanding this pattern is essential for debugging integration issues and extending the framework with new program interfaces.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User as User Code
    participant Dispatch as models.methods()
    participant Interface as *_methods class
    participant FS as Filesystem (tmpdir)
    participant QC as QC Program
    participant Parser as Output Parser
    
    User->>Dispatch: methods(method='B3LYP/6-31G*', program='gaussian')
    Dispatch->>Interface: gaussian_methods(method='B3LYP/6-31G*')
    Interface->>Interface: __init__() — validate env vars, store config
    
    User->>Interface: .predict(molecule=mol, calculate_energy_gradients=True)
    Interface->>Interface: super().predict() — normalize molDB
    
    rect rgb(240, 248, 255)
        Note over Interface,FS: Phase 1: Input Generation
        Interface->>FS: Create temp directory
        Interface->>FS: Write input file (molecule coords + method keywords)
    end
    
    rect rgb(255, 248, 240)
        Note over Interface,QC: Phase 2: Execution
        Interface->>QC: subprocess.Popen(input_file)
        QC-->>Interface: stdout/stderr
    end
    
    rect rgb(240, 255, 240)
        Note over Interface,Parser: Phase 3: Result Extraction
        Interface->>FS: Read output file(s)
        Interface->>Parser: Parse energies, gradients, etc.
        Parser-->>Interface: Structured data
        Interface->>Interface: Populate mol.electronic_states[i].energy, gradients
    end
    
    Interface-->>User: Molecule object with updated properties
```

The lifecycle has three phases. **Input generation** creates a temporary working directory (or uses the user-specified `working_directory`), translates the molecule's coordinates into the program's input format, and appends method-specific keywords. **Execution** launches the external program as a subprocess, typically with `subprocess.Popen` and `communicate()` for synchronous blocking. **Result extraction** reads one or more output files, parses energies/gradients/hessians using program-specific parsers, and populates the corresponding fields on the molecule or electronic state objects. The `save_files_in_current_directory` flag, present on all interfaces, controls whether the temporary directory is cleaned up or retained for inspection after the calculation.

Sources: [gaussian_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/gaussian_interface.py#L116-L148), [columbus_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/columbus_interface.py#L79-L103), [turbomole_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/turbomole_interface.py#L75-L103)

## Gaussian Interface

The Gaussian interface ([gaussian_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/gaussian_interface.py#L19-L148)) is the most feature-rich external interface, supporting ground-state and TD-DFT calculations with energies, gradients, Hessians, and dipole derivatives. It validates the `GAUSS_EXEDIR` environment variable at initialization time and defaults thread count to `cpu_count()`. The `predict()` method automatically injects Gaussian keywords: `force(nostep)` for gradient requests, `freq` for Hessian requests (creating a checkpoint file), and `IOp(7/33=1)` for dipole derivative requests. For multi-state TD-DFT calculations, it parses the `TD-` prefix from the method string and generates the appropriate `TD(NStates=...,Root=...)` directive.

A specialized feature of the Gaussian interface is the **external potential mode**, enabled through the `run_gaussian_job()` function's `external_task` parameter. This mechanism, implemented jointly with [gaussian_external.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/gaussian_external.py#L25-L110), allows an MLatom model to provide an external potential to Gaussian—enabling, for example, Delta-learning corrections where Gaussian computes a base property and MLatom adds a correction on-the-fly. The external script (`gaussian_external.py`) handles the `EIn`/`EOu` file protocol that Gaussian uses for external potential communication.

Sources: [gaussian_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/gaussian_interface.py#L149-L165), [gaussian_external.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/gaussian_external.py#L25-L110)

> [!TIP]
> When requesting `calculate_hessian=True` with Gaussian, the interface automatically sets `chkfilename=True`, generating a `.chk` file. This checkpoint file is also used by the `read_Hessian_matrix_from_Gaussian_chkfile()` utility function at [gaussian_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/gaussian_interface.py#L294-L327), which extracts the analytical Hessian in atomic units directly from the binary checkpoint format.

## ORCA Interface

The ORCA interface ([orca_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/orca_interface.py#L23-L216)) is the most versatile in terms of quantum chemistry method coverage, supporting TD-DFT/TDA, QD-NEVPT2, CASSCF, and the composite `CCSD(T)*/CBS` method. The binary is located via the `orcabin` environment variable. The interface distinguishes method types by parsing prefixes from the method string: `TD-` triggers full TD-DFT, `TDA-` triggers Tamm-Dancoff approximation, and `qd-nevpt2` triggers the quasi-degenerate perturbation theory path. Each method type follows a separate output parsing pipeline: `_parse_tddft_output()` for TD-DFT/DFT ground states and `_parse_qd_nevpt2_output()` for multireference methods.

A unique feature is the **per-state gradient** capability via the `calculate_energy_gradients` list argument. Instead of a single boolean, you can pass a list like `[False, True, False]` to request gradients only for a specific excited state. The interface validates that only one state has gradients requested (an ORCA limitation) and raises a descriptive error if the ground state gradient is requested for a TD-DFT calculation, which ORCA does not support.

Sources: [orca_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/orca_interface.py#L88-L183), [orca_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/orca_interface.py#L155-L172)

The `CCSD(T)*/CBS` composite method is implemented as a separate `ccsdtstarcbs` class ([orca_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/orca_interface.py#L763-L834)) that orchestrates multiple ORCA calculations with different basis sets and extracts combined energies. The `orca_methods` class delegates to this composite when `method='CCSD(T)*/CBS'` is specified, making it transparently available through the standard dispatch mechanism.

Sources: [orca_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/orca_interface.py#L84-L86), [orca_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/orca_interface.py#L763-L813)

## PySCF Interface: In-Process Execution

The PySCF interface ([pyscf_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/pyscf_interface.py#L31-L375)) differs fundamentally from all other interfaces because it operates entirely within the Python process—no subprocesses, no file I/O for communication, no environment variable requirements. This makes it significantly faster for single-molecule calculations and easier to debug, as all computation occurs in the same memory space. The `OMP_pyscf` base class ([pyscf_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/pyscf_interface.py#L23-L30)) configures OpenMP threads through PySCF's own `pyscf.lib.num_threads()` function.

The `supported_methods` list includes `HF`, `MP2`, `FCI`, `CISD`, `CCSD`, `CCSD(T)`, and the DeepMind density functionals `DM21`, `DM21m`, `DM21mu`, and `DM21mc`. The `is_method_supported()` method performs case-insensitive matching, while the main `predict_for_molecule()` method routes to appropriate PySCF API calls based on the method string. A dedicated `predict_for_molecule_DM21()` method handles the DeepMind functionals, which require a separate code path because they use `pyscf.dft.functional` rather than standard DFT functionals.

Sources: [pyscf_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/pyscf_interface.py#L50-L92), [pyscf_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/pyscf_interface.py#L313-L363)

## COLUMBUS Interface: Multi-State Dynamics

The COLUMBUS interface ([columbus_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/columbus_interface.py#L13-L283)) is the most specialized quantum chemistry interface, designed primarily for nonadiabatic dynamics simulations. It supports CASSCF and MRCI levels of theory with a uniquely rich set of multi-state properties: per-state energies for both singlet and triplet manifolds, per-state energy gradients, nonadiabatic coupling vectors (NACV) between all state pairs, and spin-orbit coupling (SOC) vectors between singlet-triplet pairs. The interface manages singlet/triplet state counting through the `nsinglets` and `ntriplets` parameters, with validation ensuring `nstates == nsinglets + ntriplets`.

The NACV extraction reads gradient-difference files from the `GRADIENTS/` directory (e.g., `cartgrd.nad.drt1.stateM.drt1.stateN.sp`), applies Bohr-to-angstrom conversion, and stores the result in a symmetric `mol.nacv[i][j]` tensor where `nacv[j][i] = -nacv[i][j]`. SOC extraction parses the `HT matrix in AU` block from the `runls` output file, converting from atomic units to cm⁻¹. Both properties are critical for surface-hopping nonadiabatic molecular dynamics, where COLUMBUS serves as the primary quantum chemistry engine.

Sources: [columbus_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/columbus_interface.py#L217-L275)

## Semiempirical and Tight-Binding Interfaces

The MNDO interface ([mndo_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/mndo_interface.py#L37-L78)) provides access to a wide range of semiempirical methods through the MNDO or Sparrow programs. The `mndo_method_keywords` dictionary maps method names to their MNDO keyword strings, and `supported_methods` is derived from this dictionary. The interface supports density matrix reading (`read_density_matrix=True`), which is essential for certain excited-state methods, and NACV calculations. The `heats_scf_methods` attribute identifies which methods produce heat-of-formation-calibrated results.

The xTB interface ([xtb_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/xtb_interface.py#L19-L106)) wraps the GFN-xTB family of tight-binding methods. Beyond basic energy and gradient calculations, it supports dipole and polarizability derivative calculations (important for IR spectra), implicit solvation through xTB's `--gbsa` flag, and stack size management for large molecules via `unlimited_stack_size`. The interface includes a structured `error_handle()` method that examines xTB's stderr output to identify and report common failure modes such as SCF convergence issues.

The DFTB+ interface ([dftbplus_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/dftbplus_interface.py#L33-L60)) generates DFTB+ input files including the `dftb_in.hsd` configuration and manages Slater-Koster file paths through the `get_skdir()` class method. It supports standard DFTB energy and gradient calculations with configurable SCF tolerance.

Sources: [mndo_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/mndo_interface.py#L19-L78), [xtb_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/xtb_interface.py#L62-L106), [dftbplus_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/dftbplus_interface.py#L58-L293)

## Dispersion Correction Interfaces

The DFT-D3 ([dftd3_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/dftd3_interface.py#L20-L125)) and DFT-D4 ([dftd4_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/dftd4_interface.py#L18-L125)) interfaces provide access to Grimme's dispersion correction schemes. DFT-D3 supports five damping function variants: `d3zero` (zero-damping), `d3bj` (Becke-Johnson), `d3bjm`, `d3zerom`, and `d3op`. Both interfaces accept a `functional` parameter for functional-specific damping parameters. The DFT-D3 interface uniquely implements a `numerical_hessian()` method for computing Hessians via finite differences of analytical gradients, useful when the dispersion correction needs to be combined with a method that does not provide analytical second derivatives.

Sources: [dftd3_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/dftd3_interface.py#L20-L63), [dftd4_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/dftd4_interface.py#L18-L56), [dftd3_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/dftd3_interface.py#L108-L125)

## Common Configuration Patterns

All external-process interfaces share a consistent set of configuration parameters for controlling execution environment and file management. These parameters are not formally enforced by the `method_model` base class but are implemented identically across all interface classes through convention.

| Parameter | Type | Default | Purpose |
|-----------|------|---------|---------|
| `save_files_in_current_directory` | `bool` | `True` (varies) | If `True`, input/output files remain in the current directory instead of a temp directory |
| `working_directory` | `str` | `None` | Custom directory for all calculation files; created if it doesn't exist |
| `directory_with_input_files` | `str` | `''` | Directory containing pre-existing input files to copy into the working directory (COLUMBUS, Turbomole) |
| `nthreads` | `int` | Varies | Number of parallel threads/processes; maps to program-specific parallelism settings |
| `method` | `str` | Varies | Method specification in the target program's syntax |

The `method_model.get_bin_env_var()` class method reads the binary path from the environment variable named by `bin_env_name`. Each interface validates this at initialization and raises a `ValueError` with a clear message if the program is not found. The standard naming convention for environment variables is `{program}bin` (e.g., `orcabin`, `mndobin`, `dftd4bin`) or a program-specific name like `GAUSS_EXEDIR` for Gaussian, `TURBODIR` for Turbomole, and `COLUMBUS` for the COLUMBUS package.

Sources: [model_cls.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/model_cls.py#L197-L202), [gaussian_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/gaussian_interface.py#L47-L48), [orca_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/orca_interface.py#L69-L71), [columbus_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/columbus_interface.py#L38-L42), [turbomole_interface.py](/dralgroup/mlatom/blob/main/mlatom/interfaces/turbomole_interface.py#L29-L31)

## Next Steps

Having understood how MLatom communicates with quantum chemistry programs through the unified `predict()` interface, the natural progression depends on your use case. If you are interested in machine learning potentials that can replace or augment these QC calculations, proceed to [Universal ML Potential Interfaces](15-universal-ml-potential-interfaces). To see how these interfaces are consumed by simulation workflows such as geometry optimization and molecular dynamics, see [Geometry Optimization Workflows](17-geometry-optimization-workflows) and [Molecular Dynamics Engine](19-molecular-dynamics-engine). For the broader model class hierarchy that these interfaces fit into, consult [Model Class Hierarchy](9-model-class-hierarchy).

# Universal ML Potential Interfaces



MLatom provides a unified interface layer to a broad ecosystem of universal machine learning potentials — pre-trained or custom-trained models that can predict energies, forces, and Hessians for molecular systems across chemical space. These interfaces normalize the considerable API diversity across programs like TorchANI, MACE, DeePMD-kit, PhysNet, sGDML, and GAP into a consistent `train → predict → save` workflow, while also exposing pre-trained foundational models for immediate drop-in use without any training step.

## Architectural Overview

The interface layer lives entirely within the `mlatom/interfaces/` directory and follows a disciplined inheritance hierarchy rooted in base classes defined in [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py). Every ML potential interface inherits from at least `ml_model`, which itself extends the foundational `model` class. Framework-specific mixins — `torch_model`, `torchani_model`, `tensorflow_model` — handle device management and thread configuration for their respective backends. This separation of concerns means adding a new potential interface requires implementing only the methods that are genuinely unique to that program, while inheriting cross-cutting concerns like hyperparameter optimization, validation, and model serialization.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    direction TB
    
    class model {
        +predict()
        +set_num_threads()
        +dump()
    }
    
    class ml_model {
        +train()
        +predict()
        +save()
        +load()
        +optimize_hyperparameters()
    }
    
    class torch_model {
        +set_num_threads()
        +config_multiprocessing()
    }
    
    class torchani_model {
        +config_multiprocessing()
    }
    
    class tensorflow_model {
        +set_num_threads()
    }
    
    class method_model {
        +is_method_supported()
        +is_program_found()
        +supported_methods
    }
    
    class downloadable_model {
        +download()
        +check_model_path()
    }
    
    model <|-- ml_model
    model <|-- torch_model
    torch_model <|-- torchani_model
    model <|-- tensorflow_model
    model <|-- method_model
    model <|-- downloadable_model
    
    ml_model <|-- ani
    ml_model <|-- msani
    ml_model <|-- mace
    ml_model <|-- physnet
    ml_model <|-- dpmd
    ml_model <|-- sgdml
    ml_model <|-- gap
    
    torchani_model <|-- ani
    torchani_model <|-- msani
    
    torch_model <|-- mace
    
    tensorflow_model <|-- physnet
    tensorflow_model <|-- dpmd
    
    method_model <|-- ani_methods
    method_model <|-- aimnet2_methods
    method_model <|-- mace_methods
    
    torchani_model <|-- ani_methods
    torchani_model <|-- aimnet2_methods
    torch_model <|-- mace_methods
    downloadable_model <|-- ani_methods
    downloadable_model <|-- mace_methods
```

## The Two Design Axes: Trainable Models vs. Pre-trained Methods

The most important architectural distinction among these interfaces is not the underlying ML framework, but rather whether the model is **trainable from user data** or is a **pre-trained foundational model** distributed by its authors. Trainable models inherit from `ml_model`, which provides `train()`, `save()`, `load()`, `predict()`, and hyperparameter optimization machinery. Pre-trained methods inherit from `method_model` (which exposes a `supported_methods` list and program-discovery logic) and typically from `downloadable_model` (which handles automatic model file retrieval). They generally implement only `predict()`.

Sources: [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L343-L379), [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L175-L207)

| Dimension | Trainable Models | Pre-trained Methods |
|---|---|---|
| **Base class** | `ml_model` | `method_model` (+ optional `downloadable_model`) |
| **Primary operation** | `train()` → `save()` → `predict()` | `predict()` only |
| **User data required** | Yes (training set) | No |
| **Hyperparameter tuning** | Built-in via `ml_model` | Not applicable |
| **Model persistence** | `.pt`, `.pb`, `.npz`, extended XYZ | Downloaded to local directory |
| **Examples** | `ani`, `mace`, `physnet`, `dpmd`, `sgdml`, `gap` | `ani_methods`, `aimnet2_methods`, `mace_methods` |

## Trainable ML Potentials

### ANI (TorchANI)

The `ani` class in [torchani_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/torchani_interface.py#L92-L821) wraps the TorchANI library to provide ANI-style neural network potentials built on the Atom-centered Symmetry Functions (AEV) representation. It inherits from both `ml_model` and `torchani_model`, making it a PyTorch-native model with TorchANI-specific multiprocessing configuration. The constructor accepts a `model_file` path for loading or a fresh set of `hyperparameters` for training. Device selection defaults to CUDA if available, falling back to CPU [torchani_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/torchani_interface.py#L146-L164).

The hyperparameter space is rich and well-structured, covering training behavior (`learning_rate`, `batch_size`, `max_epochs`), loss configuration (`force_coefficient`, `loss_type`), network architecture (`neurons`, `activation_function`), and AEV descriptor parameters (`Rcr`, `Rca`, `EtaR`, `ShfR`, `Zeta`, `ShfZ`, `EtaA`, `ShfA`). Notably, the network architecture is specified per species: the default `neurons=[[160, 128, 96]]` defines a single species with three hidden layers [torchani_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/torchani_interface.py#L105-L133). The `fix_layers()` method enables transfer learning by freezing selected layers during retraining [torchani_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/torchani_interface.py#L704-L770).

Data conversion uses `molDB2ANIdata()` or `molDB2ANIdata_state()` to bridge MLatom's `molecular_database` into TorchANI's `TransformableIterable` format, including proper handling of periodic boundary conditions when present [torchani_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/torchani_interface.py#L64-L89). A sibling class, `msani` [torchani_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/torchani_interface.py#L823-L1577), extends this architecture for multi-state (excited-state) potential energy surfaces, accepting an `nstates` parameter and managing per-state training and prediction.

Sources: [torchani_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/torchani_interface.py#L92-L821), [torchani_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/torchani_interface.py#L64-L89)

### MACE

The `mace` class in [mace_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/mace_interface.py#L117-L841) interfaces to the MACE (Multi-body Atomic Cluster Expansion) framework, an equivariant neural network potential based on E(3)-equivariant message passing. It inherits from `ml_model` and `torch_model` (but not `torchani_model`, since it does not use TorchANI's AEV computation). MACE's hyperparameter space is the most extensive of all interfaces, reflecting the framework's rich set of architectural choices: the equivariant hidden irreps (`hidden_irreps`), the type of interaction block (`interaction`), the number of interaction layers (`num_interactions`), and the body-order correlation (`correlation`) [mace_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/mace_interface.py#L129-L213).

The `train()` method internally converts MLatom's `molecular_database` into MACE's native `Configurations` format using the `load_from_molDB()` helper, which converts energies from Hartree to eV and forces by sign-flipping (MLatom stores gradients, MACE expects forces) [mace_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/mace_interface.py#L43-L85). The `get_dataset_from_molDB()` function handles automatic train/validation splitting via MACE's `SubsetCollection` [mace_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/mace_interface.py#L87-L115). MACE's checkpoint system is patched via `CheckpointHandler_modified` to integrate with MLatom's directory management [mace_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/mace_interface.py#L843-L862).

Sources: [mace_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/mace_interface.py#L117-L213), [mace_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/mace_interface.py#L43-L85)

### PhysNet

The `physnet` class in [physnet_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/physnet_interface.py#L62-L713) wraps the PhysNet TensorFlow-based potential, which uses continuous-filter convolutional layers with residual connections. It inherits from `ml_model` and `tensorflow_model`, requiring the `PhysNet` environment variable to point to a local installation [physnet_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/physnet_interface.py#L15-L34). Its hyperparameters include PhysNet-specific architectural controls: `num_blocks`, `num_residual_atomic`, `num_residual_interaction`, `num_residual_output`, `cutoff`, and physical correction terms (`use_electrostatic`, `use_dispersion`, Grimme D3 parameters) [physnet_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/physnet_interface.py#L73-L109).

The `train()` method supports TensorFlow session management with configurable `summary_interval`, `validation_interval`, and `save_interval`, and implements early stopping via a `threshold`/`patience` mechanism [physnet_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/physnet_interface.py#L221-L648). Data conversion uses `molDB2PhysNetData()` which returns a custom `_DataContainer` subclass [physnet_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/physnet_interface.py#L48-L61).

Sources: [physnet_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/physnet_interface.py#L62-L109), [physnet_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/physnet_interface.py#L221-L248)

### DeePMD-kit

The `dpmd` class in [dpmd_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/dpmd_interface.py#L66-L393) interfaces to the DeepMD-kit framework for deep potential models, inheriting from `ml_model` and `tensorflow_model`. It manages training through DeePMD-kit's JSON-based configuration system, with `update_json()` translating MLatom's hyperparameter values into the JSON structure [dpmd_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/dpmd_interface.py#L208-L250). Hyperparameters include `rcut`, `neuron`/`n_neuron` specifications, `sel` for neighbor selection, and a learning rate schedule with `start_lr`, `decay_steps`, and `decay_rate` [dpmd_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/dpmd_interface.py#L78-L98).

Data conversion via `molDB2DPdata()` writes NumPy arrays (coordinates, energies, forces) into DeePMD-kit's expected directory structure under `set.000` (training) and `set.001` (validation) [dpmd_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/dpmd_interface.py#L25-L65). The interface includes a custom `earlyStopCls` with configurable `patience` and `threshold` [dpmd_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/dpmd_interface.py#L395-L419).

Sources: [dpmd_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/dpmd_interface.py#L66-L98), [dpmd_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/dpmd_interface.py#L25-L65)

### sGDML

The `sgdml` class in [sgdml_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/sgdml_interface.py#L65-L1131) interfaces to the Symmetric Gradient Domain Machine Learning (sGDML) package, a kernel-based method that constructs force-matched potentials using symmetric gradient-domain kernels. Unlike the neural network interfaces, it has a simpler hyperparameter set focused on the kernel and training strategy: `no_E` (exclude energy matching), `gdml` (gradient-domain only), `perms` (permutation handling), `sigma` (kernel width), `E_cstr` (energy constraint), and `cprsn` (compression) [sgdml_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/sgdml_interface.py#L89-L96).

The training pipeline in `sgdml` is notably more complex than the neural network interfaces because sGDML requires an explicit model selection process. The `train()` method orchestrates `create()` (which generates training configurations across sigma values and permutation settings), `train_models()` (which runs parallel sGDML training jobs), `select()` (which picks the best model based on validation errors), and `test()` (final evaluation on a held-out test set) [sgdml_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/sgdml_interface.py#L151-L646). Data conversion via `molDB2sGDMLdata()` assembles the sGDML dataset dict with energy/force statistics and an MD5 checksum [sgdml_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/sgdml_interface.py#L32-L63).

> [!TIP]
> The sGDML interface is unique among trainable potentials in that it performs an internal model selection loop over multiple sigma values and training configurations. This is because sGDML models are defined by a single kernel width parameter — unlike neural networks which have thousands of trainable parameters — so the interface sweeps over candidate sigma values and automatically selects the best-performing model.

Sources: [sgdml_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/sgdml_interface.py#L65-L96), [sgdml_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/sgdml_interface.py#L221-L646)

### GAP (SOAP)

The `gap` class in [gap_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/gap_interface.py#L48-L244) provides an interface to the Gaussian Approximation Potential framework using Smooth Overlap of Atomic Positions (SOAP) descriptors, executed through the external QUIP/gap_fit binaries. It inherits directly from `ml_model` without any framework-specific mixin, since it communicates via subprocess calls rather than an in-process library. The `$gap_fit` and `$quip` environment variables must point to the respective executables [gap_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/gap_interface.py#L18-L26).

Hyperparameters control the SOAP descriptor: `l_max`, `n_max`, `atom_sigma`, `cutoff`, `zeta`, and `n_sparse` (the number of sparse points for the kernel approximation) [gap_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/gap_interface.py#L60-L82). Data conversion uses `molDB2extendedXYZ()` which writes the extended XYZ format expected by `gap_fit`, including PBC information and force sign conventions [gap_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/gap_interface.py#L28-L46).

Sources: [gap_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/gap_interface.py#L48-L82), [gap_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/gap_interface.py#L28-L46)

## Pre-trained Foundational Models

### ANI Methods

The `ani_methods` class in [torchani_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/torchani_interface.py#L1637-L1895) provides instant access to published ANI models without any training step. It supports a wide range of methods: `ANI-1x`, `ANI-1ccx`, `ANI-2x`, `ANI-1x-D4`, `ANI-2x-D4`, `ANI-1xnr` (a reactive potential), `ANI-1ccx-gelu`, and `ANI-1x-gelu` variants [torchani_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/torchani_interface.py#L1647). The class implements a sophisticated model composition system using `model_tree_node`: individual neural network sub-models are averaged (for ensemble prediction), and for D4-corrected variants, a D4 dispersion node is summed with the neural network average [torchani_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/torchani_interface.py#L1683-L1698).

The GELU variants (`ANI-1ccx-gelu`, `ANI-1x-gelu`) leverage the `downloadable_model` mixin to automatically fetch model files from Zenodo on first use, placing them in `ani_1ccx_gelu_model/` or `ani_1x_gelu_model/` directories with 8 cross-validation checkpoint files each [torchani_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/torchani_interface.py#L1700-L1731). The reactive `ANI-1xnr` model is loaded via a dedicated `load_ani1xnr_model()` function [torchani_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/torchani_interface.py#L1897-L1936).

Sources: [torchani_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/torchani_interface.py#L1637-L1698), [torchani_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/torchani_interface.py#L1700-L1731)

### AIMNet2 Methods

The `aimnet2_methods` class in [aimnet2_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/aimnet2_interface.py#L14-L64) provides access to AIMNet2 models, which combine neural network potentials with DFT functional information. Supported methods include `AIMNet2@b973c`, `AIMNet2@b973c-d3`, `AIMNet2@wb97m`, and `AIMNet2@wb97m-d3`, covering elements H, B, C, N, O, F, Si, P, S, Cl, As, Se, Br, I [aimnet2_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/aimnet2_interface.py#L26-L27). The constructor accepts either a specific `model_index` (for a single model) or no index (for an ensemble average) [aimnet2_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/aimnet2_interface.py#L29-L42). Single-model predictions use the `aimnet2_methods_single` class with `downloadable_model` capabilities [aimnet2_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/aimnet2_interface.py#L66-L118).

Sources: [aimnet2_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/aimnet2_interface.py#L14-L64), [aimnet2_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/aimnet2_interface.py#L66-L118)

### MACE Methods

The `mace_methods` class in [mace_methods_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/mace_methods_interface.py#L5-L88) provides access to pre-trained MACE-OFF foundational models. Supported methods include `mace-off23`, `mace-off23s`, `mace-off23m`, `mace-off23l`, `mace-off23bm`, `mace-off24`, and `mace-off24m` [mace_methods_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/mace_methods_interface.py#L17). Each method maps to a specific model file (e.g., `mace-off24` → `MACE-OFF24_medium.model`) [mace_methods_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/mace_methods_interface.py#L18-L33).

Unlike the trainable `mace` class, `mace_methods` wraps MACE's ASE calculator (`mace.calculators.mace_off`) and delegates all computation through the ASE `Atoms` interface, converting energies from eV to Hartree and forces with appropriate sign convention during prediction [mace_methods_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/mace_methods_interface.py#L54-L88). Model files are expected to be placed in the `mace_off_model/` directory; if not found, the interface raises an informative error directing the user to download them manually [mace_methods_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/mace_methods_interface.py#L59-L63).

> [!TIP]
> The `mace_methods` class uses ASE's calculator interface internally rather than the raw MACE PyTorch model. This means you can also use the returned `mace_off` calculator object directly with any ASE workflow (geometry optimization, molecular dynamics, etc.) if you need more control than MLatom's predict method provides.

Sources: [mace_methods_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/mace_methods_interface.py#L5-L88)

## Unified Method Dispatch

All pre-trained methods are accessible through a single entry point: `mlatom.models.methods()`. This function iterates through the `known_classes` list — `[aiqm1, aiqm2, aiqm3, dens, ani_methods, aimnet2_methods, mace_methods, ...]` — and checks each class's `is_method_supported()` and `is_program_found()` methods to resolve the correct interface automatically [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L624-L693). The order in `known_classes` determines the default when multiple interfaces could handle the same method name. For explicit control, the `program` parameter can be specified to bypass automatic resolution.

The unified dispatch means that calling `mlatom.models(method='ANI-1ccx')` or `mlatom.models(method='mace-off24')` works identically from the user's perspective, regardless of the underlying framework, device requirements, or model file format.

Sources: [models.py](mlatom/models.py#L624-L693)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["mlatom.models(method='...')"] --> B{method specified?}
    B -->|Yes| C["Iterate known_classes"]
    C --> D{"is_method_supported()?"}
    D -->|No| C
    D -->|Yes| E{"is_program_found()?"}
    E -->|No| C
    E -->|Yes| F["Instantiate method_class(method=...)"]
    C -->|Exhausted| G["Raise ValueError"]
    
    B -->|No, program specified| H["Instantiate {program}_methods()"]
```

## Capability Matrix

The following table summarizes the key capabilities of each interface, distinguishing between trainable models and pre-trained methods:

| Interface | Class | Framework | Train | Predict Energy | Predict Forces | Predict Hessian | Batch Prediction | Multi-state |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ANI | `ani` | PyTorch/TorchANI | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ (`batch_size`) | ❌ |
| MS-ANI | `msani` | PyTorch/TorchANI | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| ANI Methods | `ani_methods` | PyTorch/TorchANI | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| AIMNet2 | `aimnet2_methods` | PyTorch | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| MACE | `mace` | PyTorch | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ (`batch_size`) | ❌ |
| MACE Methods | `mace_methods` | PyTorch/ASE | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| PhysNet | `physnet` | TensorFlow | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| DeePMD-kit | `dpmd` | TensorFlow | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| sGDML | `sgdml` | NumPy/PyTorch | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ (`batch_size`) | ❌ |
| GAP | `gap` | External (QUIP) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |

## Predict Interface Contract

Every interface implements a `predict()` method with a shared signature contract inherited from the base `model` and `ml_model` classes. The standardized parameters are:

- `molecular_database` / `molecule` — input data (one or the other, not both)
- `calculate_energy` — whether to compute energies
- `calculate_energy_gradients` — whether to compute forces (negative gradient of energy)
- `calculate_hessian` — whether to compute the second derivative matrix
- `property_to_predict` — attribute name to store energies (default: `'estimated_y'`)
- `xyz_derivative_property_to_predict` — attribute name to store gradients
- `hessian_to_predict` — attribute name to store Hessian

The `batch_size` parameter, where supported, controls how many molecules are processed in a single forward pass. Neural network interfaces (`ani`, `msani`, `mace`, `sgdml`) expose this parameter; TensorFlow-based interfaces (`physnet`, `dpmd`) and external binary interfaces (`gap`) process the full database at once. Force sign conventions are handled internally: MLatom stores energy gradients (∂E/∂x), while some external programs expect forces (−∂E/∂x), so conversion happens at the interface boundary.

Sources: [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L78-L87), [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L365-L378)

## Hyperparameter Optimization Integration

All trainable interfaces benefit from the hyperparameter optimization infrastructure built into `ml_model`. The `optimize_hyperparameters()` method [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L609-L727) accepts an `optimization_algorithm` (e.g., grid search, Bayesian optimization), a `maximum_evaluations` budget, and delegates to `calculate_validation_loss()` [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L450-L608) for evaluation. This means any interface that defines its hyperparameters with proper `minval`/`maxval`/`optimization_space`/`dtype` metadata automatically gains hyperparameter search capability without any additional code. The ANI and MACE interfaces have the most thoroughly specified optimization spaces, making them particularly well-suited for automated hyperparameter tuning workflows.

Sources: [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L609-L727), [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L856-L905)

## Directory Structure

```
mlatom/interfaces/
├── torchani_interface.py      # ani, msani, ani_child, ani_methods, ani1xnr
├── mace_interface.py           # mace (trainable)
├── mace_methods_interface.py   # mace_methods (pre-trained MACE-OFF)
├── aimnet2_interface.py        # aimnet2_methods, aimnet2_methods_single, aimnet2_methods_ensemble
├── physnet_interface.py        # physnet
├── dpmd_interface.py           # dpmd (DeepMD-kit)
├── sgdml_interface.py          # sgdml
├── gap_interface.py            # gap (GAP/SOAP via QUIP)
├── torchani_heavy_parts.py     # shared TorchANI utilities
└── ...
```

## Next Steps

- For the full model class hierarchy and the `ml_model` base class capabilities (hyperparameter optimization, cross-validation, serialization), see [Model Class Hierarchy](9-model-class-hierarchy).
- To understand how these ML potentials are composed with semiempirical methods and DFT corrections (e.g., ANI-1x-D4, AIQM1), see [AIQM Methods and Delta Learning](11-aiqm-methods-and-delta-learning).
- For configuring hyperparameter search strategies that apply across all trainable interfaces, see [Hyperparameter Optimization](12-hyperparameter-optimization).
- To learn how these potentials plug into ASE for simulation workflows, see [ASE and Simulation Tool Integration](16-ase-and-simulation-tool-integration).
- For the quantum chemistry program interfaces (Gaussian, ORCA, PySCF, etc.) that sit alongside these ML potential interfaces, see [Quantum Chemistry Program Interfaces](14-quantum-chemistry-program-interfaces).

# ASE and Simulation Tool Integration



MLatom's architecture deliberately decouples **model evaluation** from **simulation orchestration**. While MLatom's native model classes handle energy/force/hessian prediction, the actual driving of geometry optimizations, intrinsic reaction coordinate (IRC) calculations, and quantum nuclear simulations is delegated to specialized external libraries. This page documents the adapter layer that bridges MLatom's internal data model to three external simulation engines—ASE, geomeTRIC, and pysisyphus—plus the PyVibDMC integration for diffusion Monte Carlo.

## Architecture: The Adapter Dispatch Pattern

The integration follows a consistent **Engine Adapter** pattern. Each external tool exposes a domain-specific API (ASE's `Calculator`, geomeTRIC's `Engine`, pysisyphus's `Calculator`) that expects atomic coordinates and returns energies/forces in its own unit convention. MLatom's adapter classes translate between MLatom's `molecule`/`molecular_database` data structures and each tool's expectations, while the `optimize_geometry` and `irc` classes in `simulations.py` and `irc.py` serve as dispatchers that select the appropriate backend.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "MLatom Simulation Layer"
        OG["optimize_geometry<br/>(simulations.py)"]
        IRC["irc<br/>(irc.py)"]
        TC["thermochemistry<br/>(simulations.py)"]
        DMC["dmc<br/>(simulations.py)"]
    end

    subgraph "Engine Adapters"
        ASE_C["MLatomCalculator<br/>(ase_interface.py)"]
        GEO_E["MLatomEngine<br/>(geometric_interface.py)"]
        PSY_C["mlatom_calculator<br/>(pysisyphus_interface.py)"]
    end

    subgraph "External Tools"
        ASE["ASE<br/>(LBFGS, Dimer, NEB)"]
        GEO["geomeTRIC<br/>(optimization, IRC)"]
        PSY["pysisyphus<br/>(IRC)"]
        DMC_T["PyVibDMC<br/>(DMC simulation)"]
    end

    subgraph "MLatom Model Layer"
        MODEL["model / methods<br/>(any ML or QM method)"]
    end

    OG -->|program='ase'| ASE_C
    OG -->|program='geometric'| GEO_E
    OG -->|program='scipy'| SCI["scipy.optimize"]
    IRC -->|program='geometric'| GEO_E
    IRC -->|program='pysisyphus'| PSY_C
    IRC -->|program='mlatom'| IRC_ML["irc_mlatom<br/>(built-in)"]
    TC -->|program='ASE'| ASE_T["thermochemistry()<br/>(ase_interface.py)"]
    DMC --> DMC_T

    ASE_C --> ASE
    GEO_E --> GEO
    PSY_C --> PSY

    ASE_C --> MODEL
    GEO_E --> MODEL
    PSY_C --> MODEL
    DMC_T --> MODEL
```

Sources: [simulations.py](mlatom/simulations.py#L92-L268), [ase_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/ase_interface.py#L1-L7), [geometric_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/geometric_interface.py#L1-L16), [pysisyphus_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/pysisyphus_interface.py#L1-L15)

## Program Auto-Detection and Dispatch Logic

When users instantiate `optimize_geometry` without explicitly specifying a `program`, MLatom employs a priority-based auto-detection strategy. The dispatcher checks for the presence of installed packages in a specific order, falling through to the next option if the current one is unavailable.

| Priority | Program | Detection Method | Default Algorithm |
|----------|---------|-----------------|-------------------|
| 1 | `geometric` | `importlib.util.find_spec('geometric')` | geomeTRIC's internal optimizer |
| 2 | `Gaussian` | `os.environ['GAUSS_EXEDIR']` | Gaussian's built-in |
| 3 | `ase` | `importlib.util.find_spec('ase')` | `LBFGS` |
| 4 | `scipy` | `importlib.util.find_spec('scipy')` | User-specified or scipy default |

The algorithm choice can also force program selection: specifying `optimization_algorithm='dimer'` or `'neb'` automatically overrides the program to `'ase'`, while `'qst2'` or `'qst3'` forces `'gaussian'`. The `maximum_number_of_steps` defaults to 200, and the `convergence_criterion_for_forces` defaults to 0.02 eV/Å for ASE-based optimizations. For transition state searches, only `'Gaussian'`, `'ASE'`, and `'geometric'` are supported backends.

Sources: [simulations.py](mlatom/simulations.py#L198-L221), [simulations.py](mlatom/simulations.py#L208-L213), [simulations.py](mlatom/simulations.py#L248-L250)

## ASE Integration: MLatomCalculator

The ASE integration lives entirely in [ase_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/ase_interface.py) and centers on the `MLatomCalculator` class, which extends ASE's `ase.calculators.calculator.Calculator`. This adapter is the bridge that allows any MLatom model to participate as an energy/force provider within ASE's rich ecosystem of optimizers, molecular dynamics routines, and analysis tools.

### The MLatomCalculator Adapter

`MLatomCalculator` implements the minimal ASE `Calculator` contract by declaring `implemented_properties = ['energy', 'forces']` and overriding `calculate()`. The translation pipeline inside `calculate()` follows a specific sequence: the current ASE `Atoms` object is serialized to a temporary `extxyz` file, read back into an MLatom `molecule`, and the coordinates from that file are applied to a copy of the original molecule. This workaround exists because ASE `Atoms` objects do not natively carry MLatom-specific metadata like charge or multiplicity.

The energy conversion is critical: MLatom operates internally in Hartree, while ASE uses eV. The conversion factor `ase.units.Hartree` is applied to both energy and forces (forces are negative energy gradients, hence `forces = -energy_gradients`). For optimization trajectory tracking, a global `optimization_trajectory` object accumulates `molecular_trajectory_step` entries at each step. A post-processing pass removes the duplicate energy entry that ASE produces on initialization.

> [!TIP]
> The `MLatomCalculator` uses a temporary file round-trip (write extxyz → read back) to translate between ASE `Atoms` and MLatom `molecule`. This is explicitly noted as a workaround in the source. The global variable pattern for trajectory tracking (`globals()['optimization_trajectory']`) means nested or concurrent ASE optimizations within the same process would interfere with each other.

### Geometry Optimization via ASE

The `optimize_geometry()` function in `ase_interface.py` accepts a `model`, `initial_molecule`, convergence parameters, and an `optimization_algorithm` keyword (defaulting to `'LBFGS'`). It supports arbitrary ASE optimizer names through dictionary lookup (`optimize.__dict__[optimization_algorithm]`), meaning any optimizer registered in `ase.optimize` is accessible. The function also supports **constraints** through ASE's `FixBondLengths` and `FixInternals` constraint classes, mapped from a dictionary with keys `'bond_length'`, `'bonds'`, `'angles'`, and `'dihedrals'`.

The higher-level `opt_geom_ase()` method in `simulations.py` dispatches either to `ase_interface.optimize_geometry()` for minimum energy searches or to `ase_interface.transition_state()` when `self.ts=True`, passing through `ase_kwargs` as `program_kwargs`.

Sources: [ase_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/ase_interface.py#L23-L89), [ase_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/ase_interface.py#L172-L213), [simulations.py](mlatom/simulations.py#L335-L361)

### Transition State Search via ASE

ASE provides two transition state algorithms through MLatom's interface: the **Dimer method** and the **Nudged Elastic Band (NEB)**. The `transition_state()` function routes based on the `optimization_algorithm` parameter.

The **Dimer method** (`dimer_method()`) wraps ASE's `DimerControl`, `MinModeAtoms`, and `MinModeTranslate` classes. It accepts an optional `random_seed` kwarg for reproducibility. The dimer rotates in the space perpendicular to the minimum-mode direction to find the saddle point.

The **NEB method** (`nudged_elastic_band()`) requires separate `initial_molecule` and `final_molecule` arguments (reactant and product). It creates `number_of_middle_images` intermediate images (default 3), interpolates the path using `NEB.interpolate()`, and assigns `MLatomCalculator` to each intermediate image. The `MDMin` optimizer drives the band relaxation.

| Feature | Dimer Method | NEB |
|---------|-------------|-----|
| Input | Single TS guess geometry | Reactant + Product geometries |
| `optimization_algorithm` | `'dimer'` | `'NEB'` |
| Key ASE classes | `DimerControl`, `MinModeAtoms`, `MinModeTranslate` | `NEB`, `MDMin` |
| Extra parameter | `random_seed` | `number_of_middle_images` |
| ASE kwargs | Passed to `DimerControl` | Passed to `NEB` constructor |

Sources: [ase_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/ase_interface.py#L91-L169)

### Thermochemistry via ASE

The `thermochemistry()` function in `ase_interface.py` leverages ASE's `IdealGasThermo` class to compute standard thermodynamic properties from vibrational frequencies and electronic energy. The function handles negative frequencies automatically (removes them before computation) and supports both linear and nonlinear molecular geometries. The `symmetry_number` attribute on the molecule defaults to 1 if not set.

Energy unit conversion follows a three-stage pipeline: MLatom Hartree → eV (via `ase.units.Hartree`) → kcal/mol (via `ev2kcal`) → Hartree (via `constants.kcalpermol2Hartree`). The computed properties are written directly onto the `molecule` object.

| Property | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| `molecule.ZPE` | Zero-point energy |
| `molecule.H` | Enthalpy at 298.15 K |
| `molecule.H0` | Enthalpy at 0 K |
| `molecule.U0` | Internal energy at 0 K |
| `molecule.G` | Gibbs free energy at 298.15 K |

This function is invoked by the `thermochem_ase()` method in `simulations.py`'s `thermochemistry` class, which chains a frequency calculation before the thermochemistry step.

Sources: [ase_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/ase_interface.py#L214-L261), [simulations.py](mlatom/simulations.py#L831-L833)

## geomeTRIC Integration: MLatomEngine

The geomeTRIC integration ([geometric_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/geometric_interface.py)) provides a more tightly-coupled engine adapter that handles both geometry optimization and IRC calculations. Unlike the ASE adapter's file-based translation, the geomeTRIC adapter works directly with coordinate arrays.

### The MLatomEngine Adapter

`MLatomEngine` extends `geometric.engine.Engine` and must construct a `geometric.molecule.Molecule` object during initialization. The constructor maps MLatom molecule properties—element symbols, coordinates (Å), charge, and multiplicity—into the geomeTRIC molecule format. The `build_topology(force_bonds=False)` call defers bond detection, which is appropriate for non-equilibrium geometries encountered during optimization.

The `calc_new()` method is the core evaluation hook called by geomeTRIC at each optimization step. It receives coordinates in **Bohr** and must return energy in Hartree and gradients in Hartree/Bohr. The conversion path is: received Bohr → multiplied by `constants.Bohr2Angstrom` to get Å for MLatom → model predicts energy (Hartree) and gradients (Hartree/Å) → gradients divided by `constants.Angstrom2Bohr` to return Hartree/Bohr. The trajectory is tracked via a simple list `self.trajdb` appended at each successful step.

> [!TIP]
> When geomeTRIC rejects an optimization step (e.g., line search failure), the `trajdb` list and geomeTRIC's internal `results.xyzs` can become misaligned. The `results_to_traj()` function handles this by performing RMSD-based alignment between stored trajectory molecules and geomeTRIC's result coordinates, skipping entries that don't match within a 1e-8 Å threshold.

### Geometry Optimization via geomeTRIC

The `optimize_geometry()` function in `geometric_interface.py` supports both minimum energy and transition state searches (controlled by the `ts` boolean). For transition state optimization, the hessian is pre-computed at the initial geometry and written to disk, as geomeTRIC requires an initial hessian for TS optimizations. The function wraps `geometric.optimize.run_optimizer()` with a `try/except` block that gracefully handles non-convergence: if `geometric.errors.GeomOptNotConvergedError` is raised, the trajectory accumulated in `trajdb` is still returned with a success flag.

The dispatcher in `simulations.py`'s `opt_geom_geometric()` stores both the `optimization_trajectory` and a `successful` flag. On failure, the initial geometry (with a single-point energy evaluation) is used as the "optimized" molecule.

Sources: [geometric_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/geometric_interface.py#L17-L51), [geometric_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/geometric_interface.py#L53-L98), [simulations.py](mlatom/simulations.py#L389-L404)

### IRC via geomeTRIC

The `generate_irc()` function in `geometric_interface.py` handles intrinsic reaction coordinate calculations. It follows the same pre-computation pattern as TS optimization: the hessian is computed and written to disk before launching geomeTRIC with `irc=True`. The default prediction kwargs ensure energy and gradients are calculated (`calculate_energy=True, calculate_energy_gradients=True`).

After geomeTRIC completes, reaction coordinates are extracted from the step indices in the log (`results.comms`). The trajectory is split at the TS point (where reaction coordinate equals 0) into forward and backward branches. The top-level `irc_geometric()` function in [irc.py](mlatom/irc.py) combines these branches using the `irc.combine()` classmethod, which reverses the forward trajectory and concatenates it with the backward trajectory through the shared TS point.

Sources: [geometric_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/geometric_interface.py#L144-L204), [irc.py](mlatom/irc.py#L458-L462)

## pysisyphus Integration: mlatom_calculator

The pysisyphus interface ([pysisyphus_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/pysisyphus_interface.py)) is specifically designed for IRC calculations. pysisyphus uses a fundamentally different model interface compared to geomeTRIC: instead of a single evaluation function, it requests **energy, forces, and hessian separately** through distinct method calls (`get_energy()`, `get_forces()`, `get_hessian()`). This is inefficient for models that compute these quantities simultaneously, which the source code explicitly notes as a design limitation.

### The mlatom_calculator Adapter

The `mlatom_calculator` extends pysisyphus's `Calculator` and uses a **caching dictionary** (`mlatom_results`, a class variable) to avoid redundant computations. When pysisyphus calls `get_energy()` and subsequently `get_forces()` at the same geometry, the cached result from the energy calculation is reused. The cache entry is deleted after retrieval to prevent stale data.

The constructor accepts initial energy, gradients, and hessian from the TS molecule, which avoids a redundant calculation at the starting geometry. Unit conversions are handled at the boundary: pysisyphus operates in Bohr, so coordinates are converted to Å before MLatom prediction, and gradients are converted from Hartree/Å to Hartree/Bohr on output. The hessian conversion divides by `(Angstrom2Bohr)²` to transform from Hartree/Å² to Hartree/Bohr².

### IRC via pysisyphus

The `generate_irc()` function supports directional control (`'forward'`, `'backward'`, or `'both'`) and configurable IRC algorithms (default: `'eulerpc'`). The pysisyphus `IRC_DICT` maps algorithm names to IRC integrator classes. Unlike geomeTRIC, pysisyphus **can** generate single-direction IRC paths.

After the IRC run completes, results are reassembled into a `molecular_database`. The trajectory ordering convention differs between tools: pysisyphus returns `forward (reversed) → TS → backward`, while Gaussian returns `backward (reversed) → TS → forward`. The interface normalizes this by reversing the trajectory for `'forward'` direction and negating reaction coordinates for `'backward'` direction.

> [!TIP]
> The pysisyphus interface includes a documented warning about a potential stale-cache problem: if the initial IRC step does not retrieve all three properties (energy, forces, hessian) from the TS, the cached results persist and corrupt subsequent steps. The `reset:bool=True` parameter and deletion-after-retrieval pattern mitigate this, but the design remains fragile for edge cases.

Sources: [pysisyphus_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/pysisyphus_interface.py#L32-L115), [pysisyphus_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/pysisyphus_interface.py#L117-L193)

## IRC Program Comparison

The `irc` class in [irc.py](mlatom/irc.py) dispatches to four possible backends. Each has distinct capabilities and limitations that influence which is appropriate for a given task.

| Feature | `mlatom` (built-in) | `geometric` | `pysisyphus` | `Gaussian` |
|---------|---------------------|-------------|--------------|------------|
| Direction control | Forward / Backward / Both | Both only | Forward / Backward / Both | Forward / Backward / Both |
| Hessian estimation | Bofill, SR1, PSB, or recalculate | geomeTRIC internal | Euler predictor-corrector | Gaussian internal |
| Integrator | LQA (local quadratic approximation) | geomeTRIC default | Configurable (eulerpc, etc.) | Gaussian default |
| Coordinate system | Mass-weighted | Cartesian | Mass-weighted (Bohr) | Gaussian internal |
| TS frequency validation | Automatic (runs `freq` if needed) | Automatic | Automatic | Skipped (Gaussian computes own) |
| Dependency | None | `geometric` | `pysisyphus` | Gaussian + `$GAUSS_EXEDIR` |

The built-in `mlatom` IRC implementation ([irc.py](mlatom/irc.py#L518-L659)) uses a **local quadratic approximation (LQA)** integrator and supports three Hessian update schemes: **Bofill** (default), **SR1** (symmetric rank-1), and **PSB** (Powell-symmetric-Broyden). The first displacement is derived from the imaginary-frequency normal mode, scaled by the user-specified `init_length` parameter. Each subsequent step uses the integrator to compute a mass-weighted step from the current gradient and (estimated) Hessian. Propagation terminates when either the gradient norm falls below `thred` (default 1e-5) or `n_steps` is exhausted.

Sources: [irc.py](mlatom/irc.py#L14-L70), [irc.py](mlatom/irc.py#L520-L658), [irc.py](mlatom/irc.py#L727-L775)

## PyVibDMC Integration: Diffusion Monte Carlo

The `dmc` class in [simulations.py](mlatom/simulations.py#L867-L958) wraps the external `PyVibDMC` package to perform diffusion Monte Carlo simulations for zero-point energy calculations. This integration follows a **potential function callback** pattern rather than an adapter class pattern.

The `potential_function()` method accepts walker coordinates from PyVibDMC (in Bohr) and returns energies. It constructs a `molecular_database` from the batch of coordinates, calls `model.predict()` for energy evaluation, and applies an `energy_scaling_factor`. PyVibDMC's `Potential_Direct` wrapper consumes this callback. The `initialize()` method uses PyVibDMC's `InitialConditioner` for harmonic oscillator sampling to generate the initial walker distribution.

The `run()` method configures and launches the full DMC simulation with parameters for walker count, timestep length (converted from fs to atomic units via `constants.fs2au`), equilibration, and descendant weighting. Results are loaded from the HDF5 output file via `pyvibdmc.SimInfo`, and `get_zpe()` returns the zero-point energy in Hartree, averaged from a configurable starting step.

Sources: [simulations.py](mlatom/simulations.py#L867-L958)

## Unit Conversion Reference

Each integration boundary involves unit conversions between MLatom's internal conventions and the external tool's conventions. This table summarizes the critical conversion points.

| Quantity | MLatom Internal | ASE | geomeTRIC | pysisyphus | PyVibDMC |
|----------|----------------|-----|-----------|------------|----------|
| Energy | Hartree | eV (×`Hartree`) | Hartree | Hartree | Hartree |
| Coordinates | Å | Å | Bohr (÷`Angstrom2Bohr`) | Bohr (÷`Angstrom2Bohr`) | Bohr |
| Forces | Hartree/Å | eV/Å | Hartree/Bohr | Hartree/Bohr | N/A |
| Hessian | Hartree/Å² | N/A | N/A | Hartree/Bohr² (÷`Angstrom2Bohr²`) | N/A |

Sources: [ase_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/ase_interface.py#L203-L212), [geometric_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/geometric_interface.py#L38-L51), [pysisyphus_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/pysisyphus_interface.py#L49-L78), [simulations.py](mlatom/simulations.py#L890-L894)

## Continuation

This page covered the simulation tool integration layer. The following pages provide deeper dives into specific workflows and the underlying model system:

- **[Geometry Optimization Workflows](17-geometry-optimization-workflows)** — End-to-end optimization pipelines including constrained optimization, convergence behavior, and trajectory analysis
- **[Nonadiabatic and Surface-Hopping Dynamics](20-nonadiabatic-and-surface-hopping-dynamics)** — Advanced dynamics simulations that build on these same model interfaces
