# Geometry Optimization Workflows



Geometry optimization is the computational process of finding stationary points on a molecular potential energy surface (PES) — typically energy minima or first-order saddle points (transition states). In MLatom, this capability is orchestrated through a unified class that routes requests to multiple backend engines depending on what software is available in the environment. The design philosophy decouples the model (any energy/gradient provider) from the optimization algorithm, enabling ML potentials, semi-empirical methods, and quantum chemistry programs to drive geometry searches through an identical interface.

Sources: [simulations.py](mlatom/simulations.py#L92-L154)

## Architecture Overview

The geometry optimization subsystem follows a hub-and-spoke architecture. The central orchestrator is `optimize_geometry`, which accepts a model, an initial molecule, and a set of control parameters. During `__init__`, the class inspects the runtime environment, selects an appropriate backend engine, and immediately invokes the corresponding optimization method. This eager-evaluation pattern means results are available as soon as the object is constructed.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[User creates optimize_geometry] --> B{program specified?}
    B -->|Yes| C[Use specified program]
    B -->|No| D{geometric installed?}
    D -->|Yes| C
    D -->|No| E{GAUSS_EXEDIR set?}
    E -->|Yes| C
    E -->|No| F{ase installed?}
    F -->|Yes| C
    F -->|No| G{scipy installed?}
    G -->|Yes| C
    G -->|No| H[Raise ValueError]
    
    C --> I{program value}
    I -->|Gaussian| J[opt_geom_gaussian]
    I -->|ASE| K[opt_geom_ase]
    I -->|geometric| L[opt_geom_geometric]
    I -->|scipy / other| M[opt_geom]
    
    J --> N[optimized_molecule]
    K --> N
    L --> N
    M --> N
    
    subgraph "Model Prediction Path"
        O[model._predict_geomopt] --> P[calculate_energy=True]
        O --> Q[calculate_energy_gradients=True]
    end
    
    J -.->|invokes| O
    K -.->|invokes| O
    L -.->|invokes| O
    M -.->|invokes| O
```

The auto-detection priority follows a strict cascade: **geometric** → **Gaussian** (if `$GAUSS_EXEDIR` is set) → **ASE** → **scipy**. This priority reflects a preference for purpose-built geometry optimizers over generic scientific libraries, as seen in the constructor logic at lines 198–203 of `simulations.py`.

Sources: [simulations.py](mlatom/simulations.py#L155-L268)

## The `optimize_geometry` Class

### Constructor and Initialization

The constructor accepts a comprehensive set of parameters that control every aspect of the optimization workflow. Two molecule arguments exist for backward compatibility — `initial_molecule` and `molecule` — but they cannot both be provided simultaneously, raising a `ValueError` if they are. When `molecule` is used, the optimized result is written back into the same object (in-place overwrite), whereas `initial_molecule` leaves the original untouched.

The constructor automatically enforces two essential model prediction flags: `calculate_energy=True` and `calculate_energy_gradients=True`. These are injected into `model_predict_kwargs` even if the user did not specify them, because every geometry optimizer requires both energies and gradients to proceed. Additional bookkeeping parameters — trajectory dump settings, format, filename — are also packed into `model_predict_kwargs` so that the model's `_predict_geomopt` helper can handle them during each step.

A critical design detail is the **trajectory dumping mechanism**. When `dump_trajectory_interval` is set (including being forced to `1` for Gaussian optimizations), a `molecular_trajectory` object is created and begins dumping to disk immediately in the specified format (`json` or `h5md`). This enables post-hoc analysis of the optimization path even for very long runs.

Sources: [simulations.py](mlatom/simulations.py#L155-L275)

### Parameter Reference

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `model` | `model` / `methods` | `None` | Any model providing energies and forces |
| `model_predict_kwargs` | `dict` | `{}` | Additional model prediction keyword arguments |
| `initial_molecule` | `molecule` | `None` | Starting geometry (non-destructive) |
| `molecule` | `molecule` | `None` | Starting geometry (overwritten with result) |
| `ts` | `bool` | `False` | Enable transition state search |
| `reactants` | `molecule` | `None` | Reactant for TS methods (qst2/qst3) |
| `products` | `molecule` | `None` | Product for TS methods (qst2/qst3) |
| `program` | `str` | auto-detect | Backend engine |
| `program_kwargs` | `dict` | `{}` | Engine-specific keyword arguments |
| `optimization_algorithm` | `str` | `None` | Specific algorithm (e.g., `'LBFGS'`, `'dimer'`) |
| `maximum_number_of_steps` | `int` | `200` | Step limit for ASE/scipy/geometric |
| `convergence_criterion_for_forces` | `float` | `0.02` | Force convergence in eV/Å (ASE) |
| `working_directory` | `str` | `'.'` | Directory for output files |
| `constraints` | `dict` | `None` | Geometric constraints (ASE/geometric) |
| `dump_trajectory_interval` | `int` | `None` | Dump every N steps (`None` = disabled) |
| `filename` | `str` | auto UUID | Trajectory output filename |
| `format` | `str` | `'json'` | Trajectory format (`json` or `h5md`) |
| `print_properties` | `bool`/`str` | `None` | Print progress (`None`, `'all'`) |

Sources: [simulations.py](mlatom/simulations.py#L92-L154)

## Backend Engines

### Geometric (Preferred Default)

The `geometric` library from the Grimme group is the first-choice engine when available. The integration is implemented in `mlatom/interfaces/geometric_interface.py` through a custom engine class `MLatomEngine` that subclasses `geometric.engine.Engine`. This engine translates between MLatom's molecule representation and geometric's internal coordinate system.

The `MLatomEngine.calc_new` method performs the critical unit conversion: geometric operates in **Bohr**, so incoming coordinates are converted from Bohr to Ångström before being set on the MLatom molecule, and the resulting gradients are converted back by dividing by `Angstrom2Bohr`. The energy is returned in Hartree (MLatom's native unit), while the gradient is flattened to a 1D array as geometric expects.

For **transition state searches**, the geometric backend first computes the Hessian at the initial geometry and writes it to a temporary file, then passes this initial Hessian to `geometric.optimize.run_optimizer` with `transition=True`. If optimization fails to converge (raised as `GeomOptNotConvergedError`), the last computed geometry is still returned as the result rather than the initial geometry. If a completely different error occurs, the initial geometry is used instead.

The `results_to_traj` function reconstructs a full optimization trajectory by reconciling geometric's internal step list with MLatom's trajectory database. A potential misalignment can occur when geometric rejects steps — the function handles this by comparing RMSD between stored molecules and reported coordinates to filter out rejected steps.

Sources: [geometric_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/geometric_interface.py#L17-L98)

### ASE (Atomic Simulation Environment)

The ASE backend provides the widest algorithm variety, including both minimum and transition state search methods. The integration works through a custom `MLatomCalculator` that subclasses ASE's `Calculator` class. Energy unit conversion is handled explicitly: MLatom energies in Hartree are multiplied by `ase.units.Hartree`, and forces (negative gradients) are similarly scaled.

For **minimum energy optimizations**, ASE's `optimize` dispatch table is used directly — meaning any ASE optimizer name can be passed as `optimization_algorithm` (default: `'LBFGS'`). The convergence criterion maps to ASE's `fmax` parameter in eV/Å.

For **transition state searches**, two specialized algorithms are available through ASE:

- **Dimer method** (`optimization_algorithm='dimer'`): Uses ASE's `DimerControl`, `MinModeAtoms`, and `MinModeTranslate` classes. Supports a `random_seed` kwarg passed through `ase_kwargs`.
- **NEB (Nudged Elastic Band)** (`optimization_algorithm='neb'`): Requires both `reactants` and `products` molecules, and uses ASE's `NEB` class with `MDMin` as the image optimizer. The `number_of_middle_images` parameter (default 3) controls path resolution.

A notable implementation detail is that the ASE backend uses global variables (`initial_molecule`, `optimization_trajectory`) to pass context into the `MLatomCalculator.calculate` method. The code comments acknowledge this as an "ugly solution" — it's a pragmatic workaround for ASE's calculator interface not cleanly supporting external molecule objects. Additionally, ASE has a quirk of recording duplicate energy entries at the start of optimization, which is detected and corrected by comparing the first two step energies and shifting step indices.

Sources: [ase_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/ase_interface.py#L23-L169)

### Gaussian

The Gaussian backend delegates all optimization work to the Gaussian quantum chemistry program through its external interface. When the program is selected, the model is serialized to `model.json` and a Gaussian input file (`gaussianN.com`) is generated with the appropriate task keyword — `opt` for minimum energy or `ts` for transition state. For the specialized `qst2` and `qst3` algorithms, reactant and product geometries are included in the input file.

Success detection is performed by scanning the Gaussian log file for the string `'Stationary point found'`. If found, `self.successful` is set to `True` and the optimized molecule is extracted from the last step of the optimization trajectory. If convergence is not achieved, the initial molecule is returned with all atomic coordinates set to `[None, None, None]` — a sentinel state indicating failure.

The Gaussian backend always forces `dump_trajectory_interval=1`, as the trajectory file is needed to reconstruct the optimization path from disk after Gaussian completes.

Sources: [simulations.py](mlatom/simulations.py#L277-L333)

### SciPy (Fallback)

The SciPy backend serves as the minimal-fallback option when no dedicated optimization software is installed. It wraps `scipy.optimize.minimize` with a closure-based objective function that takes flat coordinate arrays, reshapes them into molecular geometry, invokes `model._predict_geomopt`, and returns both the energy and gradient.

This backend has the most limited feature set: it supports no constraints, no transition state search, and relies entirely on the SciPy optimizer's own convergence criteria. The optimization algorithm is passed directly to SciPy's `method` parameter with no default value — if `None`, SciPy will choose its own.

Sources: [simulations.py](mlatom/simulations.py#L362-L387)

### Program Selection Matrix

| Feature | Gaussian | ASE | Geometric | SciPy |
|---------|----------|-----|-----------|-------|
| Minimum energy optimization | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Transition state search | ✓ | ✓ (dimer/NEB) | ✓ | ✗ |
| QST2/QST3 | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ |
| Constraints | ✗ | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ |
| Custom optimizer | ✗ | ✓ | ✗ | ✓ |
| Max steps control | N/A | ✓ | ✓ | N/A |
| Force convergence | N/A | ✓ | ✓ | N/A |
| Graceful non-convergence | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ | ✗ |

Sources: [simulations.py](mlatom/simulations.py#L208-L268), [ase_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/ase_interface.py#L91-L169), [geometric_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/geometric_interface.py#L53-L98)

## Model Integration and the `_predict_geomopt` Path

All optimization backends ultimately invoke energy and gradient predictions through a single code path: `model._predict_geomopt()`. This method is defined in the base `model` class in `model_cls.py` and acts as a wrapper around `predict()` that adds optimization-specific side effects.

The `_predict_geomopt` method receives the standard prediction kwargs plus several internal parameters: `return_string` (controls whether to return a string for external program interfaces), `dump_trajectory_interval` (controls intermediate trajectory dumping), `filename` and `format` (for trajectory I/O), and `print_properties` (for progress output). This indirection allows the model to handle trajectory bookkeeping centrally while keeping the optimization engines clean of I/O concerns.

The base `model` class is documented as a "Parent (super) class for models to enable useful features such as logging during geometry optimizations." All concrete model implementations — `krr`, `kreg`, `ani_methods`, `aiqm1`, `mace_methods`, etc. — inherit from this class either directly or through intermediate mixins like `torch_model`, `method_model`, or `downloadable_model`, ensuring that every model type can participate in geometry optimizations without engine-specific adaptation.

Sources: [model_cls.py](mlatom/model_cls.py#L20-L87)

## Constraint System

Geometric constraints are supported in both the ASE and geometric backends, passed through the `constraints` parameter. The constraint dictionary uses a structured format that is translated into backend-native constraint objects.

For **ASE**, the constraint dictionary supports:

| Key | Value Format | ASE Translation |
|-----|-------------|-----------------|
| `bond_length` | `[[idx0, idx1], ...]` | `FixBondLengths` |
| `bonds` | `[[target, [idx0, idx1]], ...]` | `FixInternals(bonds=...)` |
| `angles` | `[[target, [idx0, idx1, idx2]], ...]` | `FixInternals(angles_deg=...)` |
| `dihedrals` | `[[target, [idx0, idx1, idx2, idx3]], ...]` | `FixInternals(dihedrals_deg=...)` |

Both `FixBondLengths` and `FixInternals` constraints are applied as a combined list via `atoms.set_constraint()`. The geometric backend passes constraints through `geometric_kwargs` directly to the geometric library's optimization routine.

> [!TIP]
> Constraints are silently ignored by the Gaussian and SciPy backends. If your optimization requires constraints (e.g., constrained dihedral scans), explicitly set `program='ASE'` or `program='geometric'` to ensure they are enforced. The constructor does not validate constraint compatibility with the selected backend.

Sources: [simulations.py](mlatom/simulations.py#L222-L223), [ase_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/ase_interface.py#L42-L68)

## Transition State Search

### Algorithm Routing

When `ts=True` is set, the `optimize_geometry` constructor validates that the selected program supports transition state search — only Gaussian, ASE, and geometric are permitted. Additionally, the `optimization_algorithm` parameter can force the program selection:

- Algorithms `'dimer'` and `'neb'` automatically switch the program to ASE.
- Algorithms `'qst2'` and `'qst3'` automatically switch to Gaussian.

This cross-parameter validation ensures that incompatible algorithm/program combinations are resolved before optimization begins.

### The `gen_ts` Function

For more elaborate transition state generation, the standalone `gen_ts()` function provides access to the **ECTS** (Elaborate Constrained Transition State) method implemented in `gen_ts_methods.py`. This function accepts separate `reactant` and `product` molecules (unlike `optimize_geometry` which uses `reactants`/`products` for QST methods), along with control parameters for the number of transition states (`n_ts`), path points (`n_path`), and averaging options.

Sources: [simulations.py](mlatom/simulations.py#L406-L437)

## IRC (Intrinsic Reaction Coordinate) Calculations

IRC calculations trace the minimum energy path connecting a transition state to reactant and product valleys. MLatom provides IRC functionality through two external engines.

### Geometric IRC

The geometric IRC interface in `geometric_interface.py` follows the same `MLatomEngine` pattern as geometry optimization. It requires a pre-computed Hessian (written to a temporary file as `hessian.txt`), then invokes `geometric.optimize.run_optimizer` with `irc=True`. The reaction coordinates are extracted from geometric's comment lines (step indices), and the trajectory is post-processed to handle the forward/backward directionality.

### PySyphus IRC

The pysisyphus interface provides a more sophisticated IRC implementation with multiple algorithm choices (default: `'eulerpc'`). The `mlatom_calculator` class adapts MLatom models to pysisyphus's `Calculator` interface, handling energy, forces, and Hessian separately through cached results to avoid redundant calculations — a critical optimization since pysisyphus calls `get_energy`, `get_forces`, and `get_hessian` independently.

Unit conversions in pysisyphus are handled at the calculator level: gradients are converted to forces by negation and dividing by `Angstrom2Bohr`, while Hessian elements are divided by `Angstrom2Bohr²`. The resulting trajectory uses mass-weighted reaction coordinates from pysisyphus's internal computation.

> [!TIP]
> The pysisyphus interface carries a documented warning about a potential bug: if the initial IRC step fails to retrieve all three results (energy, gradients, Hessian) from the transition state, cached values from the initial step may persist into subsequent steps and cause errors. This is a known limitation of pysisyphus's separated property retrieval pattern.

### Native MLatom IRC

MLatom also includes a built-in IRC implementation in `mlatom/irc.py` with its own LQA (Local Quadratic Approximation) integrator (`integrator_lqa` class) and Hessian update methods including Powell (`psb`), SR1 (`sr1`), and Bofill (`bofill`) algorithms. The `irc` class manages IRC trajectories with full support for forward/backward direction splitting, trajectory persistence (JSON and XYZ formats), plotting, and result loading from previous calculations.

Sources: [geometric_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/geometric_interface.py#L144-L204), [pysisyphus_interface.py](mlatom/interfaces/pysisyphus_interface.py#L1-193), [irc.py](mlatom/irc.py#L14-L832)

## Numerical Gradients and Hessian

When a model does not provide analytical gradients, MLatom can compute them numerically through `numerical_gradients()` in `simulations.py`. This function uses **two-point central finite differences** with a default displacement of `1e-5` Å. For a molecule with N atoms, it requires `3N + 1` single-point energy evaluations (3N displaced geometries plus the reference).

The implementation supports **parallel execution** via `joblib.Parallel`. When multiple threads are used, the model's thread count is temporarily set to 1 per worker to avoid oversubscription, then restored after computation. This is essential for models with internal parallelism (e.g., Fortran-backed KREG). The function can optionally return the full molecular database of displaced geometries for debugging or analysis purposes.

A companion function `numerical_hessian()` handles numerical Hessian computation with a larger default displacement of `5.29167e-4` Å (approximately 0.001 Bohr), which is appropriate for the second-order finite differences used in Hessian calculations.

Sources: [simulations.py](mlatom/simulations.py#L960-L1010)

## Usage Patterns

### Basic Minimum Energy Optimization

```python
import mlatom as ml

# Define the molecule and model
mol = ml.data.molecule()
mol.read_from_xyz_file(filename='ethanol.xyz')
aiqm1 = ml.models.methods(method='AIQM1', qm_program='MNDO')

# Run optimization (auto-selects backend)
geomopt = ml.simulations.optimize_geometry(
    model=aiqm1,
    initial_molecule=mol,
    program='ASE'
)

# Access results
optmol = geomopt.optimized_molecule
geo = optmol.get_xyz_coordinates()
energy = optmol.energy
gradient = optmol.get_energy_gradients()
```

### Constrained Optimization with Geometric

```python
geomopt = ml.simulations.optimize_geometry(
    model=my_model,
    initial_molecule=mol,
    program='geometric',
    constraints={
        'bonds': [[1.09, [0, 1]]],
        'dihedrals': [[180.0, [0, 1, 2, 3]]]
    },
    maximum_number_of_steps=500
)
```

### Transition State Search

```python
# Dimer method via ASE
ts_opt = ml.simulations.optimize_geometry(
    model=my_model,
    initial_molecule=ts_guess,
    ts=True,
    program='ASE',
    optimization_algorithm='dimer'
)

# QST3 via Gaussian
ts_opt = ml.simulations.optimize_geometry(
    model=my_model,
    molecule=ts_guess,
    ts=True,
    reactants=reactant_mol,
    products=product_mol,
    program='Gaussian',
    optimization_algorithm='qst3'
)
```

### Trajectory Inspection

```python
# Enable trajectory dumping during optimization
geomopt = ml.simulations.optimize_geometry(
    model=my_model,
    initial_molecule=mol,
    program='geometric',
    dump_trajectory_interval=1,
    filename='opt_traj.json'
)

# Iterate through optimization steps
for step in geomopt.optimization_trajectory.steps:
    print(f"Step {step.step}: E = {step.molecule.energy:.6f} Ha")
```

Sources: [simulations.py](mlatom/simulations.py#L134-L151)

## Parallel Geometry Optimization

The `run_in_parallel()` function in `simulations.py` enables batch optimization across multiple molecules simultaneously. It uses `joblib.Parallel` for distribution and handles thread-per-model allocation intelligently: when there are fewer molecules than available threads, each model receives multiple threads; when there are more molecules than threads, each gets one.

The function supports optional temporary directory creation for each parallel job (useful for external program backends that may have file I/O conflicts), error-tolerant execution via `proceed_on_error`, and thread-count management for models with internal parallelism — the same pattern used by `numerical_gradients`.

Sources: [simulations.py](mlatom/simulations.py#L25-L90)

## CLI Integration

From the command line, geometry optimization is dispatched through `MLtasks.geomopt()` in `mlatom/MLtasks.py`, which parses the `geomopt` task from CLI arguments. The task loads the method/model, the molecular database, and delegates to `optimize_geometry`. A companion function `optfreq()` combines geometry optimization with frequency analysis — the natural next step for verifying that a stationary point is a true minimum (all real frequencies) or transition state (exactly one imaginary frequency).

Sources: [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L378-L454)

---

**Next Steps**: After completing geometry optimization, you will typically want to verify the nature of the stationary point through frequency analysis — see [Frequency and Thermochemistry Calculations](18-frequency-and-thermochemistry-calculations). For transition states, IRC analysis provides additional validation of the reaction path — see [Nonadiabatic and Surface-Hopping Dynamics](20-nonadiabatic-and-surface-hopping-dynamics) for advanced dynamics. To understand the model types that can drive these optimizations, consult [Model Class Hierarchy](9-model-class-hierarchy). For deeper exploration of how external programs are wrapped, see [Quantum Chemistry Program Interfaces](14-quantum-chemistry-program-interfaces) and [ASE and Simulation Tool Integration](16-ase-and-simulation-tool-integration).

# Frequency and Thermochemistry Calculations



This page documents MLatom's frequency analysis and thermochemistry pipeline — the machinery that converts a stationary-point geometry into vibrational spectra, thermodynamic corrections, and heats of formation. The system unifies three computational backends (Gaussian, PySCF, and a built-in TorchANI-derived engine) behind a single `freq` class, then layers thermochemical analysis on top via the `thermochemistry` class. Understanding this pipeline is essential for validating molecular minima, predicting IR/Raman spectra, and computing Gibbs free energies that feed into [Geometry Optimization Workflows](17-geometry-optimization-workflows) and [Active Learning Pipeline](24-active-learning-pipeline).

## Architectural Overview

The frequency and thermochemistry subsystem lives entirely in [`mlatom/simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py) and connects to three external backends through the interfaces layer. The core data flow follows a strict topological ordering: model prediction → Hessian assembly → eigenvalue decomposition → normal mode extraction → intensity calculation → thermodynamic property assembly.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Input
        M[molecule object]
        MD[model / method]
    end

    subgraph "freq class"
        direction TB
        Init["freq.__init__()"]
        AutoDetect{Auto-detect<br/>program?}
        GW["Gaussian backend"]
        PW["PySCF backend"]
        Torch["Built-in TorchANI<br/>engine"]
        
        Init --> AutoDetect
        AutoDetect -->|"GAUSS_EXEDIR set"| GW
        AutoDetect -->|"pyscf installed"| PW
        AutoDetect -->|"fallback"| Torch
        
        GW --> FreqResult["frequencies, force_constants,<br/>reduced_masses, normal_modes"]
        PW --> FreqResult
        Torch --> FreqResult
    end

    subgraph "Optional Intensities"
        IR["ir_intensities()"]
        RM["raman_intensities()"]
        FreqResult -->|"ir=True"| IR
        FreqResult -->|"raman=True"| RM
        IR --> IRResult["molecule.infrared_intensities"]
        RM --> RMResult["molecule.raman_intensities"]
    end

    subgraph "thermochemistry class"
        TC["thermochemistry.__init__()"]
        FreqResult --> TC
        ASE_TC["ase_interface.thermochemistry()"]
        HOF["calculate_heats_of_formation()"]
        TC --> ASE_TC
        ASE_TC --> ThermProps["ZPE, H, H0, U0, G"]
        ThermProps --> HOF
        HOF --> DeltaHf["DeltaHf298"]
    end

    M --> Init
    MD --> Init
```

## Frequency Analysis Engine

The `freq` class ([`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L440-L763)) is the central orchestrator. Upon instantiation, it automatically selects a computational backend, invokes the model for the Hessian, solves the vibrational eigenvalue problem, and optionally computes spectral intensities — all in a single constructor call.

### Constructor and Backend Selection

The constructor accepts a model (or QM method), a molecule, and several control flags. Backend selection follows a priority chain: if `program` is explicitly provided, it is used; otherwise the system probes for PySCF first, then checks the `GAUSS_EXEDIR` environment variable for Gaussian, and finally falls back to the built-in TorchANI-derived numerical engine ([`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L520-L538)).

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `model` | `model` or `methods` | `None` | Any model or method providing energies, forces, and Hessian |
| `molecule` | `data.molecule` | `None` | Molecule at a stationary point (energy minimum or transition state) |
| `program` | `str` | auto-detected | One of `'Gaussian'`, `'PySCF'`, `'ASE'`, or any other string for the built-in engine |
| `ir` | `bool` | `False` | Calculate infrared intensities (requires dipole derivative support) |
| `raman` | `bool` | `False` | Calculate Raman intensities (requires polarizability derivative support) |
| `normal_mode_normalization` | `str` | `'mass deweighted normalized'` | Normal mode convention: see Normal Mode Normalization section below |
| `anharmonic` | `bool` | `False` | Request anharmonic frequency calculation (Gaussian only) |
| `anharmonic_kwargs` | `dict` | `{}` | Additional keywords for anharmonic calculations (Gaussian only) |
| `working_directory` | `str` | `'.'` | Directory for temporary/intermediate files |

When `ir=True`, the constructor automatically injects `calculate_dipole_derivatives=True` into the model's prediction kwargs ([`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L515-L516)). Similarly, `raman=True` injects `calculate_polarizability_derivatives=True` ([`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L517-L519)). This design ensures models are queried for exactly the properties needed without requiring the user to manually wire these flags.

### The Built-in TorchANI-Derived Engine

The default computational path — `freq_modified_from_TorchANI` ([`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L650-L762)) — is adapted from TorchANI (citing Gao et al., J. Chem. Inf. Model. 2020, 60, 3408). It performs the complete harmonic analysis pipeline in four stages.

**Stage 1 — Model prediction.** The model is called with `calculate_energy=True`, `calculate_energy_gradients=True`, and `calculate_hessian=True` to obtain the full Hessian matrix ([`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L685-L686)). If the model only provides energies, the system falls back to [`numerical_hessian()`](mlatom/simulations.py#L1011-L1037), which computes second derivatives via two-point numerical differentiation of gradients.

**Stage 2 — Mass-weighted eigenvalue problem.** The Hessian is converted to mass-weighted coordinates through Löwdin diagonalization. Given Hessian **H** and diagonal mass matrix **T**, the system solves **T**⁻¹/² **H** **T**⁻¹/² **q'** = ω² **q'** where **q'** = **T**¹/² **q** ([`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L690-L701)). The eigenvalues yield angular frequencies, which are converted to wavenumbers (cm⁻¹) via the unit converter `17091.7006789297` ([`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L688-L716)).

**Stage 3 — Normal mode transformation.** Eigenvectors (the columns of the eigenvalue solution) represent mass-weighted normalized (MWN) modes. These are then transformed to the requested normalization convention ([`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L722-L738)):

- **MWN** → **MDU**: divide by √(mass) for each Cartesian component
- **MDU** → **MDN**: normalize each mode vector to unit length

Reduced masses are computed as the square of the MDU normalization factors (in AMU), and force constants are converted from Ha/(AMU·Å²) to mDyne/Å using the factor `4.359744650780506` ([`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L688), [`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L728-L731)).

**Stage 4 — Attribute assignment.** The resulting `frequencies` (cm⁻¹), `force_constants` (mDyne/Å), `reduced_masses` (AMU), and per-atom `normal_modes` arrays are stored directly on the molecule object ([`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L754-L761)). By default, all eigenvalues are returned (including translational/rotational modes), since filtering logic was commented out due to ambiguity around negative frequency handling at saddle points ([`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L742-L753)).

> [!TIP]
> The built-in engine does **not** filter out translational and rotational modes (the first 5–6 eigenvalues). Downstream consumers such as the thermochemistry module handle this filtering themselves. If you are consuming frequencies directly, be aware that the array includes these non-vibrational entries.

### Gaussian and PySCF Backends

The **Gaussian backend** (`freq_gaussian`, [`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L548-L569)) delegates the entire frequency calculation to Gaussian via an external interface. It serializes the model and molecule to JSON, invokes Gaussian with either `Freq` or `Freq(anharmonic)` keywords, and then parses the output back. Anharmonic calculations are supported by passing `anharmonic=True` and optional `anharmonic_kwargs` such as `['NoRaman']` ([`gaussian_interface.py`](mlatom/interfaces/gaussian_interface.py#L188-L199)).

The **PySCF backend** (`freq_pyscf`, [`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L571-L576)) calls `model.predict()` with `calculate_hessian=True`, then delegates thermodynamic analysis to `pyscf_interface.thermo_calculation()`. This path also invokes `thermo_modified_from_pyscf()` for the full statistical thermodynamics treatment ([`pyscf_interface.py`](mlatom/interfaces/pyscf_interface.py#L376-L537)).

### Numerical Differentiation Utilities

For models that lack analytical Hessians, MLatom provides [`numerical_hessian()`](mlatom/simulations.py#L1011-L1037) and [`numerical_gradients()`](mlatom/simulations.py#L960-L1009). The Hessian function uses a nested two-point scheme: outer loop displaces each coordinate by `displacement` (default 5.29167×10⁻⁴ Å ≈ 0.001 bohr) and computes numerical gradients at each displaced geometry, which themselves use two-point differentiation with `displacement4grads` (default 1×10⁻⁵ Å). All single-point calculations are parallelized via `joblib` ([`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L995-L1004)).

| Function | Default displacement | Parallelized | Output location |
|----------|---------------------|--------------|-----------------|
| `numerical_gradients()` | 1×10⁻⁵ Å | Yes (via joblib) | `molecule.energy_gradients` |
| `numerical_hessian()` | 5.29167×10⁻⁴ Å | Yes (inner gradients) | `molecule.hessian` |

## Normal Mode Normalization Conventions

Different quantum chemistry packages output normal modes in different coordinate representations. MLatom's frequency engine supports all three major conventions, which is critical when interfacing with external programs or when composing model trees in [Model Class Hierarchy](9-model-class-hierarchy).

The transformation chain and orthogonality properties are summarized below. Let **L** = **T**⁻¹/² **Q** where **Q** are the eigenvectors and **T** is the mass matrix.

| Convention | Abbreviation | Formula from eigenvectors | Orthogonal? | Normalized? | Used by |
|------------|-------------|--------------------------|-------------|-------------|---------|
| Mass-weighted normalized | MWN | **L** (raw eigenvectors) | Yes | Yes | Internal computation |
| Mass-deweighted unnormalized | MDU | **L** · diag(1/√mᵢ) | No | No | ASE |
| Mass-deweighted normalized | MDN | MDU / ‖MDU‖ | No | Yes | Gaussian, ORCA (default in MLatom) |

When `ir=True` or `raman=True` with a non-Gaussian backend, the intensity calculation methods internally convert the stored modes from the requested normalization back through the chain: MDN → MWN (by rescaling with √mass and re-normalizing) → MDU (by dividing by √mass), because the dipole/polarizability derivative contraction requires mass-deweighted unnormalized modes ([`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L587-L604), [`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L617-L633)).

> [!TIP]
> If you switch `normal_mode_normalization` to `'mass weighted normalized'`, the `ir_intensities()` and `raman_intensities()` methods will return early without computation ([`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L605), [`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L635)). Always use `'mass deweighted normalized'` or `'mass deweighted unnormalized'` when requesting spectral intensities.

## IR and Raman Intensity Calculation

### Infrared Intensities

The `ir_intensities()` method ([`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L581-L611)) computes IR intensities in km/mol from dipole derivatives (expected in Debye/Å) using the formula:

*I*ₖ = κ · Σₜ (∂μₜ/∂Qₖ)²

where κ is a composite physical constant involving the fine structure constant, Avogadro's number, Bohr-to-Ångström conversion, and Debye unit conversion ([`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L585)). The dipole derivatives are reshaped to a (3N×3) matrix and contracted with the mass-deweighted unnormalized normal modes via `np.dot` and `np.einsum` ([`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L606-L611)).

### Raman Intensities

The `raman_intensities()` method ([`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L613-L647)) computes Raman scattering activities from polarizability derivatives. For each normal mode, the isotropic (ᾱ²) and anisotropic (γ²) invariants are computed:

ᾱ² = (α'ₓₓ + α'ᵧᵧ + α'ᵤᵤ)² / 9

γ² = [(α'ₓₓ − α'ᵧᵧ)² + (α'ₓₓ − α'ᵤᵤ)² + (α'ᵧᵧ − α'ᵤᵤ)² + 6(α'²ₓᵧ + α'²ₓᵤ + α'²ᵧᵤ)] / 2

The final Raman activity is 45·ᾱ² + 7·γ², converted to Å⁴/AMU using unit conversion constants ([`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L640-L647)). These activities feed into the [`raman`](mlatom/spectra.py#L497-L537) spectrum class for Lorentzian broadening.

## Thermochemistry Calculations

The `thermochemistry` class ([`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L764-L866)) builds directly on top of the `freq` class, adding statistical thermodynamic analysis and heats of formation. It always begins by running a frequency calculation, then dispatches to the appropriate backend for thermodynamic property evaluation.

### Initialization and Dispatch

The constructor ([`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L814-L829)) follows the same backend auto-detection logic as `freq`: PySCF is preferred, then Gaussian, with ASE available as an explicit option. After frequency analysis completes, if the program is ASE, it calls `ase_interface.thermochemistry()`; otherwise it proceeds directly to `calculate_heats_of_formation()`.

### ASE Thermochemistry Backend

The ASE path ([`ase_interface.py`](mlatom/interfaces/ase_interface.py#L214-L261)) wraps ASE's `IdealGasThermo` class. It first filters out negative frequencies (printing a warning for each), converts frequencies from cm⁻¹ to eV, and determines molecular geometry (linear vs. nonlinear) from `molecule.shape`. The `IdealGasThermo` object is constructed with vibrational energies, potential energy (converted from Hartree), molecular geometry, symmetry number, and spin multiplicity. All thermodynamic quantities are computed at 298.15 K and 101325 Pa, then converted from eV → kcal/mol → Hartree ([`ase_interface.py`](mlatom/interfaces/ase_interface.py#L249-L260)).

### Available Thermodynamic Properties

After a `thermochemistry` calculation, the following attributes are populated on the molecule object:

| Property | Description | Backend availability |
|----------|-------------|---------------------|
| `ZPE` | Zero-point vibrational energy | All |
| `H0` | Enthalpy at 0 K | All |
| `U0` | Internal energy at 0 K (equal to H0) | All |
| `H` | Enthalpy at 298.15 K | All |
| `G` | Gibbs free energy at 298.15 K | All |
| `DeltaE2U` | Thermal correction to internal energy | Gaussian only |
| `DeltaE2H` | Thermal correction to enthalpy | Gaussian only |
| `DeltaE2G` | Thermal correction to Gibbs energy | Gaussian only |
| `U` | Internal energy at 298.15 K | Gaussian only |
| `S` | Entropy at 298.15 K | Gaussian only |
| `atomization_energy_0K` | Atomization energy at 0 K | All (if model supports atoms) |
| `ZPE_exclusive_atomization_energy_0K` | ZPE-corrected atomization energy | All (if model supports atoms) |
| `DeltaHf298` | Heat of formation at 298 K | All (if model supports atoms) |

### Heats of Formation

The `calculate_heats_of_formation()` method ([`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L835-L865)) computes ΔHf₂₉₈ by an atomization energy scheme. For each atom in the molecule, it creates a single-atom molecule, predicts its energy, and sums atomic contributions. The atomization energy is then:

Eₐₜₒₘ = Σ E(atom) − U₀(molecule)

The heat of formation is assembled as:

ΔHf₂₉₈ = Σ H₀(atom) − Eₐₜₒₘ + (H₂₉₈ − H₀)(molecule) − Σ ΔH(atom)

where ΔH(atom) = 1.4811 kcal/mol × conversion factor is applied to each atom ([`simulations.py`](mlatom/simulations.py#L848-L862)). If the model cannot predict single-atom energies (common for some ML potentials), the method silently returns without setting `DeltaHf298`.

## Usage Examples

### Basic Frequency Calculation with ML Model

```python
import mlatom as ml

# Load optimized geometry
mol = ml.data.molecule()
mol.read_from_xyz_file(filename='ethanol.xyz')

# Use any supported model or method
model = ml.models.methods(method='AIQM1', qm_program='MNDO')

# Run frequency analysis (auto-detects backend)
ml.simulations.freq(model=model, molecule=mol)
print(f"Frequencies (cm⁻¹): {mol.frequencies}")
```

### Frequency with IR and Raman Intensities

```python
import mlatom as ml

mol = ml.data.molecule()
mol.read_from_xyz_file(filename='benzene.xyz')

model = ml.models.methods(method='wB97X/6-31G*', qm_program='Gaussian')

# Request both IR and Raman in a single call
ml.simulations.freq(
    model=model, 
    molecule=mol, 
    ir=True, 
    raman=True,
    program='ASE'
)
print(f"IR intensities (km/mol): {mol.infrared_intensities}")
print(f"Raman activities (Å⁴/AMU): {mol.raman_intensities}")
```

### Full Thermochemistry with Heat of Formation

```python
import mlatom as ml

mol = ml.data.molecule()
mol.read_from_xyz_file(filename='ethanol.xyz')
mol.multiplicity = 1
mol.shape = 'nonlinear'
mol.symmetry_number = 1  # set if known for better accuracy

model = ml.models.methods(method='AIQM1', qm_program='MNDO')

# Complete thermochemistry analysis
ml.simulations.thermochemistry(model=model, molecule=mol, program='ASE')

print(f"ZPE:             {mol.ZPE:.6f} Hartree")
print(f"H0:              {mol.H0:.6f} Hartree")
print(f"H (298.15 K):    {mol.H:.6f} Hartree")
print(f"G (298.15 K):    {mol.G:.6f} Hartree")
if hasattr(mol, 'DeltaHf298'):
    print(f"ΔHf (298 K):     {mol.DeltaHf298:.6f} Hartree")
```

### Numerical Hessian for Models Without Analytical Hessians

```python
import mlatom as ml
import numpy as np

mol = ml.data.molecule()
mol.read_from_xyz_file(filename='molecule.xyz')

model = ml.models.methods(method='AIQM1', qm_program='MNDO')

# Compute Hessian numerically, then run frequency analysis
ml.simulations.numerical_hessian(mol, model)
ml.simulations.freq(model=model, molecule=mol, program='ASE')
```

The complete frequency-to-spectra pipeline continues in [IR and Raman Spectra Calculation](21-ir-and-raman-spectra-calculation), where the computed frequencies and intensities are broadened into continuous spectra using the `ir` and `raman` classes from [`spectra.py`](mlatom/spectra.py#L455-L537). For broader context on how these calculations fit into optimization workflows, see [Geometry Optimization Workflows](17-geometry-optimization-workflows); for the model capabilities required (Hessian prediction, dipole derivatives), consult [Model Class Hierarchy](9-model-class-hierarchy) and [Quantum Chemistry Program Interfaces](14-quantum-chemistry-program-interfaces).

# Molecular Dynamics Engine



The Molecular Dynamics (MD) engine in MLatom propagates nuclear motion on potential energy surfaces provided by any supported model—whether a machine learning potential like AIQM1 or a conventional quantum chemistry method. It implements a Velocity Verlet integrator with support for both NVE and NVT ensembles, three thermostat families, multiple initial condition sampling strategies, and both single-trajectory and batch-parallel execution modes. This page covers the core MD machinery; for dynamics involving electronic transitions, see [Nonadiabatic and Surface-Hopping Dynamics](20-nonadiabatic-and-surface-hopping-dynamics).

Sources: [md.py](mlatom/md.py#L1-L9), [md_parallel.py](mlatom/md_parallel.py#L1-L9)

## Architecture Overview

The MD engine is organized as a layered system: initial conditions feed into a propagation loop that delegates thermostatting to pluggable thermostat objects, and trajectory output is handled through the molecular trajectory data layer.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Entry Points"
        A["md_cmd.py<br/>CLI interface"]
        B["md class<br/>Python API"]
        C["md_parallel class<br/>Batch trajectories"]
    end

    subgraph "Propagation Core"
        D["Velocity Verlet Integrator"]
        E["nve propagation_algorithm<br/>(passthrough)"]
        F["Thermostat propagation_algorithm<br/>(modifies velocities)"]
    end

    subgraph "Thermostat Hierarchy"
        G["Thermostat (base)"]
        H["Andersen_thermostat"]
        I["Nose_Hoover_thermostat"]
        J["Langevin_thermostat"]
    end

    subgraph "Initial Conditions"
        K["generate_initial_conditions()"]
        K1["user-defined"]
        K2["random / Maxwell-Boltzmann"]
        K3["Wigner sampling"]
        K4["harmonic-quantum-boltzmann"]
    end

    subgraph "Output & Analysis"
        L["molecular_trajectory"]
        M["md2vibr.py<br/>Vibrational spectra"]
    end

    B --> D
    C --> D
    A --> B
    D --> E
    D --> F
    F --> H
    F --> I
    F --> J
    H --> G
    I --> G
    J --> G
    K --> B
    K --> A
    K --> K1 & K2 & K3 & K4
    D --> L
    L --> M
```

The design follows a **strategy pattern** for thermostatting: the `md` class holds a reference `self.propagation_algorithm` that points to either an `nve()` passthrough object or a thermostat instance. Both expose the same two-phase interface (`update_velocities_first_half_step` and `update_velocities_second_half_step`), making them interchangeable behind the propagation loop.

Sources: [md.py](mlatom/md.py#L132-L135), [thermostat.py](mlatom/thermostat.py#L13-L18)

## Velocity Verlet Integration

The core integrator follows the standard Velocity Verlet scheme adapted for MLatom's internal unit system (energy in Hartree, distance in Ångström, time in femtoseconds). At each propagation step after the initial one, the algorithm executes:

**1. First velocity half-step** — Delegated to the propagation algorithm (thermostat or NVE passthrough).

**2. Coordinate update** — Positions advance according to `coord = coord + v·dt + 0.5·a·dt²` [md.py](mlatom/md.py#L190).

**3. Second velocity half-step (pre-force)** — `v = v + 0.5·a·dt` [md.py](mlatom/md.py#L193).

**4. Force evaluation** — The model predicts energy and gradients; acceleration is computed as `a = -∇E / m · (1/ram2au) · (Bohr²/Å²) · (fs²/au²)` to convert from Hartree/Bohr forces into Å/fs² accelerations [md.py](mlatom/md.py#L200-L201).

**5. Second velocity half-step (post-force)** — `v = v + 0.5·a·dt` [md.py](mlatom/md.py#L204).

**6. Optional momentum removal** — If `eliminate_momentum=True`, both center-of-mass translation and rigid-body rotation are stripped from velocities [md.py](mlatom/md.py#L207-L211).

**7. Thermostat second half-step** — Completes the velocity modification for the current timestep [md.py](mlatom/md.py#L217-L218).

The loop terminates either when `step × dt ≥ maximum_propagation_time` or when a user-defined `stop_function` returns `True`. At step zero, the engine only computes initial forces and records the starting geometry—no position or velocity updates occur.

Sources: [md.py](mlatom/md.py#L158-L247), [md.py](mlatom/md.py#L264-L276)

## The `md` Class: Single-Trajectory Dynamics

The primary entry point for running one MD trajectory. Instantiating `ml.md()` automatically triggers propagation via its constructor.

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `model` | `model` or `methods` | `None` | Any model providing energies and gradients |
| `molecule_with_initial_conditions` | `data.molecule` | `None` | Molecule with initial coordinates and velocities |
| `molecule` | `data.molecule` | `None` | Alias (mutually exclusive with above) |
| `ensemble` | `str` | `'NVE'` | Ensemble type: `'NVE'` or `'NVT'` |
| `thermostat` | `Thermostat` | `None` | Thermostat instance (required for NVT) |
| `time_step` | `float` | `0.1` | Integration timestep in femtoseconds |
| `maximum_propagation_time` | `float` | `1000` | Maximum propagation time in femtoseconds |
| `dump_trajectory_interval` | `int` or `None` | `None` | Dump interval in steps (`None` disables) |
| `filename` | `str` or `None` | `None` | Trajectory output file |
| `format` | `str` | `'h5md'` | Output format: `'h5md'` or `'json'` |
| `eliminate_momentum` | `bool` | `False` | Remove translational and angular momentum each step |
| `stop_function` | `callable` | `None` | User-defined early termination callback |
| `stop_function_kwargs` | `dict` | `None` | Keyword arguments for `stop_function` |

The constructor automatically detects molecular linearity to set degrees of freedom (3N−5 for linear, 3N−6 for nonlinear) and begins propagation immediately. The resulting trajectory is accessible at `dyn.molecular_trajectory` as a `data.molecular_trajectory` object. Each step records `time`, `step`, `total_energy`, and `temperature` alongside the molecular state.

Sources: [md.py](mlatom/md.py#L99-L156), [md.py](mlatom/md.py#L219-L226)

## The `md_parallel` Class: Batch Trajectory Propagation

For workflows that require propagating many independent trajectories simultaneously (e.g., ensemble-averaged property calculations or nonadiabatic MD), `md_parallel` operates on a `molecular_database` of initial conditions rather than a single molecule. The key architectural differences from `md` are:

- **Batch force evaluation**: All active trajectories are predicted in a single model call at each step [md_parallel.py](mlatom/md_parallel.py#L168-L170).
- **Per-trajectory stop functions**: Each trajectory is independently tracked by a `stop_array` boolean mask; terminated trajectories are excluded from subsequent force evaluations [md_parallel.py](mlatom/md_parallel.py#L231-L248).
- **Excess energy redistribution**: An `excess_energy` parameter injects kinetic energy uniformly across the trajectory duration via `rescale_velocity`, scaling velocities at each step to match the target kinetic energy [md_parallel.py](mlatom/md_parallel.py#L209-L214).
- **Trajectory length tracking**: `molecular_trajectory.traj_len` stores the final step index for each trajectory, which is essential for computing ensemble averages when trajectories terminate at different times [md_parallel.py](mlatom/md_parallel.py#L255-L257).

The class does not currently expose a `Langevin_thermostat` import, limiting parallel NVT dynamics to Andersen and Nose-Hoover thermostats.

Sources: [md_parallel.py](mlatom/md_parallel.py#L17-L151), [md_parallel.py](mlatom/md_parallel.py#L261-L264)

## Thermostat System

All thermostats extend a common `Thermostat` base class and expose the two-phase velocity update interface expected by the propagation loop. The system supports three distinct thermostatting strategies.

### Andersen Thermostat

The Andersen thermostat implements stochastic collisions: at each timestep, each atom has a probability `p = γ · dt` of having its velocity replaced by a random sample from the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution at the target temperature. The velocity modulus is computed from the atom's mass and the target temperature, accounting for the unit conversion chain (K → kcal/mol → Hartree → Å/fs units). The `gamma` parameter (collision rate, default 0.2 fs⁻¹) controls the strength of thermostatting—higher values produce tighter temperature control at the cost of dynamical realism.

Sources: [thermostat.py](mlatom/thermostat.py#L20-L93)

### Nose-Hoover Thermostat

The Nose-Hoover chain thermostat is the most sophisticated option, implementing a multi-stage integration based on the Martyna-Klein-Tuckerman scheme (DOI: 10.1080/00268979600100761). It nests three configurable parameters:

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `nose_hoover_chain_length` | 3 | Number of thermostat "beads" in the chain |
| `multiple_time_steps` (Nc) | 3 | Number of sub-divisions per timestep |
| `number_of_yoshida_suzuki_steps` (Nys) | 7 | Integration order (1, 3, 5, or 7) |
| `nose_hoover_chain_frequency` | 1/16 ≈ 0.0625 fs⁻¹ | Oscillation frequency of chain variables |
| `temperature` | 300 K | Target temperature |
| `degrees_of_freedom` | auto | Can be a negative offset from 3N |

The Yoshida-Suzuki coefficients are precomputed at initialization for the selected order (1, 3, 5, or 7). The effective masses `NHC_Q` follow the convention where Q₁ = N_dof·kT/ω² and Qᵢ = kT/ω² for i > 1, ensuring proper ergodic sampling. The thermostat applies a cumulative velocity scaling factor computed from the chain variables' evolution, which can be restored across checkpoint restarts via the `NHC_xi` and `NHC_vxi` keyword arguments.

Sources: [thermostat.py](mlatom/thermostat.py#L95-L278)

### Langevin Thermostat

The Langevin thermostat applies friction and stochastic kicks using the BAOAB-like splitting scheme (DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevE.75.056707). At each half-step, velocities are damped by factor `C₁ = exp(−τ·dt/2)` and then perturbed by Gaussian noise with standard deviation `C₂ = √(k_BT·(1−C₁²)/m)`. The `tau` parameter (default 0.001 fs⁻¹) controls friction strength. Unlike Andersen, which acts on individual atoms stochastically, Langevin applies continuous friction to all atoms simultaneously, making it particularly suitable for condensed-phase simulations.

Sources: [thermostat.py](mlatom/thermostat.py#L280-L337)

### Thermostat Comparison

| Feature | Andersen | Nose-Hoover | Langevin |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deterministic | No (stochastic) | Yes (deterministic) | No (stochastic) |
| Velocity modification | Replace per-atom | Scale globally | Damp + perturb per-atom |
| Key parameter | `gamma` (collision rate) | `NHC_frequency` (chain freq) | `tau` (friction coeff) |
| Configurable chain length | N/A | Yes (`NHC_length`) | N/A |
| Parallel trajectory support | Yes | Yes | No (single-trajectory only) |
| Typical use case | Gas-phase sampling | Canonical ensemble properties | Condensed-phase dynamics |

Sources: [md.py](mlatom/md.py#L96-L98), [md_parallel.py](mlatom/md_parallel.py#L96-L97)

## Initial Condition Generation

Initial conditions are prepared through the `ml.generate_initial_conditions()` function, which supports multiple sampling strategies. The choice of method determines what information the input molecule must carry (coordinates only, or coordinates plus Hessian/frequencies).

| Method | Required on molecule | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `'user-defined'` | Coordinates | Loads positions and velocities from separate XYZ/VXYZ files |
| `'random'` | Coordinates | Generates random velocities at a target temperature or kinetic energy |
| `'maxwell-boltzmann'` | Coordinates | Samples velocities from the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution |
| `'wigner'` | Coordinates + Hessian | Wigner nuclear sampling (modified from Newton-X) |
| `'harmonic-quantum-boltzmann'` | Coordinates + frequencies | Harmonic quantum Boltzmann sampling (J. Phys. Chem. A 1998, 102, 3648) |

All methods except `'user-defined'` can automatically eliminate angular momentum by default. The Wigner sampler requires a Hessian matrix (obtainable via `ml.models.methods.predict(molecule=mol, calculate_hessian=True)`), while the harmonic quantum Boltzmann sampler requires pre-computed normal mode frequencies. An optional excitation energy window filter can reject samples whose vertical excitation energies fall outside a specified range—useful for targeted nonadiabatic dynamics studies.

> [!TIP]
> When using the `'random'` or `'wigner'` methods, the `degrees_of_freedom` parameter can be specified as a negative integer (e.g., `-6`) which is interpreted as `3N - 6`, automatically accounting for the number of atoms. This is the default convention throughout the MD engine and CLI interface.

Sources: [initial_conditions.py](mlatom/initial_conditions.py#L105-L304), [initial_conditions.py](mlatom/initial_conditions.py#L219-L226)

## CLI Interface

The command-line interface in `md_cmd.py` maps directly to the Python API through the `MD_CMD.dynamics()` classmethod. All key parameters have CLI counterparts:

| CLI Flag | Python Equivalent | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `dt` | `time_step` | 0.1 fs |
| `trun` | `maximum_propagation_time` | 1000 fs |
| `initXYZ` | (file path argument) | `''` |
| `initVXYZ` | (file path argument) | `''` |
| `initConditions` | `generation_method` | `''` (user-defined) |
| `ensemble` | `ensemble` | `'nve'` |
| `thermostat` | thermostat type | `''` |
| `temperature` | `temperature` | 300 K |
| `gamma` | `gamma` (Andersen) | 0.2 fs⁻¹ |
| `initTemperature` | `initial_temperature` | 300 K |
| `trajH5MDout` | `filename` (H5MD) | `'traj.h5'` |
| `trajTextOut` | output plain text | `'traj'` |

The CLI automatically detects linear molecules to set the correct degrees of freedom and always enables angular momentum elimination (`noang=1`). The `randomSeed` option allows reproducible initial condition generation.

Sources: [md_cmd.py](mlatom/md_cmd.py#L12-L51), [md_cmd.py](mlatom/md_cmd.py#L58-L222)

## Trajectory Output and Checkpointing

The MD engine supports two trajectory serialization formats:

- **H5MD** (`.h5`): HDF5-based format, efficient for large trajectories and compatible with the molecular trajectory data layer. Each dump interval appends to the file incrementally.
- **JSON**: Plain-text JSON format, suitable for inspection and post-processing.

When `dump_trajectory_interval` is set, the engine writes trajectory snapshots at that cadence. If no `filename` is provided, a UUID-based name is generated automatically. The `dump_md_checkpoint` method writes a human-readable checkpoint file containing the last step's coordinates, velocities, ensemble type, and full thermostat state—enabling exact restart of interrupted simulations.

Sources: [md.py](mlatom/md.py#L137-L145), [md.py](mlatom/md.py#L237-L245), [md.py](mlatom/md.py#L249-L262)

## Gap-Driven Dynamics

The `gap_md` class in `gap_md.py` extends the single-surface MD engine to handle dynamics on two electronic states with automatic surface switching. It wraps a standard model with a `gap_model` adapter that intercepts energy and gradient predictions, returning values for either the lower or upper surface based on whether the current nuclear geometry places the system above or below a configurable energy gap threshold. At each step, velocities are rescaled by a factor `√(1 − ΔE/E_kin)` to approximately conserve total energy across surface hops. This provides a lightweight alternative to full nonadiabatic surface hopping when only two states are relevant.

Sources: [gap_md.py](mlatom/gap_md.py#L16-L37), [gap_md.py](mlatom/gap_md.py#L91-L158)

## Post-Processing: Vibrational Spectra from Trajectories

The `md2vibr.py` module converts MD trajectories into vibrational spectra through time-correlation analysis. The `vibrational_spectrum` class accepts a `molecular_database` (or trajectory) and timestep, then computes either infrared spectra (from dipole moment autocorrelation) or power spectra (from velocity autocorrelation). Key processing steps include Hann windowing, mean removal, zero-padding, and normalization. The Fourier transform implementation uses numpy's FFT with proper scaling for frequency-domain representation.

Sources: [md2vibr.py](mlatom/md2vibr.py#L16-L188)

## Usage Example: Complete NVT Dynamics

The following workflow demonstrates a typical MD simulation with Nose-Hoover thermostatting, from initial condition generation through trajectory analysis:

```python
import mlatom as ml

# 1. Load molecular geometry
mol = ml.data.molecule()
mol.read_from_xyz_file(filename='ethanol.xyz')

# 2. Set up the model
aiqm1 = ml.models.methods(method='AIQM1')

# 3. Generate initial conditions (user-defined velocities)
init_cond_db = ml.generate_initial_conditions(
    molecule=mol,
    generation_method='user-defined',
    file_with_initial_xyz_coordinates='ethanol.xyz',
    file_with_initial_xyz_velocities='ethanol.vxyz'
)
init_mol = init_cond_db.molecules[0]

# 4. Configure thermostat
nose_hoover = ml.md.Nose_Hoover_thermostat(
    temperature=300,
    molecule=init_mol,
    degrees_of_freedom=-6  # 3N - 6
)

# 5. Run dynamics (propagation starts automatically)
dyn = ml.md(
    model=aiqm1,
    molecule_with_initial_conditions=init_mol,
    ensemble='NVT',
    thermostat=nose_hoover,
    time_step=0.5,
    maximum_propagation_time=10.0,
    dump_trajectory_interval=1,
    filename='traj.h5',
    format='h5md'
)

# 6. Access results
traj = dyn.molecular_trajectory
traj.dump(filename='traj', format='plain_text')

# 7. Optional: save checkpoint for restart
dyn.dump_md_checkpoint(filename='md_chk')
```

> [!TIP]
> Energy and distance units in MLatom are always **Hartree** and **Ångström** respectively. The acceleration conversion factor `1/ram2au · (Bohr/Å)² · (fs/au)²` at [md.py#L172](mlatom/md.py#L172) handles the internal unit transform from model-predicted Hartree/Bohr gradients to Å/fs² accelerations. If using a custom model with different native units, you must ensure consistency before passing it to the MD engine.

Sources: [md.py](mlatom/md.py#L57-L94), [md.py](mlatom/md.py#L172-L173)

## Next Steps

- **[Nonadiabatic and Surface-Hopping Dynamics](20-nonadiabatic-and-surface-hopping-dynamics)** — For dynamics involving electronic state transitions, including fewest-switches surface hopping (FSSH) and Landau-Zener-based hopping algorithms.
- **[IR and Raman Spectra Calculation](21-ir-and-raman-spectra-calculation)** — For harmonic-frequency-based spectra as an alternative to the trajectory-correlation approach in `md2vibr.py`.
- **[Molecular Trajectory and HDF5 I/O](8-molecular-trajectory-and-hdf5-i-o)** — For details on the `molecular_trajectory` data structure used to store and serialize MD results.
