# UV-Vis Spectra and Nuclear Ensemble Approach



Computing accurate UV-Vis absorption spectra requires more than a single-point electronic structure calculation. Nuclear motion broadens spectral lines, shifts peak positions, and in some cases creates entirely new spectral features invisible at the equilibrium geometry. MLatom provides two complementary approaches to address this — the **single-point convolution (SPC)** method for quick estimates from a single geometry, and the **Nuclear Ensemble Approach (NEA)** for physically rigorous spectra that account for vibronic effects. Both are unified under a `uvvis` spectrum class that handles unit conversions, broadening, and visualization in a single consistent API.

Sources: [spectra.py](mlatom/spectra.py#L1-L16), [ML_NEA.py](mlatom/ML_NEA.py#L1-L9)

## Architectural Overview

The UV-Vis spectroscopy subsystem spans three layers: a pure-Python spectrum manipulation layer in `spectra.py`, a high-performance C++ cross-section engine in `cs.cpp`, and an end-to-end workflow orchestrator in `ML_NEA.py` that automates everything from molecular dynamics sampling through quantum chemistry calculations to spectrum generation. These layers share physical constants defined in `constants.py` and operate on the same [`molecule`](6-molecule-and-atom-classes) / [`molecular_database`](7-molecular-database-management) data structures used throughout MLatom.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "User API Layer"
        A["uvvis class<br/>(spectra.py)"]
        B["uvvis.spc()"]
        C["uvvis.nea()"]
        D["plot_uvvis()"]
    end

    subgraph "Spectrum Infrastructure"
        E["spectrum base class<br/>broaden / normalize<br/>interpolate / sample"]
        F["Broadening Functions<br/>Gaussian / Lorentzian / SPC"]
    end

    subgraph "Computation Layer"
        G["cs.so (C++/OpenMP)<br/>cross-section kernel"]
        H["Physical Constants<br/>hartree↔eV↔nm conversions"]
    end

    subgraph "ML-NEA Pipeline (ML_NEA.py)"
        I["NewtonXCalc<br/>Wigner sampling"]
        J["GaussCalc<br/>TD-DFT calculations"]
        K["ML_calc<br/>ML model predictions"]
        L["CrossSection_calc<br/>TD / ML / SPC"]
    end

    B --> E
    C --> G
    C --> E
    A --> D
    E --> F
    F --> H
    I --> J
    J --> L
    K --> L
    L --> G
```

The core physical constant linking wavelength and energy is `ev_nm_conversion_constant = h·c × 10⁹`, providing the conversion functions `eV2nm()` and `nm2eV()` used across all spectrum calculations.

Sources: [spectra.py](mlatom/spectra.py#L17-L114), [cs.cpp](mlatom/MLatomF_src/cs.cpp#L1-L17), [constants.py](mlatom/constants.py#L53-L62)

## The `spectrum` Base Class and the `uvvis` Subclass

All spectral types in MLatom inherit from the `spectrum` base class, which provides a general-purpose xy-data container with manipulation primitives. The constructor accepts either raw `x`/`y` arrays, pre-paired `xy_pairs`, or an `xy` matrix, and stores them internally as both column vectors and transposed pairs for flexible downstream access. Key capabilities include linear and cubic interpolation via SciPy, Riemann-sum normalization (average, sqrt, max, and MSC methods), spectrum broadening by arbitrary functions, range clipping, and data persistence to `.npy` or text formats.

The `broaden()` class method is the central convolution engine: it iterates over each point in a line spectrum, evaluates a user-supplied broadening function at every target wavelength, and accumulates the component curves into the final spectrum. Three built-in broadening functions are provided — `normalized_Gaussian`, `Gaussian`, and `Lorentzian` — each parameterized by peak position, intensity/scaling factor, x-range, and width parameter. This same mechanism is reused by both SPC and NEA to produce continuous spectra from discrete excitation data.

The `uvvis` subclass extends `spectrum` with UV-Vis-specific semantics. Its constructor accepts physical quantities directly — `wavelengths_nm`, `energies_eV`, `molar_absorbance`, and `cross_section` — and automatically derives the complementary representations using the conversion factor `1 Å²/molecule = 1/3.82353×10⁻⁵ M⁻¹cm⁻¹`. This means you can construct a spectrum from any consistent unit pair and immediately access all other representations without manual conversion.

Sources: [spectra.py](mlatom/spectra.py#L17-L282)

## Single-Point Convolution (SPC) Method

The SPC method generates a UV-Vis spectrum from excitation energies and oscillator strengths computed at a **single molecular geometry** (typically the equilibrium structure). It is the faster of the two approaches and is useful for quick spectral estimates, screening studies, or when nuclear ensemble data is unavailable. The implementation follows the methodology described in doi:[10.1007/s00894-020-04355-y](http://doi.org/10.1007/s00894-020-04355-y).

The method proceeds in three stages. First, excitation energies stored in Hartree on the molecule object are converted to eV using `constants.hartree2eV`. Second, a wavelength grid is automatically constructed spanning ±3 band widths beyond the extreme excitation energies. Third, the `broaden()` engine is invoked with a custom `spc_broadening_func` that computes Gaussian-broadened extinction coefficients at each wavelength:

$$\varepsilon(\lambda) = \frac{0.619 \cdot n \cdot f}{\delta \cdot 3.82353 \times 10^{-5}} \exp\!\left(-\frac{\left[\frac{hc}{\lambda} - \Delta E + \Delta E_{\text{shift}}\right]^2}{\delta^2}\right)$$

where `n` is the refractive index, `f` the oscillator strength, `δ` the band width in eV, and `ΔE_shift` an optional peak shift parameter. The prefactor 0.619 encodes the physical conversion from oscillator strength to molar absorbance.

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `molecule` | `mlatom.data.molecule` | required | Molecule with `excitation_energies` (Hartree) and `oscillator_strengths` |
| `band_width` | `float` | `0.3` | Gaussian broadening width in eV |
| `shift` | `float` | `0.0` | Energy shift applied to all peaks, in eV |
| `refractive_index` | `float` | `1.0` | Solvent refractive index correction |

The SPC method is a class method, invoked as `mlatom.spectra.uvvis.spc(molecule=mol, band_width=0.3)`. It returns a fully populated `uvvis` object with all unit representations available as attributes.

Sources: [spectra.py](mlatom/spectra.py#L287-L366)

## Nuclear Ensemble Approach (NEA) — Core API

The NEA produces a vibrationally-resolved UV-Vis spectrum by sampling an ensemble of nuclear geometries (typically via Wigner distribution from harmonic frequencies or from ab initio molecular dynamics trajectories) and computing vertical excitation properties at each geometry. This captures vibronic broadening, Herzberg-Teller effects, and temperature-dependent peak shifts that SPC cannot reproduce. The MLatom implementation follows the original NEA formulation from *Theor. Chem. Acc.* **2012**, *131*, 1237.

The `nea()` class method accepts a `molecular_database` where each molecule carries `excitation_energies` and `oscillator_strengths`. It automatically determines the energy range from the ensemble min/max, then delegates the cross-section calculation to a compiled C++ shared library (`cs.so`) via Python's `ctypes` FFI. The C++ kernel uses OpenMP parallelism to evaluate the absorption cross section at each wavelength point by summing Gaussian-broadened contributions across all ensemble geometries and all excited states:

$$\sigma(\tilde{E}) = \frac{C}{N \cdot \tilde{E}} \sum_{i=1}^{N_{\text{geom}}} \sum_{s=1}^{N_{\text{states}}} E_s^{(i)} \cdot f_s^{(i)} \cdot \exp\!\left(-\frac{(\tilde{E} - E_s^{(i)})^2}{2\delta^2}\right)$$

where `C` is a physical prefactor incorporating `π·e²/(2mₑ·c·ε₀)·h/(2π)·10²⁰` (converting to Å²·eV units), `N` is the number of ensemble geometries, and `δ` is the broadening width.

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `molecular_database` | `mlatom.data.molecular_database` | required | Ensemble with `excitation_energies` (Hartree) and `oscillator_strengths` |
| `wavelengths_nm` | `np.ndarray` | auto | Wavelength grid in nm; auto-computed if `None` |
| `broadening_width` | `float` | `0.05` | Gaussian broadening width in eV (narrower than SPC default) |

Note that the NEA default broadening width (0.05 eV) is significantly narrower than SPC's default (0.3 eV) because the nuclear ensemble itself provides much of the spectral broadening. The Python layer prepares C-type arrays from the molecular database, loads `cs.so` from the same directory as `spectra.py`, invokes the `cs_calc` entry point, and converts the resulting cross sections back to molar absorbance using the same conversion factor as SPC.

Sources: [spectra.py](mlatom/spectra.py#L368-L453), [cs.cpp](mlatom/MLatomF_src/cs.cpp#L49-L71)

## The C++ Cross-Section Kernel (`cs.so`)

The compiled shared library `cs.so` (built from [cs.cpp](mlatom/MLatomF_src/cs.cpp)) is the computational bottleneck solver for NEA cross-section calculations. It exposes a single `extern "C"` function `cs_calc` that accepts flat C arrays for excitation energies and oscillator strengths (indexed as `[state][geometry]`), the number of states, the number of geometry points, broadening parameters, and output buffers.

The function first precomputes `devided = -δ²/2` to avoid redundant division inside the inner loop, then distributes wavelength points across OpenMP threads with `schedule(dynamic)` for load balancing. Each thread calls `calc_at_de()` which iterates over all states and geometries, retrieving data via a `getValue()` accessor that maps the flat array layout to 2D indexing. The result at each energy point is `cs_coeff × Σ(E·f·Gauss) / (N·Ẽ)`.

The same `cs.so` library is used by both the main `uvvis.nea()` API and the standalone `ML_NEA.py` pipeline's `CrossSection_calc._calc_with_data()` method, ensuring consistent numerical results across both usage paths.

Sources: [cs.cpp](mlatom/MLatomF_src/cs.cpp#L1-L71)

> [!TIP]
> The C++ cross-section library (`cs.so`) must be pre-compiled from `MLatomF_src/cs.cpp` and placed alongside `spectra.py`. The `uvvis.nea()` method locates it via `os.path.abspath(__file__)` — if you encounter a missing shared library error, ensure the compiled `.so` file exists in the `mlatom/` directory.

## The ML-NEA Pipeline (ML_NEA.py)

Beyond the core API, MLatom ships a standalone end-to-end pipeline in `ML_NEA.py` that automates the entire NEA workflow — from generating the nuclear ensemble through Newton-X molecular dynamics, computing TD-DFT excitations with Gaussian, training ML models for excitation energies/oscillator strengths, and finally generating both QC-NEA and ML-NEA spectra. This pipeline was implemented by Bao-Xin Xue and is designed for reproducible paper-scale workflows.

### Pipeline Architecture

The pipeline is organized into several cooperating classes, each responsible for one stage of the workflow:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Sampling"
        A["NewtonXCalc<br/>Wigner/MD sampling"] --> B["xyz.dat<br/>N geometries"]
    end

    subgraph "QC Calculations"
        B --> C["GaussCalc<br/>TD-DFT on each geometry"]
        C --> D["E{s}.dat / f{s}.dat<br/>excitation data"]
    end

    subgraph "ML Augmentation"
        D --> E["ML_calc<br/>train ML model"]
        E --> F["predict remaining<br/>geometries"]
        F --> G["mix_single_file_data()<br/>QC+ML blended"]
    end

    subgraph "Spectrum Generation"
        D --> H["TD_cross_section<br/>QC-NEA spectrum"]
        G --> I["ML_cross_section<br/>ML-NEA spectrum"]
        H --> J["Plot & Compare"]
        I --> J
    end
```

### Cross-Section Calculation Variants

The `CrossSection_calc` base class defines the computational framework shared by all spectrum generators. It encapsulates all physical constants (Boltzmann constant, Planck constant, speed of light, electron charge/mass, vacuum permittivity) and pre-computes the cross-section prefactor `cs_coeff = π·e²/(2mₑ·c·ε₀)·h/(2π)·10²⁰` in units of Å²·eV. Two concrete implementations exist:

| Class | Purpose | Data Source |
|-------|---------|-------------|
| `TD_cross_section` | QC-NEA from TD-DFT results | `E{s}.dat` / `f{s}.dat` files |
| `ML_cross_section` | ML-NEA with mixed QC/ML data | Trained ML model predictions blended with QC data |

The `ML_cross_section` class inherits from both `CrossSection_calc` and `ML_calc`, giving it access to the ML model training and prediction machinery. Its `mix_single_file_data()` method implements a key strategy: for geometries where QC calculations were actually performed, the original QC values are used; for the remaining geometries, ML predictions replace QC values (clamped to non-negative). This delta-learning-like approach lets you achieve near-QC accuracy with only a fraction of the QC calculations.

The `SPC_cross_section` class provides a pure-Python reference implementation of the SPC formula, useful for validation or environments where the C++ library is unavailable. It implements the same `0.619·n·f/δ · exp(...)` formula found in the main API's `spc_broadening_func`.

Sources: [ML_NEA.py](mlatom/ML_NEA.py#L1155-L1196), [ML_NEA.py](mlatom/ML_NEA.py#L1336-L1610), [ML_NEA.py](mlatom/ML_NEA.py#L1061-L1083)

### Workflow Control and the Newton-X Interface

The `NewtonXCalc` class provides a Python interface to the Newton-X program for generating nuclear ensembles. It manages the full workflow: transferring equilibrium geometry and frequency data to the Newton-X working directory, launching Wigner-sampled or MD trajectories, and extracting the resulting ensemble as a multi-XYZ file. The `RecurPaperProcedure` class at the top of the control hierarchy orchestrates the full paper-reproduction workflow, including conditional logic for detecting existing optimization outputs, managing temporary directories, and comparing QC-NEA vs. ML-NEA results.

The `Config` and `ProcedureCtl` classes handle user-facing configuration — setting the number of TD points (`nTDpoints`), the number of QC training points (`nQMpoints`), the broadening parameter `deltaQCNEA`, and flags for plotting comparison figures. The `ControlPartProxy` class provides a simplified API entry point that can invoke either the full paper procedure or a programmatic API.

Sources: [ML_NEA.py](mlatom/ML_NEA.py#L786-L889), [ML_NEA.py](mlatom/ML_NEA.py#L2255-L2562)

## Spectrum Visualization and Plotting

MLatom provides two complementary plotting pathways for UV-Vis spectra. The `uvvis.plot()` instance method is a thin wrapper that delegates to `plot_uvvis()`, which is the full-featured plotting function. `plot_uvvis()` handles both pre-computed spectra objects and on-the-fly SPC generation directly from molecule data, and supports an interactive band-width slider via `ipywidgets` for Jupyter notebook environments.

The function orchestrates several visualization features: optional oscillator strength stick plots on a secondary y-axis, spectrum normalization, peak shifting, wavelength range clipping, and component analysis that identifies which molecular geometries or excited states contribute most to spectral features above a threshold. It delegates the actual rendering to the generic `plot_spectra()` function, which manages the matplotlib figure creation and styling.

| Feature | Parameter | Description |
|---------|-----------|-------------|
| Stick spectra | `oscillator_strength=True` | Overlay oscillator strengths as vertical bars on y2-axis |
| SPC on-the-fly | `spc=True` | Generate SPC spectra from molecule/DB at plot time |
| Interactive width | `band_width_slider=True` | Jupyter slider for real-time band width adjustment |
| Peak analysis | `print_peaks=True` | Print dominant peak positions and intensities |
| Component analysis | `analyze_component=True` | Report geometry/state contributions per peak |
| Normalize | `normalize=True` | Scale spectra to unit integral for comparison |

Sources: [spectra.py](mlatom/spectra.py#L1188-L1282), [spectra.py](mlatom/spectra.py#L284-L285)

## Practical Usage Patterns

### Generating an SPC Spectrum from a Single Geometry

```python
import mlatom
import numpy as np

# Assume 'mol' has excitation_energies (Hartree) and oscillator_strengths
uvvis_spectrum = mlatom.spectra.uvvis.spc(
    molecule=mol,
    band_width=0.3,
    shift=0.0,
    refractive_index=1.33  # e.g., water
)
uvvis_spectrum.plot(filename='spc_spectrum.png')
print(uvvis_spectrum.wavelengths_nm)   # wavelength grid
print(uvvis_spectrum.molar_absorbance) # ε in M⁻¹ cm⁻¹
print(uvvis_spectrum.cross_section)    # σ in Å²/molecule
```

### Generating an NEA Spectrum from a Nuclear Ensemble

```python
# 'db' is a molecular_database with excitation properties per geometry
uvvis_nea = mlatom.spectra.uvvis.nea(
    molecular_database=db,
    broadening_width=0.05
)
uvvis_nea.plot(filename='nea_spectrum.png')
```

### Interactive SPC with Band-Width Tuning (Jupyter)

```python
mlatom.spectra.plot_uvvis(
    molecule=mol,
    spc=True,
    band_width=0.3,
    band_width_slider=True
)
```

## Unit Conversions Reference

All UV-Vis calculations depend on a consistent set of physical constants and conversion factors. The following table summarizes the key relationships used throughout the codebase:

| From | To | Factor | Constant Location |
|------|----|--------|-------------------|
| Hartree | eV | `27.2114079527` | `constants.hartree2eV` |
| eV | nm | `h·c × 10⁹ / E` | `constants.eV2nm()` |
| nm | eV | `h·c × 10⁹ / λ` | `constants.nm2eV()` |
| M⁻¹ cm⁻¹ | Å²/molecule | `× 3.82353 × 10⁻⁵` | Hardcoded in `uvvis.__init__` |
| Å²/molecule | M⁻¹ cm⁻¹ | `÷ 3.82353 × 10⁻⁵` | Hardcoded in `uvvis.__init__` |

> [!TIP]
> Molecule objects must carry `excitation_energies` in **Hartree**, not eV. The `uvvis.spc()` and `uvvis.nea()` methods perform the conversion internally via `constants.hartree2eV`, but passing eV values directly will produce incorrectly shifted spectra.

Sources: [constants.py](mlatom/constants.py#L39-L62), [spectra.py](mlatom/spectra.py#L325-L326), [spectra.py](mlatom/spectra.py#L431)

## Relationship to Other Subsystems

UV-Vis spectrum computation sits at the convergence of several MLatom subsystems. The input data — excited-state energies and oscillator strengths — comes from either quantum chemistry program interfaces (see [Quantum Chemistry Program Interfaces](14-quantum-chemistry-program-interfaces)) or ML models trained on such data (see [Model Class Hierarchy](9-model-class-hierarchy)). The nuclear ensemble itself is typically generated from frequency calculations (see [Frequency and Thermochemistry Calculations](18-frequency-and-thermochemistry-calculations)) or from nonadiabatic molecular dynamics trajectories (see [Nonadiabatic and Surface-Hopping Dynamics](20-nonadiabatic-and-surface-hopping-dynamics)). Once spectra are computed, the `spectrum_comparison` class (covered in [Spectrum Comparison Metrics](23-spectrum-comparison-metrics)) provides metrics like Pearson correlation, cosine similarity, and KL divergence for quantitative spectral comparison.

# Spectrum Comparison Metrics



Quantifying spectral similarity is a fundamental requirement when validating machine-learned spectra against reference quantum-chemical calculations or experimental data. MLatom provides a comprehensive suite of 15 comparison metrics within the `spectrum_comparison` class, unified behind a single dispatcher that handles pre-processing alignment, metric computation, and optional similarity transformation in one call. This page documents the architecture, every available metric, and the alignment pipeline that ensures apples-to-apples comparisons even when spectra originate from different computational sources with mismatched discretizations.

## Architecture Overview

The entire comparison subsystem lives in [`spectrum_comparison`](mlatom/spectra.py#L539-L1016), a utility class inside `mlatom/spectra.py` (credited to Yangtao Chen and Yifan Hou). It is deliberately stateless—all methods are `@classmethod`s—so it functions as a namespace rather than an object with identity. Every metric expects two pre-aligned intensity arrays (`spectra_ref`, `spectra_pred`) of shape `(n_wavelength,)`, and the public entry point `spectrum_comparison()` manages alignment before dispatching to the appropriate metric function.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["spectrum_comparison()"] --> B{"line_up?"}
    B -- Yes --> C["line_up_spectra()<br/>interpolate both spectra<br/>to common grid"]
    B -- No --> D["Use raw .y arrays"]
    C --> E["Dispatch by metric name"]
    D --> E
    E --> F["Correlation metrics<br/>PCC, SCC, Tanimoto, cosine"]
    E --> G["Divergence metrics<br/>KLD, JD, JSD"]
    E --> H["Error metrics<br/>MSE, RMSE, MAE, RMSD,<br/>Euclidean, EMD"]
    E --> I["Spectral-specific<br/>SIS, ADV, RIC"]
    
    G --> J["loss2similarity()<br/>exp(-α·loss)"]
    H --> J
    J --> K["Similarity ∈ [0, 1]"]
    F --> L["Raw coefficient<br/>(no transformation)"]
    I --> L
```

This architecture separates **concerns** cleanly: alignment is an orthogonal pre-processing step, metric computation is pure math, and similarity transformation is an optional post-processing layer. The `loss2similarity` bridge function at [line 627](mlatom/spectra.py#L627-L636) converts any non-negative loss `L` into a similarity score via `exp(-α·L)`, where `α` is a tunable hyperparameter (default 0.2). This is applied to most error/divergence metrics but **not** to correlation coefficients, which are already bounded.

## The Alignment Pipeline: `line_up_spectra`

Before any metric can operate, both spectra must share an identical x-axis grid. The [`line_up_spectra`](mlatom/spectra.py#L607-L621) method computes the intersection of the two spectral ranges, then interpolates both onto a common grid.

The logic is straightforward:
1. **Range intersection**: `range_lb = max(min(s1), min(s2))`, `range_ub = min(max(s1), max(s2))` — any x-region outside both spectra is discarded at [line 611–612](mlatom/spectra.py#L611-L612).
2. **Grid construction**: If `align_list` is `None`, a uniformly spaced grid with 2 points per unit of x-range is created via `np.linspace(range_lb, range_ub, int((range_ub-range_lb)*2+1))` at [line 614](mlatom/spectra.py#L614). Otherwise the user-supplied `align_list` is clipped to the intersection bounds.
3. **Interpolation**: Each spectrum's [`sample()`](mlatom/spectra.py#L82-L87) method is called, which internally delegates to `scipy.interpolate.interp1d` (linear or cubic) and returns a new `spectrum` object on the unified grid.

> [!TIP]
> The default grid density of **2 points per unit x-range** may be too coarse for UV-Vis spectra (nm scale) but adequate for IR/Raman (cm⁻¹ scale). Always pass an explicit `align_list` when comparing high-resolution spectra to avoid interpolation artifacts that inflate error metrics.

## Metric Catalog

All 15 metrics are registered in the [`spectrum_comparison()`](mlatom/spectra.py#L544-L605) dispatcher via case-insensitive string matching. The following table provides a complete taxonomy.

### Correlation-Based Metrics

| Metric Key | Method | Range | Symmetric | Transformation | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `PCC` | [`pearson_coefficient`](mlatom/spectra.py#L639-L661) | [−1, 1] | ✅ | None (raw) | [JCTC 2020](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jctc.0c01279) |
| `SCC` | [`spearman_coeffient`](mlatom/spectra.py#L664-L687) | [−1, 1] | ✅ | None (raw) | — |
| `Tanimoto` | [`tanimoto_coefficient`](mlatom/spectra.py#L690-L708) | [−0.33, 1] | ✅ | None (raw) | — |
| `cosine` | [`cosine`](mlatom/spectra.py#L955-L971) | [−1, 1] | ✅ | None (raw) | — |

The **Pearson** coefficient at [line 656–660](mlatom/spectra.py#L656-L660) is computed as `Σ(ref−ref̄)(pred−pred̄) / √(Σ(ref−ref̄)² · Σ(pred−pred̄)²)`, making it sensitive to linear relationships but insensitive to global scaling or offset. The **Spearman** coefficient at [line 680–686](mlatom/spectra.py#L680-L686) replaces values with ranks before applying the same formula, capturing monotonic (nonlinear) relationships. The **Tanimoto** coefficient at [line 707](mlatom/spectra.py#L707) follows the vector formulation `Σ(a·b) / (Σa² + Σb² − Σa·b)`, familiar from cheminformatics fingerprint similarity.

### Information-Theoretic Divergence Metrics

| Metric Key | Method | Symmetric | Transformation | α parameter |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `KLD` | [`KL_divergence_transformed`](mlatom/spectra.py#L711-L728) | ❌ | `exp(-0.2·L)` | 0.2 |
| `JD` | [`jeffery_divergence_transformed`](mlatom/spectra.py#L731-L748) | ❌ | `exp(-0.2·L)` | 0.2 |
| `JSD` | [`JS_divergence_transformed`](mlatom/spectra.py#L751-L769) | ✅ | `exp(-0.8·L)` | **0.8** |

The **KL divergence** at [line 727](mlatom/spectra.py#L727) is `Σ ref · log(ref / (pred + ε))` with `ε = 1e-8` for numerical stability. Because `D_KL(P‖Q) ≠ D_KL(Q‖P)`, `spectrum1` is always treated as the reference distribution. The **Jeffery divergence** at [line 747](mlatom/spectra.py#L747) computes `Σ (ref − pred) · log(ref / (pred + ε))`, which is also asymmetric. The **Jensen-Shannon divergence** at [line 767–768](mlatom/spectra.py#L767-L768) symmetrizes by computing `½ D_KL(ref‖M) + ½ D_KL(pred‖M)` where `M = (ref+pred)/2`, and notably uses a **higher α of 0.8** at [line 769](mlatom/spectra.py#L769) to counteract the typically smaller magnitude of JSD values.

> [!TIP]
> All divergence metrics assume the intensity values represent probability-like distributions (non-negative). Passing raw (un-normalized) spectral intensities will produce unreliable results. Always call `spectrum.normalize()` before computing KLD, JD, or JSD.

### Error and Distance Metrics

| Metric Key | Method | Symmetric | Transformation |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MSE` | [`mse_transformed`](mlatom/spectra.py#L792-L809) | ✅ | `exp(-0.2·L)` |
| `RMSE` | [`rmse_transformed`](mlatom/spectra.py#L812-L829) | ✅ | `exp(-0.2·L)` |
| `MAE` | [`mae_transformed`](mlatom/spectra.py#L832-L849) | ✅ | `exp(-0.2·L)` |
| `RMSD` | [`rmsd_transformed`](mlatom/spectra.py#L912-L930) | ✅ | `exp(-0.2·L)` |
| `EMD` | [`earth_mover_distance_transformed`](mlatom/spectra.py#L772-L789) | ✅ | `exp(-0.2·L)` |
| `Euclidean` | [`euclidean_transformed`](mlatom/spectra.py#L933-L951) | ✅ | `1/(1+d)` |

Both `RMSE` and `RMSD` are implemented identically as `√(mean((ref−pred)²))` at [line 828](mlatom/spectra.py#L828) and [line 929](mlatom/spectra.py#L929) respectively — the duplicate names exist for compatibility with literature conventions. The **EMD** at [line 788](mlatom/spectra.py#L788-L789) delegates to `scipy.stats.wasserstein_distance`, making it the only metric that can theoretically handle unequal-length arrays (though alignment normally equalizes them). The **Euclidean** metric at [line 950–951](mlatom/spectra.py#L950-L951) uses an alternative transformation `1/(1+d)` instead of the exponential decay, providing a slightly softer falloff curve.

### Spectral-Specific Metrics

| Metric Key | Method | Extra Parameters | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SIS` | [`spectral_information_similarity`](mlatom/spectra.py#L852-L909) | `threshold=1e-10` | [chemprop-IR](https://github.com/gfm-collab/chemprop-IR) |
| `ADV` | [`absolute_difference_value_search`](mlatom/spectra.py#L974-L993) | None | [J. Cheminf.](https://journals.pan.pl/dlibra/publication/122822/edition/107074/content) |
| `RIC` | [`relative_integral_change`](mlatom/spectra.py#L996-L1015) | Requires `align_list` | — |

The **SIS** metric at [lines 900–908](mlatom/spectra.py#L900-L908) first floors both spectra at `threshold` to avoid `log(0)`, then computes a symmetric information distance `Σ(n₁·log(n₁/n₂) + n₂·log(n₂/n₁))` and converts to similarity as `1/(1+Σdistance)`. The original convolution-based implementation from chemprop-IR is preserved as commented-out code at [lines 868–899](mlatom/spectra.py#L868-L899).

The **ADV** metric at [line 991–993](mlatom/spectra.py#L991-L993) computes `1 − Σ|ref−pred| / Σ|ref|`, which is a normalized L1 error expressing the fraction of reference spectral area that is "lost" in the prediction.

The **RIC** metric at [lines 1011–1014](mlatom/spectra.py#L1011-L1014) is unique in requiring the `align_list` parameter directly (rather than just aligned y-arrays). It computes `1 − Σ|ref−pred|·dx / Σ(ref·dx)` via Riemann sums, measuring the relative change in integrated area under the curve.

## The `loss2similarity` Bridge

The [`loss2similarity`](mlatom/spectra.py#L627-L636) function is the universal adapter for converting unbounded loss values into bounded similarity scores:

```python
similarity = exp(-α * loss)
```

When `loss = 0` (perfect match), similarity is exactly 1.0. As loss grows, similarity decays exponentially toward 0. The default `α = 0.2` at [line 627](mlatom/spectra.py#L627) means a loss of 5 yields similarity ≈ 0.37, and a loss of 10 yields ≈ 0.14. The **Jensen-Shannon divergence** is the exception, using `α = 0.8` at [line 769](mlatom/spectra.py#L769) because JSD values are typically an order of magnitude smaller than raw error metrics.

Metrics that bypass this transformation entirely — PCC, SCC, Tanimoto, cosine, ADV, and RIC — return their raw mathematical values, which are already naturally bounded.

## Usage Patterns

### Direct Dispatch

The primary entry point is the class method [`spectrum_comparison()`](mlatom/spectra.py#L544-L605), which accepts two `spectrum` objects and a metric name string:

```python
from mlatom import spectra

# Assuming spec_ref and spec_pred are spectrum() instances
similarity = spectra.spectrum_comparison.spectrum_comparison(
    spectrum1=spec_ref,
    spectrum2=spec_pred,
    metric='SIS',
    align_method_dict={'interpolate_method': 'linear'},
    metric_arg_dict={'threshold': 1e-10, 'std_dev': 10},
    line_up=True
)
```

The `align_method_dict` is forwarded to [`line_up_spectra`](mlatom/spectra.py#L608-L621) and supports `interpolate_method` (`"linear"` or `"cubic"`) and `align_list`. The `metric_arg_dict` is forwarded as `**kwargs` to the specific metric function, enabling per-metric parameters like `threshold` for SIS or `alpha` for `loss2similarity`.

### Bypassing Alignment

When spectra are already on the same grid (e.g., from identical simulation parameters), set `line_up=False` to skip interpolation overhead. The raw `.y` arrays are then passed directly to the metric function at [lines 552–554](mlatom/spectra.py#L552-L554).

### Metric Selection Guidance

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Q1{"Do you need shape-only<br/>comparison<br/>(ignore intensity scale)?"}
    Q1 -- Yes --> Q2{"Linear or nonlinear<br/>relationship?"}
    Q2 -- Linear --> PCC["PCC or cosine<br/>scale/offset invariant"]
    Q2 -- Monotonic/any --> SCC["SCC<br/>rank-based, robust to outliers"]
    Q1 -- No --> Q3{"Do intensities represent<br/>probability distributions?"}
    Q3 -- Yes --> JSD["JSD<br/>symmetric, bounded"]
    Q3 -- No --> Q4{"Do you need<br/>integrated area sensitivity?"}
    Q4 -- Yes --> RIC["RIC<br/>Riemann-sum based"]
    Q4 -- No --> RMSE["RMSE or MSE<br/>standard error metrics"]
```

For **active learning loops** (see [Active Learning Pipeline](24-active-learning-pipeline)), the divergence metrics (KLD, JSD) are particularly informative because they quantify information loss in a physics-motivated way. For **spectral assignment validation** in UV-Vis workflows (see [UV-Vis Spectra and Nuclear Ensemble Approach](22-uv-vis-spectra-and-nuclear-ensemble-approach)), correlation coefficients (PCC, SCC) provide intuitive shape-overlap scores.

## Relationship to Other MLatom Modules

The `spectrum_comparison` class operates downstream of the spectral generation pipeline. The [`spectrum`](mlatom/spectra.py#L17-L217) base class provides the data structures and interpolation machinery that `line_up_spectra` consumes. The specialized subclasses — [`uvvis`](mlatom/spectra.py#L220-L454), [`ir`](mlatom/spectra.py#L455-L496), and [`raman`](mlatom/spectra.py#L497-L537) — generate the spectrum objects that are ultimately compared. The broader [`plot_spectra`](mlatom/spectra.py#L1020-L1186) function provides the visual inspection counterpart to these quantitative metrics, with normalization and peak-shifting capabilities that should be applied consistently before comparison.

For scalar property accuracy assessment (energies, gradients), MLatom uses a separate statistics module at [`mlatom/stats.py`](mlatom/stats.py) providing `mae`, `mse`, `rmse`, and `correlation_coefficient` — these are **not** spectrum-aware and do not handle alignment, making them unsuitable for spectral data where x-axis correspondence matters.

## Summary Table

| Category | Metrics | Return Range | Best For |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Correlation** | PCC, SCC, Tanimoto, cosine | [−1, 1] | Shape matching, scale-invariant comparison |
| **Divergence** | KLD, JD, JSD | [0, 1] (transformed) | Distributional comparison, information-theoretic |
| **Error** | MSE, RMSE, MAE, RMSD, Euclidean, EMD | [0, 1] (transformed) | Point-wise accuracy, general-purpose |
| **Spectral** | SIS, ADV, RIC | [0, 1] or raw | Domain-specific spectral similarity |

---

**Next steps**: For understanding how spectra are generated before comparison, see [IR and Raman Spectra Calculation](21-ir-and-raman-spectra-calculation) and [UV-Vis Spectra and Nuclear Ensemble Approach](22-uv-vis-spectra-and-nuclear-ensemble-approach). To learn how spectrum comparison fits into iterative model improvement, see [Active Learning Pipeline](24-active-learning-pipeline). For the underlying spectral data model, see the `spectrum` class at [lines 17–217](mlatom/spectra.py#L17-L217).

# Active Learning Pipeline



The Active Learning (AL) pipeline in MLatom automates the construction of machine learning potential energy surfaces by iteratively expanding a training set with configurations sampled from molecular dynamics, geometry optimizations, or other simulations. At its core, the system uses a **dual-model uncertainty quantification (UQ) strategy**: a main model trained on energies and gradients, paired with an auxiliary model trained on energies only. Disagreement between the two models identifies high-uncertainty geometries that require labeling with a reference quantum chemistry method, closing the feedback loop that drives efficient data acquisition.

Sources: [al.py](mlatom/al.py#L16-L17), [al_utils.py](mlatom/al_utils.py#L9-L10)

## Pipeline Architecture

The AL pipeline is orchestrated by the `al` class and decomposed into clearly separated concerns across three modules. The `al` class manages the overall iteration lifecycle and state persistence, the `Sampler` class encapsulates exploration strategies for discovering new configurations, and the `ml_model` / `ml_model_msani` classes handle model training, prediction, and uncertainty quantification. A lightweight stop-function mechanism bridges prediction and sampling by terminating simulations when a molecule is flagged as uncertain.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "al class — Orchestrator"
        A[Initialize] --> B{Initial dataset<br/>provided?}
        B -- Yes --> D[Load initial dataset]
        B -- No --> C[Sample initial pool<br/>via Sampler]
        C --> C1{Refinement method}
        C1 -- "cross-validation" --> C2[CV error + learning curve fit]
        C1 -- "validation" --> C3[Hold-out validation error]
        C1 -- "one-shot" --> D
        C2 --> C4{Converged?}
        C3 --> C4
        C4 -- No --> C
        C4 -- Yes --> D
    end

    subgraph "Iteration Loop"
        D --> E["label_points()<br/>Reference calculations"]
        E --> F["create_ml_model()<br/>Train main + aux models"]
        F --> G["use_ml_model()<br/>Sample via ML-driven simulation"]
        G --> H{Converged?}
        H -- No --> E
        H -- Yes --> I[Done]
    end

    subgraph "Sampler — Exploration"
        S1[Wigner]
        S2[Random]
        S3[Fixed]
        S4[Geometry Optimization]
        S5[Molecular Dynamics]
        S6[Batch MD]
        S7[MD + Excess Energy]
        S8[Harmonic Quantum Boltzmann]
        S9[Surface Hopping MD]
    end

    subgraph "Uncertainty Quantification"
        U1[Main Model<br/>energies + gradients] --> U3["Δ = |E_main − E_aux|"]
        U2[Auxiliary Model<br/>energies only] --> U3
        U3 --> U4{"Δ > threshold?"}
        U4 -- Yes --> U5[mol.uncertain = True]
        U4 -- No --> U6[mol.uncertain = False]
        U5 --> U7[Stop simulation,<br/>add to label pool]
    end
```

Sources: [al.py](mlatom/al.py#L378-L426), [al_utils.py](mlatom/al_utils.py#L1254-L1260), [al_utils.py](mlatom/al_utils.py#L2492-L2494)

## The `al` Class — Orchestrating the Loop

The `al` class is the central coordinator. Its constructor accepts a wide range of keyword arguments covering every aspect of the pipeline — from the reference method to the sampling strategy to convergence criteria — then immediately launches the main loop unless debug mode is enabled. State is persisted across restarts through an `al_info.json` file and per-iteration subdirectories under `iterations/`.

### Constructor and Configuration

All configuration flows through keyword arguments. The constructor establishes sensible defaults for common parameters while requiring an explicit `reference_method` (a quantum chemistry method for labeling). The `molecule` argument, if provided, triggers automatic geometry optimization and frequency calculation via `optfreq()` to produce the equilibrium structure used as the origin for initial condition sampling.

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `job_name` | `str` | `'AL'` | Prefix for output files |
| `reference_method` | model instance | *(required)* | Quantum chemistry method for labeling |
| `baseline_method` | model instance | `None` | Baseline for delta learning |
| `molecule` | molecule | `None` | Equilibrium geometry (triggers opt+freq) |
| `initial_dataset` | molecular_database | `None` | Pre-built dataset (skips initial sampling) |
| `initial_points_refinement` | `str` | `'cross-validation'` | Strategy: `'cross-validation'`, `'validation'`, or `'one-shot'` |
| `init_ncvsplits` | `int` | `5` | CV splits for cross-validation refinement |
| `init_RMSE_threshold` | `float` | `None` | RMSE target to stop initial sampling |
| `init_train_energies_only` | `bool` | `True` | Energy-only training during initial sampling |
| `ml_model` | `str` or class | `'ml_model'` | ML model class (`'ANI'`, `'KREG'`, `'MACE'`, `'msani'`, `'delta_msani'`) |
| `device` | `str` | auto-detect | `'cuda'` or `'cpu'` |
| `validation_set_fraction` | `float` | `0.1` | Fraction held out for validation during training |
| `reuse_previous_model` | `bool` | `False` | Skip retraining if model file exists |
| `train_model_from_scratch_interval` | `int` | `5` | Retrain from scratch every N iterations |
| `sampler` | `Sampler` or `str` | `Sampler('batch_md')` | Exploration sampler |
| `new_points` | `int` | `None` | Max sampled points per iteration |
| `min_new_points` | `int` | `5` | Convergence threshold for new points |
| `max_iterations` | `float` | `inf` | Hard cap on iterations |
| `init_sampling_only` | `bool` | `False` | Exit after initial point sampling |

Sources: [al.py](mlatom/al.py#L50-L376)

### The Main Iteration Loop

The `main()` method implements a straightforward while-loop that continues until convergence or the maximum iteration count is reached. Each iteration executes four sequential phases, and timing is reported for each:

1. **Label** — `label_points()` sends the molecular pool to the reference method for energy and gradient calculations, using parallel execution when `label_nthreads > 1`.
2. **Train** — `create_ml_model()` splits the accumulated labeled database into training/validation sets, trains both the main and auxiliary models, and computes the UQ threshold on the validation set.
3. **Sample** — `use_ml_model()` runs ML-driven simulations (MD, geometry optimization, etc.) using the newly trained model. Simulations are stopped early via the stop function when a molecule is flagged as uncertain, and those molecules are collected into the next pool to label.
4. **Convergence check** — If the number of newly sampled points falls below `min_new_points`, the pipeline declares convergence and exits.

> [!TIP]
> The pipeline supports **restart from any iteration**. On startup, if `al_info.json` exists with a non-zero `iteration` count, `main()` reconstructs the labeled database by loading all `labeled_db.json` files from prior iteration directories, then resumes the loop from the recorded iteration number. This makes long-running active learning jobs resilient to interruptions.

Sources: [al.py](mlatom/al.py#L378-L426)

## Initial Data Pool Sampling

Before the iterative loop begins, the pipeline must establish a seed set of labeled configurations. Three strategies control how this initial pool is built, selectable via the `initial_points_refinement` parameter.

### Cross-Validation Refinement (Default)

This is the most rigorous approach. It alternates between sampling a batch of new initial conditions (via the `initdata_sampler`) and evaluating model quality through k-fold cross-validation. A learning curve is fitted to the sequence of `(Ntrain, RMSE)` pairs using a power-law model `eRMSE = a · N^b`. Sampling stops when the predicted improvement from adding `init_ntrain_next` more points drops below 10% of the current error — that is, when `[e(N) − e(N+ΔN)] / e(N) < 0.1`. This ensures the initial pool is large enough for meaningful model training but avoids wasteful over-sampling.

Sources: [al.py](mlatom/al.py#L462-L543)

### Validation Refinement

Analogous to cross-validation, but uses a single random hold-out split (controlled by `init_validation_set_fraction`, default 0.2) instead of k-fold. The same learning curve convergence criterion applies. This is faster per iteration since only one model is trained instead of `init_ncvsplits` models.

Sources: [al.py](mlatom/al.py#L575-L597)

### One-Shot Sampling

The simplest strategy: sample initial conditions once via the `initdata_sampler`, label them all with the reference method, and proceed directly to the iterative loop. No quality assessment or adaptive expansion occurs. This is useful when the user has domain knowledge about an appropriate initial set size.

Sources: [al.py](mlatom/al.py#L600-L617)

### Alternative: Pre-built Initial Dataset

If an `initial_dataset` (a `molecular_database` instance) is provided, all sampling is bypassed entirely. The pre-built dataset is saved as `init_cond_db.json` and used directly as the molecular pool to label. This supports workflows where training data has been curated externally.

Sources: [al.py](mlatom/al.py#L437-L445)

## Sampling Strategies — The `Sampler` Class

The `Sampler` class in `al_utils.py` acts as a strategy dispatcher. It accepts either a string identifier or a callable, mapping string names to built-in sampling methods. Each method generates a molecular database of configurations, annotates each molecule with a `sampling` attribute indicating its source, and returns the database to the AL pipeline.

| Sampler Name | Constructor String | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **Wigner** | `'wigner'` | Samples nuclear displacements from the Wigner distribution at a given temperature |
| **Random** | `'random'` | Adds uniform random perturbations to equilibrium coordinates |
| **Fixed** | `'fixed'` | Returns a user-provided molecule or database unchanged |
| **Geometry Optimization** | `'geomopt'` | Runs geometry optimizations from sampled initial conditions; collects steps where UQ triggers |
| **Molecular Dynamics** | `'md'` | Runs individual MD trajectories in parallel; collects final uncertain configurations |
| **Batch Molecular Dynamics** | `'batch_md'` | Uses the `md_parallel` engine for vectorized multi-trajectory propagation |
| **MD with Excess Energy** | `'md_excess_energy'` | MD trajectories initialized with Poisson-distributed excess vibrational energies |
| **Harmonic Quantum Boltzmann** | `'harmonic-quantum-boltzmann'` | Samples from the harmonic quantum Boltzmann distribution |
| **Surface Hopping MD** | `'lzsh'` | Nonadiabatic surface-hopping dynamics for excited-state PES construction |

### How Samplers Interact with UQ

Every simulation-type sampler (MD, geometry optimization, surface hopping) integrates with the stop-function mechanism. The `internal_stop_function` inspects the `mol.uncertain` flag — set during prediction by comparing the main and auxiliary model energies — and returns `stop=True` when uncertainty exceeds the threshold. In MD, this terminates the trajectory immediately, and the terminal configuration is added to the pool to label. In geometry optimization, steps where uncertainty is detected mid-optimization are collected. An optional `uq_threshold` parameter on the sampler allows overriding the threshold from a previous iteration without retraining.

> [!TIP]
> The `batch_molecular_dynamics` sampler is the default for the iterative loop and is recommended for most use cases. It leverages the `md_parallel` module for efficient vectorized propagation of many trajectories simultaneously, making it significantly faster than the per-trajectory parallelization used by the standard `molecular_dynamics` sampler.

Sources: [al_utils.py](mlatom/al_utils.py#L9-L518), [al_utils.py](mlatom/al_utils.py#L2492-L2497)

## Dual-Model Uncertainty Quantification

The UQ mechanism is the intelligence layer that determines *which* configurations warrant expensive reference labeling. Rather than relying on ensemble disagreement or gradient-based heuristics, MLatom employs a principled approach based on model disagreement between two models trained with different information content.

### Architecture: Main Model vs. Auxiliary Model

| Aspect | Main Model | Auxiliary Model |
|--------|-----------|----------------|
| **Training data** | Full (energies + gradients) | Energy values only |
| **Purpose** | Primary prediction engine | UQ calibration signal |
| **File suffix** | `mlmodel.pt` (or `.npz` for KREG) | `aux_mlmodel.pt` (or `.npz`) |
| **Prediction output** | `mol.energy`, `mol.energy_gradients` | `mol.aux_energy`, `mol.aux_energy_gradients` |

During prediction, both models evaluate every molecule. The uncertainty for a molecule is computed as the absolute energy difference:

```
uq = |E_main − E_aux|
```

A molecule is flagged as uncertain (`mol.uncertain = True`) when `uq` exceeds the dynamically computed threshold. The threshold defaults to the **M+3·MAD** statistic (median + 3 × median absolute deviation) of the UQ values on the validation set, making it robust to outliers. Alternative metrics include `'max'` (use the maximum UQ value) or custom `'m+n*MAD'` patterns like `'m+2.5mad'`.

Sources: [al_utils.py](mlatom/al_utils.py#L1409-L1426), [al_utils.py](mlatom/al_utils.py#L1436-L1456)

### Threshold Persistence and Adaptation

The UQ threshold is computed once — on the first iteration's validation set — and stored in `al_info['uq_threshold']`. On subsequent iterations, the saved threshold is reused, providing consistent stopping behavior across the pipeline's lifetime. However, samplers can override this threshold via the `uq_threshold` keyword argument, enabling looser or tighter exploration without retraining.

Sources: [al_utils.py](mlatom/al_utils.py#L1396-L1405)

## ML Model Training Within the Pipeline

The `ml_model` class (for standard models like ANI, KREG, MACE) and `ml_model_msani` class (for the Msani/VecMsani architectures) manage the training lifecycle within each AL iteration. Both follow the same pattern.

### Training Workflow

1. **Data splitting** — The accumulated labeled database is randomly split into 90% subtraining and 10% validation sets. If a `training_db.json` already exists in the working directory (from a prior failed or restarted iteration), it is reloaded instead of re-splitting.
2. **Main model training** — If no saved model file exists, a fresh main model is initialized and trained on both energies and gradients (unless `use_gradients_in_training=False`). If a model file is found, training is skipped.
3. **Auxiliary model training** — A separate model is trained on energies only, using the same subtraining/validation split.
4. **UQ threshold calibration** — Both models predict on the validation set, UQ values are extracted, and the threshold is set via the `threshold_metric` method.
5. **Summary generation** — Training and validation metrics are written to a summary file in the iteration working directory.

The `ml_model_trainer` class acts as a factory, dispatching to model-specific training routines (`main_model_trainer_kreg`, `main_model_trainer_ani`, `main_model_trainer_mace`, `main_model_trainer_msani`) based on the `ml_model_type` configuration.

Sources: [al_utils.py](mlatom/al_utils.py#L1046-L1228), [al_utils.py](mlatom/al_utils.py#L1313-L1410)

## Delta Learning Support

The pipeline natively supports delta learning workflows where the ML model learns the *difference* between a high-level reference method and a lower-level baseline (e.g., learning the correction from DFT to CCSD(T)). The `delta_ml_model_trainer` extends `ml_model_trainer` and overrides the training methods to compute delta properties on-the-fly before model fitting.

At the configuration level, providing `baseline_method` to the `al` constructor activates delta labeling. During `label_points_moldb()`, both the reference and baseline methods are called for each molecule, and the delta energy and delta gradients are stored on the molecule object. The `ml_model_delta_msani` class further extends `ml_model_msani` with delta-aware training and prediction, automatically adding baseline predictions back during inference.

Sources: [al_utils.py](mlatom/al_utils.py#L1230-L1252), [al.py](mlatom/al.py#L742-L764)

## Filesystem Layout

Each active learning job produces a structured output directory. Understanding this layout is essential for monitoring progress and restarting interrupted jobs.

```
<job_directory>/
├── al_info.json                          # Pipeline state (iteration, UQ threshold, model paths)
├── init_cond_db.json                     # Initial conditions database
├── labeled_db.json                       # Cumulative labeled database
├── valdb.json                            # Latest validation split
├── iterations/
│   ├── 0/
│   │   ├── labeled_db.json              # Points labeled in iteration 0
│   │   ├── db_to_label.json             # Full-sampling-info pool for next iteration
│   │   ├── training_db.json             # Full training set snapshot
│   │   ├── mlmodel.pt                   # Main model (iteration 0)
│   │   ├── aux_mlmodel.pt               # Auxiliary model (iteration 0)
│   │   └── trajs/                       # Optional trajectory dumps
│   ├── 1/
│   │   ├── labeled_db.json
│   │   ├── db_to_label.json
│   │   ├── training_db.json
│   │   ├── mlmodel.pt
│   │   ├── aux_mlmodel.pt
│   │   └── trajs/
│   └── ...
```

Sources: [al.py](mlatom/al.py#L340-L360), [al.py](mlatom/al.py#L388-L426)

## Labeling with Reference Methods

The `label_points_moldb()` method handles the computationally expensive step of calculating reference energies and gradients for unlabeled molecules. It supports both single-threaded and multi-threaded execution. In parallel mode (`nthreads > 1`), it uses `run_in_parallel` with temporary working directories to avoid file conflicts between concurrent quantum chemistry calculations. The method gracefully handles failed calculations — molecules where the reference method raises an exception are counted and excluded from the labeled database rather than crashing the pipeline.

Sources: [al.py](mlatom/al.py#L620-L672), [al.py](mlatom/al.py#L723-L806)

## Convergence and Stopping Criteria

The pipeline converges when the exploration sampler produces fewer than `min_new_points` (default 5) uncertain configurations in an iteration. This indicates the ML model has become sufficiently accurate across the configuration space explored by the sampler. A hard cap on iterations is enforced by `max_iterations` (default infinity). The combination of these two criteria — a soft data-driven convergence check and a hard computational budget — provides both efficiency and safety guarantees.

Sources: [al.py](mlatom/al.py#L698-L718)

---

For deeper understanding of the underlying model architectures that power the AL pipeline, see [Model Class Hierarchy](9-model-class-hierarchy) and [Kernel Ridge Regression Models](10-kernel-ridge-regression-models). To learn how the sampling strategies connect to the broader simulation engine, consult [Molecular Dynamics Engine](19-molecular-dynamics-engine). For strategies on initial data selection and validation, proceed to [Data Sampling and Cross-Validation Strategies](25-data-sampling-and-cross-validation-strategies).

# Data Sampling and Cross-Validation Strategies



The fidelity of any machine learning potential rests on two pillars: **how training data is partitioned** and **how model generalization is measured**. MLatom implements a layered sampling architecture where the Fortran backend (`MLatomF`) handles high-performance index generation and the Python frontend orchestrates active-learning loops, slice-based structured sampling, and nested cross-validation pipelines. This page dissects every sampling primitive, the data-flow contracts between layers, and the cross-validation topologies available for both static model evaluation and adaptive data acquisition.

## Architectural Overview

MLatom's sampling subsystem spans three tiers. The **Fortran tier** performs the low-level combinatorics of fold generation and index shuffling. The **Python task tier** (`MLtasks`) bridges CLI arguments to both backends, managing temporary index files and converting between 1-based Fortran indices and 0-based NumPy arrays. The **active learning tier** (`al.py`, `al_utils.py`) uses sampling primitives as building blocks within iterative uncertainty-driven loops. A separate **slice-based subsystem** (`sliceData.py`) provides distance-ordered partitioning for equilibrium-structure-centric datasets.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "CLI Entry Points"
        A1["sample task"]
        A2["createMLmodel task"]
        A3["estAccMLmodel task"]
        A4["learningCurve task"]
        A5["al task"]
        A6["slice / sampleFromSlices / mergeSlices"]
    end

    subgraph "Python Orchestration Layer"
        B1["MLtasks.sampling()"]
        B2["MLtasks.training()"]
        B3["MLtasks.estAccMLmodel()"]
        B4["MLtasks.learningCurve()"]
        B5["data.sample()"]
        B6["ml_database.split()"]
        B7["al.get_initial_data_pool_cross_validation()"]
        B8["sliceData.sliceDataCls"]
    end

    subgraph "Fortran Backend"
        C1["sampling.f90 :: sample()"]
        C2["dataset.f90 :: splitAndSample()"]
        C3["dataset.f90 :: getSubtrainValidate()"]
        C4["dataset.f90 :: getTotalTrainTest()"]
    end

    A1 --> B1
    A2 --> B1
    A3 --> B1
    A3 --> B3
    A4 --> B1
    A4 --> B4
    A5 --> B7
    A6 --> B8

    B1 -->|"delegates via interface_MLatomF"| C1
    B5 --> C1
    B6 --> B5
    B7 --> B5

    C1 --> C2
    C1 --> C3
    C1 --> C4
    B3 --> B2
```

Sources: [sampling.f90](mlatom/MLatomF_src/sampling.f90#L1-L127), [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L363-L374), [data.py](mlatom/data.py#L3331-L3383)

## Core Sampling Primitives

### The `data.sample()` Function

The foundational sampling entry point in the Python layer is `data.sample()`, a standalone function that operates on any molecular database instance. It accepts a `sampling` mode string, a `number_of_splits` integer, and either `fraction_of_points_in_splits` or `split_equally` flags. The function validates that the sum of fractions does not exceed 1.0, distributes rounding residuals to the first slices, then either shuffles indices randomly or uses user-defined index lists. The return value is a list of molecular database objects, one per split, constructed by iterating over the computed index ranges and appending the corresponding molecules.

Sources: [data.py](mlatom/data.py#L3331-L3383)

### The `ml_database.split()` Method

The `ml_database` class exposes sampling through its `split()` method, which is a thin delegation to `data.sample()`, passing `self` as the database to split. This design means every molecular database instance — whether holding small molecules, trajectory frames, or reaction steps — inherits a uniform splitting interface. The method returns a list of new `ml_database` instances, preserving the original database type via `type(molDB)()`.

Sources: [data.py](mlatom/data.py#L131-L133)

### The Fortran `sampling` Module

The Fortran backend's `sampling.f90` contains a single `sample()` subroutine that orchestrates all index generation for the compiled MLatomF workflow. It first calls `dataset.getTotalTrainTest()` to determine how many points belong in training versus test sets, handling both absolute counts and fractional specifications (values < 1.0 are interpreted as proportions of `NitemsTot`). When cross-validation testing is enabled (`CVtest`), the subroutine allocates fold arrays (`indicesCVtestSplits` and `CVtestFolds`) and calls `splitAndSample()` to distribute indices across folds. For each fold, it constructs complementary train/test partitions by concatenating all non-holdout folds into the training index array. If nested cross-validation for hyperparameter optimization (`CVopt`) is also requested, the subroutine recursively calls `splitAndSample()` within each training fold to create inner CV splits.

Sources: [sampling.f90](mlatom/MLatomF_src/sampling.f90#L20-L127), [dataset.f90](mlatom/MLatomF_src/dataset.f90#L91-L200)

## Sampling Modes and Data Partitioning

MLatom supports four distinct sampling modes that determine how data points are assigned to subsets. The choice of mode propagates through the entire pipeline, from index generation to model training and accuracy estimation.

| Mode | Description | Typical Use Case |
|------|-------------|------------------|
| `random` | Fisher-Yates shuffle of all indices, then sequential assignment by split size | Default for most training/test splits |
| `user-defined` | External index files (1-based) specify exact membership of each subset | Reproducible benchmarks, predefined chemical space partitions |
| `none` | No shuffling; indices are assigned in their original file order | Ordered datasets where randomization is undesirable |
| Distance-based slicing | Euclidean distance sorting from equilibrium geometry, then equal-range slicing | PES datasets centered on a minimum-energy structure |

### Random Sampling

The default and most widely used mode. In the Python layer, `data.sample()` delegates to `random.shuffle(all_indices)` before sequential slicing. In the Fortran layer, `splitAndSample()` performs an analogous permutation. The `MLtasks.sampling()` function, when invoked for `createMLmodel` or `estAccMLmodel` tasks, suppresses all user-defined index inputs (`iTrainIn`, `iSubtrainIn`, `iValidateIn`, `iTestIn` are set to empty strings) and generates fresh random splits into a temporary directory. After generation, indices are read back with `np.loadtxt(...).astype(int) - 1` to convert from Fortran's 1-based indexing to Python's 0-based convention.

Sources: [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L791-L833), [data.py](mlatom/data.py#L3357-L3359)

### User-Defined Sampling

When `sampling=user-defined`, the pipeline reads pre-existing index files rather than generating new ones. The `MLtasks.sampling()` function skips the Fortran delegation entirely when the sampling mode matches, and instead directly loads the user-supplied index files specified via `iTrainIn`, `iSubtrainIn`, `iValidateIn`, `iTestIn`, `iCVtestPrefIn`, and `iCVoptPrefIn`. This mode is essential for reproducible studies where the exact train/test partition must be consistent across multiple experiments or publications.

Sources: [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L785-L790)

### Distance-Based Slice Sampling

The `sliceData` module implements a fundamentally different sampling paradigm optimized for potential energy surface datasets. The workflow proceeds in three stages:

1. **Sort by distance**: An equilibrium descriptor vector (`eqX`) is loaded, and all data point descriptors (`xx`) are sorted by their Euclidean distance to this reference. The `sortByDistance()` method computes distances using the L2 norm across all descriptor dimensions and stores a sorted index mapping.

2. **Slice**: The sorted dataset is divided into `nslices` equal-sized spatial shells. Each slice corresponds to a contiguous range in the distance-ordered list, with the final slice absorbing any rounding remainder. Index files, descriptor files, and distance files are written to per-slice subdirectories.

3. **Sample from slices**: When `sampleFromSlices` is invoked, each slice independently samples `Ntrain / nslices` points using the standard MLatom sampling engine. This ensures **spatial uniformity** across the training set — a critical requirement for PES models that must generalize across both near-equilibrium and far-from-equilibrium geometries.

4. **Merge**: The `mergeSlices` operation interleaves sampled points across slices in a round-robin fashion to construct the final `itrain.dat`, `isubtrain.dat`, `ivalidate.dat`, and `itest.dat` files. The subtraining set uses 80% of the training pool, and unsampled points from all slices are pooled into the test set.

Sources: [sliceData.py](mlatom/sliceData.py#L13-L212)

## Cross-Validation Topologies

Cross-validation in MLatom is not a monolithic concept — the framework implements **three distinct CV roles**, each serving a different purpose in the model development lifecycle. Understanding the distinction between CVtest, CVopt, and the subtraining/validation split is essential for correctly configuring MLatom workflows.

### Role 1: CVtest — Estimating Predictive Accuracy

CVtest is the outermost cross-validation layer, used to produce an unbiased estimate of model generalization error. When `CVtest=True`, the dataset is split into `NcvTestFolds` folds. For each fold `j`, the model is trained on all folds except `j`, and predictions are made on fold `j`. After iterating through all folds, predictions from every held-out set are concatenated into a single combined test set, and statistics (MAE, RMSE, correlation) are computed across the full dataset.

A special case is **leave-one-out (LOO)** cross-validation, activated by setting `LOOtest=True` (which internally forces `NcvTestFolds = NitemsTot`). LOO is computationally expensive but provides the most thorough utilization of limited data.

The `estAccMLmodel` task in `MLtasks.py` orchestrates this loop: for each test fold, it concatenates the remaining folds into a combined training index array (`i_cv_train`), trains a model, predicts on the held-out test fold, and accumulates results. After all folds complete, it calls `analyzing()` on the combined predictions.

Sources: [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L97-L151), [sampling.f90](mlatom/MLatomF_src/sampling.f90#L52-L72)

### Role 2: CVopt — Hyperparameter Optimization

CVopt is an inner cross-validation layer, nested either within each CVtest fold or within the single training set (when CVtest is disabled). It is used exclusively for **selecting optimal hyperparameters** (e.g., kernel widths for KRR, network architectures for neural networks). When `CVopt=True`, the training data is further split into `NcvOptFolds` inner folds. Each hyperparameter candidate is evaluated by training on `NcvOptFolds - 1` inner folds and validating on the held-out inner fold. The hyperparameter with the lowest aggregate validation error is selected for the final model.

In the Fortran backend, this nesting is explicit: the `sample()` subroutine iterates over CVtest folds, and within each fold, conditionally calls `splitAndSample()` on the training indices to create CVopt splits. The nested index files use a composite naming scheme: `{CVtestPref}{j}{CVoptPref}{i}.dat`, where `j` is the outer fold and `i` is the inner fold.

The Python `training()` function passes CVopt splits to `model.optimize_hyperparameters()` as `cv_splits_molecular_databases`, enabling the model to evaluate each hyperparameter candidate across all inner folds.

Sources: [sampling.f90](mlatom/MLatomF_src/sampling.f90#L85-L95), [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L886-L918)

### Role 3: Subtraining/Validation — Simple Hold-Out for Hyperparameters

When full CVopt is too expensive, MLatom falls back to a single hold-out split of the training set into **subtraining** (80% by default) and **validation** (20%) sets. This is handled by `getSubtrainValidate()` in the Fortran backend or by a simple `split(number_of_splits=2, fraction_of_points_in_splits=[0.8, 0.2])` call in Python. The validation set is used for early stopping and hyperparameter selection, while the subtraining set is used for actual model fitting.

Sources: [dataset.f90](mlatom/MLatomF_src/dataset.f90#L91-L200), [al.py](mlatom/al.py#L575-L597)

### Nested Cross-Validation Topology

When both CVtest and CVopt are enabled simultaneously, MLatom constructs a **nested cross-validation** topology. The outer loop partitions data into test folds for accuracy estimation, while the inner loop partitions each outer training set into optimization folds for hyperparameter selection. This prevents information leakage from the test set into hyperparameter choices.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Full Dataset"
        D["N data points"]
    end
    D --> F1["Fold 1 (test)"]
    D --> F2["Fold 2 (test)"]
    D --> F3["Fold k (test)"]
    D --> Fk["Fold K (test)"]

    F2 --> T1["Fold 2 \nInner Fold 1 (val)"]
    F2 --> T2["Fold 2 \nInner Fold 2 (val)"]
    F2 --> T3["Fold 2 \nInner Fold M (val)"]
    F2 --> Tk["Fold 2 \nInner Fold M (val)"]

    style F1 fill:#e74c3c,stroke:#c0392b,color:#fff
    style F3 fill:#e74c3c,stroke:#c0392b,color:#fff
    style Fk fill:#e74c3c,stroke:#c0392b,color:#fff
    style T1 fill:#3498db,stroke:#2980b9,color:#fff
    style Tk fill:#3498db,stroke:#2980b9,color:#fff
```

Sources: [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L812-L830), [sampling.f90](mlatom/MLatomF_src/sampling.f90#L75-L100)

## The `MLtasks.sampling()` Bridge Function

The `sampling()` function in `MLtasks.py` is the critical bridge between the high-level task interface and the low-level sampling engines. Its signature exposes the full parameter space: dataset files (`XYZfile`, `XfileIn`), sampling mode (`sampling`), set sizes (`Ntrain`, `Nsubtrain`, `Nvalidate`, `Ntest`), index file paths for both input and output, and CV configuration flags (`CVtest`, `CVopt`, `NcvTestFolds`, `NcvOptFolds`). The function operates through the following sequence:

1. **Argument normalization**: Copies relevant keys from the parent `args` object (or constructs a fresh `mlatom_args` if called programmatically), then overlays any explicitly passed keyword arguments.
2. **Conditional Fortran delegation**: If the sampling mode is not `user-defined`, the function delegates to the Fortran backend via `interface_MLatomF.ifMLatomCls.run()`, writing indices to temporary files. After the Fortran call completes, it reads the generated index files back into NumPy arrays.
3. **CV fold loading**: When CVtest or CVopt is enabled, the function loads multi-fold index files by iterating over fold numbers and appending each fold's indices to a list of arrays. For the doubly-nested case (CVtest + CVopt), it constructs a nested list structure: `i_cvopt[j][i]` represents inner fold `i` within outer fold `j`.
4. **Index conversion**: All loaded indices are converted from Fortran's 1-based convention to Python's 0-based convention via `.astype(int) - 1`.

Sources: [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L751-L858)

## Active Learning Sampling Strategies

Within the active learning pipeline ([Active Learning Pipeline](24-active-learning-pipeline)), sampling strategies determine how candidate data points are generated for labeling. The `Sampler` class in `al_utils.py` provides multiple generation methods, each producing a molecular database of candidate geometries that are subsequently evaluated by a reference quantum chemistry method.

| Sampler Method | Description | Key Parameters |
|---|---|---|
| `fixed` | Uses pre-existing molecular geometries from a database | `molecular_database` |
| `random` | Generates random displacements from an equilibrium structure | `scale` (Å), `number_of_initial_conditions` |
| `wigner` | Wigner distribution sampling from harmonic frequencies | `initial_temperature`, `use_hessian` |
| `geometry_optimization` | Samples low-energy geometries via ML-predicted optimization | `uq_threshold`, `program` |
| `molecular_dynamics` | Samples configurations from MD trajectories | `maximum_propagation_time`, `time_step`, `ensemble` |
| `batch_molecular_dynamics` | Parallelized batch MD with round-robin trajectory allocation | Same as MD + `batch_parallelization` |
| `surface_hopping_molecular_dynamics` | Nonadiabatic dynamics sampling across electronic states | Inherited MD parameters |

Sources: [al_utils.py](mlatom/al_utils.py#L9-L519)

## Adaptive Initial Pool Sampling with Cross-Validation

The `al.py` module implements a sophisticated adaptive sampling loop for determining the minimum viable initial training set in active learning. The `get_initial_data_pool_cross_validation()` method iteratively adds batches of sampled points to the training pool, and after each batch, evaluates the model's expected accuracy using either cross-validation or hold-out validation. The loop terminates when one of two stopping criteria is met:

1. **Threshold-based**: If `init_RMSE_threshold` is set, the loop stops when the cross-validation RMSE drops below this value. This provides a hard quality guarantee.

2. **Learning curve extrapolation**: When no threshold is set, the method fits a power law of the form `e(N) = a · N^b` to the log-log relationship between training set size and RMSE. It then extrapolates to predict the RMSE at `N + init_ntrain_next` points. If the predicted relative improvement `(e(N) - e(N+ΔN)) / e(N)` falls below 10%, the loop terminates — the marginal return of additional data has become negligible. The linear regression is performed using `scipy.stats.linregress` on the log-transformed data, and a positive slope (which would indicate the RMSE is increasing with more data, a sign of overfitting or numerical noise) is explicitly handled by skipping that iteration.

Within each iteration, the method delegates to either `init_cross_validation()` (which calls `data.sample()` with `split_equally=True` to create equal-sized CV folds) or `init_validation()` (which uses `molecular_database.split()` with an 80/20 fraction). The cross-validation path trains a full model per fold, while the validation path trains a single model on the subtraining set. Both paths compute RMSE using `stats.rmse()`.

> [!TIP]
> The learning curve extrapolation in `get_initial_data_pool_cross_validation()` requires at least `minimum_number_of_fitting_points` data points before attempting regression. Positive regression slopes are silently skipped rather than treated as errors, since they often reflect transient noise in early sampling iterations when the model capacity is poorly matched to the data.

Sources: [al.py](mlatom/al.py#L462-L597)

## Learning Curve Generation

The `learningCurve()` task in `MLtasks.py` automates the systematic evaluation of model accuracy as a function of training set size. It accepts a comma-separated list of training set sizes (`lcNtrains`) and a corresponding list of repeat counts (`lcNrepeats`). For each training size, the function:

1. Creates a dedicated directory structure: `lcDir/Ntrain_{n}/repeat_{j}/{modeldirname}/`
2. Invokes `sampling()` to generate random train/subtrain/validate/test splits (or reuses existing index files if present)
3. Delegates to `CLItasks(args).run()` which executes the full `estAccMLmodel` pipeline
4. Aggregates results across repeats, computing mean and standard deviation of RMSE
5. Writes CSV files (`lcy.csv`, `lcygradxyz.csv`, `lctimetrain.csv`, `lctimepredict.csv`) with per-size statistics

A `.running` sentinel file prevents concurrent execution of the same repeat, and completed repeats are detected via the presence of `result.json`, enabling resumption of interrupted learning curve studies.

Sources: [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L216-L350)

## Model Training with Subtraining/Validation Splits

The `training()` function in `MLtasks.py` demonstrates how sampling indices flow into the model fitting pipeline. When hyperparameter optimization is enabled, the function passes `molecular_database[i_subtrain]` as the subtraining set, `molecular_database[i_validate]` as the validation set, and a list of `molecular_database[i_split]` for each CVopt fold. The molecular database class supports integer array indexing via its `__getitem__` method, which constructs a new database containing only the referenced entries. After hyperparameter optimization (if applicable), the model is trained on the full `molecular_database[i_train]` set — note this is the **outer** training set, not the subtraining set, ensuring the final model benefits from all available labeled data.

Sources: [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L886-L918), [data.py](mlatom/data.py#L163-L170)

## Error Metrics for Validation

Once cross-validation or test-set predictions are generated, MLatom's `stats.py` module provides the statistical primitives for quantifying accuracy:

| Metric | Function | Formula |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Mean Absolute Error | `mae()` | `Σ|y_est - y_ref| / N` |
| Mean Signed Error | `mse()` | `Σ(y_est - y_ref) / N` |
| Root-Mean-Square Error | `rmse()` | `√(Σ(y_est - y_ref)² / N)` |
| Pearson Correlation | `correlation_coefficient()` | Standard Pearson r |
| Largest Positive Outlier | `largest_positive_outlier()` | `max(y_est - y_ref)` |
| Largest Negative Outlier | `largest_negative_outlier()` | `min(y_est - y_ref)` |
| Linear Regression | `linear_regression()` | `y_est = a + b·x` with R² and standard errors |

The `analyzing()` function in `MLtasks.py` wraps these metrics, computing them for scalar values (energies) and gradient vectors separately, and returning a structured result dictionary with both per-split and aggregate statistics.

Sources: [stats.py](mlatom/stats.py#L9-L122), [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L919-L1046)

## Configuration Reference

The following table summarizes all sampling-related arguments accepted by the `mlatom_args` class, as used across the sampling pipeline:

| Argument | Type | Default | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `sampling` | str | `'random'` | Sampling mode: `random`, `user-defined`, `none` |
| `Nuse` | int/str | `'ALL'` | Total number of data points to use (or `'ALL'`) |
| `Ntrain` | int/float | `0.8 × Ntot` | Training set size (float < 1.0 = fraction) |
| `Nsubtrain` | int/float | — | Subtraining set size for hyperparameter optimization |
| `Nvalidate` | int/float | — | Validation set size |
| `Ntest` | int/float | `Ntot - Ntrain` | Test set size |
| `CVtest` | bool | `False` | Enable cross-validation for accuracy estimation |
| `CVopt` | bool | `False` | Enable cross-validation for hyperparameter optimization |
| `LOOtest` | bool | `False` | Leave-one-out test CV |
| `LOOopt` | bool | `False` | Leave-one-out optimization CV |
| `NcvTestFolds` | int | 5 | Number of CV test folds |
| `NcvOptFolds` | int | 5 | Number of CV optimization folds |
| `iTrainIn` / `iTrainOut` | str | — | Train index file (input/output) |
| `iSubtrainIn` / `iSubtrainOut` | str | — | Subtrain index file |
| `iValidateIn` / `iValidateOut` | str | — | Validate index file |
| `iTestIn` / `iTestOut` | str | — | Test index file |
| `iCVtestPrefIn` / `iCVtestPrefOut` | str | — | CV test fold index file prefix |
| `iCVoptPrefIn` / `iCVoptPrefOut` | str | — | CV opt fold index file prefix |
| `nslices` | int | 3 | Number of distance-based slices |
| `eqXfileIn` | str | — | Equilibrium descriptor file for slice sampling |

Sources: [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L751-L757), [sliceData.py](mlatom/sliceData.py#L216-L231)

## Practical Workflow Patterns

### Standard Train/Test Split with Hyperparameter Optimization

The most common workflow for model creation and evaluation combines a random train/test split with an internal subtrain/validate partition:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Full Dataset"] -->|"Ntrain=1000"| B["Training Set"]
    A -->|"Ntest=250"| C["Test Set"]
    B -->|"Nsubtrain=800"| D["Subtraining"]
    B -->|"Nvalidate=200"| E["Validation"]
    D -->|"Train"| F["ML Model"]
    E -->|"Select σ, λ"| F
    F -->|"Predict"| G["Test Accuracy"]
```

### Nested CV for Unbiased Hyperparameter Selection

For rigorous model comparison where hyperparameter choices must not contaminate the test estimate:

1. Enable `CVtest=True` with `NcvTestFolds=5`
2. Enable `CVopt=True` with `NcvOptFolds=4`
3. For each outer fold, the inner 4-fold CV selects optimal hyperparameters
4. The outer fold test predictions are aggregated for the final accuracy estimate

### Active Learning Initial Pool Determination

When configuring active learning, set `option='cross-validation'` in `get_initial_data_pool_cross_validation()` to automatically determine the minimum initial training set size. The method iteratively samples, labels, and evaluates until the learning curve flattens, at which point the active learning loop can begin with a well-conditioned model.

> [!TIP]
> When using nested cross-validation (CVtest + CVopt), the index file naming follows the pattern `{CVtestPref}{j}{CVoptPref}{i}.dat`. If you provide custom `iCVoptPrefOut` values, ensure they do not collide with the `iCVtestPrefOut` prefix to avoid file overwrites. The `MLtasks.sampling()` function handles this by checking for the compound file pattern `*icvtest1icvopt1.dat`.

Sources: [MLtasks.py](mlatom/MLtasks.py#L812-L830), [al.py](mlatom/al.py#L462-L543)
